Afghanistan.d:
Afghanistan's governments have long been run in part by people that foreign powers paid, trained or protected, and Pakistan's military intelligence service, the ISI, has reached furthest. Since the Taliban took Kabul in 2021, the interior ministry and Kabul's security have been run by the Haqqani network, a militant group inside the Taliban that the top US military officer once called an arm of the ISI. Pakistan denies interfering.

Before 2021 the reach came through cash and agents. For more than a decade the CIA delivered bags of money to President Hamid Karzai's office, tens of millions of dollars that went on to relatives, politicians and warlords, and Iran's government paid his chief of staff in the same way; Karzai confirmed both. In 2012 the Afghan intelligence service told parliament it had arrested 15 government employees, including senior officials and a general, for spying for the ISI or Iran. The drug trade reached in too: the official in charge of fighting it was accused of using his post to give smugglers safe passage.

For people living there, the police in the capital answer to a faction accused of serving a neighbouring spy service, and for twenty years the men around the president were kept loyal with foreign money rather than by voters. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Afghanistan 9 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and 1.5 for courts, police and watchdogs, so residents have almost nowhere to take a complaint.

Angola.d:
Angola's state runs mainly on oil, and the state oil company, Sonangol, which awards offshore contracts, is where foreign firms have reached in most often. Oil traders, builders of oil platforms, construction groups and a management consultancy have all paid Angolan officials through local agents and bank accounts abroad to win state business, and the reach goes beyond oil to public works, the Ministry of the Economy and the central bank. The clearest view comes from the Dutch platform builder SBM Offshore, which admitted that from 1997 to 2012 the 'commissions' it paid its Angolan agents were passed on to at least nine Sonangol officials. Most of what is known comes from admissions and court cases in Switzerland and the United States; the Angolan officials who took the money are mostly unnamed.

The same pattern ran through the rebuilding of the country after its civil war. China International Fund, a Hong Kong company, ran Chinese-financed reconstruction in partnership with generals close to the former president José Eduardo dos Santos, and in 2022 Angolan prosecutors indicted two of those generals and the company, alleging that money meant for public housing went to private ends and that about $1.5 billion in Chinese payments for Angolan oil never reached Angola. The generals went on trial in 2024.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Angola 8 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 4 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For Angolans, this means the oil revenue and foreign loans that should pay for housing, schools, hospitals and wages have repeatedly been split with foreign companies and well-placed officers, and most of the officials paid have never been named at home.

Australia.d:
In Australia outsiders reach in through four routes: crime groups buying police and border officers, developers and mining money reaching state and local politicians, foreign governments cultivating politicians, and industries placing their people where national policy is shaped.

The police route is the oldest. Public inquiries in Queensland in the late 1980s and New South Wales in the mid-1990s found that brothel, illegal casino and drug operators paid officers as a matter of routine. The buying has since moved to the border: drug importers in Sydney and Melbourne recruit 'trusted insiders' in Border Force, the state police and freight firms to keep their parcels and containers from being inspected, and in 2024 federal and state police formed a strike team just to find them.

In the states, money goes to whoever decides land and mineral rights. Anti-corruption commissions in New South Wales and Victoria have found councillors and an MP serving developers who paid them, and Labor MP Eddie Obeid and a state minister were jailed over a coal licence covering Obeid land. A Queensland minister was jailed for secretly taking money from businessmen.

Foreign governments work through people. A donor tied to China's United Front, the Chinese Communist Party's network for building influence abroad, paid a senator's bills, and the senator then backed China's line against his own party's policy. ASIO, the domestic security agency, says another country's spies recruited a former politician, and an army private is charged with obtaining defence information for Russia. Firms reach national policy too: a PwC partner advising the Treasury on tax-avoidance laws passed its plans to colleagues. For people here, the officer checking cargo may be paid by the trade they are meant to stop, and the planning decision next door may have been paid for.

Bahrain.d:
Bahrain is a small Gulf kingdom whose largest industry outside oil is aluminium, and the clearest record of outsiders reaching in runs through the state-controlled smelter, Aluminium Bahrain, known as Alba. To keep long-term contracts supplying Alba with alumina, the raw material for aluminium, the US company Alcoa placed a London-based middleman with close ties to senior members of the royal family between itself and the smelter. His offshore companies marked up prices by about $188 million between 2005 and 2009, and he used that margin to pay tens of millions of dollars in kickbacks to the Bahraini officials who controlled the tenders. Alcoa's subsidiary pleaded guilty to bribery in the United States in 2014.

The other record concerns the rivalry between Sunni-led Gulf states and Shia Iran, which Bahrain accuses of backing Shia militants; Tehran denies it. In 2017 a Bahraini military court said a cell funded by people based in Iran and Iraq had chosen a serving soldier to kill the armed forces' commander-in-chief, a killing that never took place. Rights groups objected to civilians being tried in military courts and alleged torture, so this rests on a contested verdict from the state's own side.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Bahrain 4.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 5.3 for its courts, police and watchdogs, both in the middle of the range. For Bahrainis, a state company that belongs to the public paid inflated prices for its raw material for years, and the difference went to the officials running its tenders and the middleman connected to the royal family. That case was brought abroad, and the officials who took the money have not been named at home.

Belgium.d:
Belgium is where outsiders reach into Europe and the Western alliance. Brussels hosts the main EU institutions and NATO's headquarters, and more cocaine reaches Europe through Antwerp than through any other port, so foreign governments, companies and drug networks all want people inside.

Spy services have sought people on NATO's staff for decades, from Soviet and East German agents in the Cold War to an intern at its military headquarters arrested in 2026 on suspicion of spying, reportedly for China. Hungarian intelligence officers posing as diplomats tried to recruit Hungarians at the European Commission, and Belgian intelligence reported that Morocco placed its own people in charge of Brussels' Great Mosque and inside Belgium's official Muslim body.

Money reaches the people who negotiate and vote. Belgian prosecutors say Qatar and Morocco paid cash to members of the European Parliament in a case known as Qatargate, and suspect people linked to a Chinese telecoms company of paying MEPs to oppose limits on foreign 5G equipment; most of those accused deny it. At home, a Senate vice-president joined the legal team of billionaires linked to Kazakhstan and visited the justice minister in 2011, the year a wider settlement law let one of them pay to close his case. An inquiry found he breached professional ethics; he denied wrongdoing.

In Antwerp, cocaine networks pay port workers, terminal staff, customs officers and police to pull containers out and pass on access codes, and an investigating judge wrote in 2025 that inquiries had also led to arrests of municipal clerks and justice staff. For people in Belgium and across the EU, rules on trade, technology and human rights may have been shaped by foreign payments, and the clerks, guards and officers handling their cases may work for the networks they are meant to stop.

Bolivia.d:
Bolivia is one of the world's main producers of coca, the plant cocaine is made from, and for more than forty years traffickers have bought the part of the state meant to stop them: the interior ministry, the anti-drug police and the offices that issue documents. The pattern took shape in the 1980 'Cocaine Coup', when the leading trafficker helped pay for a military takeover and his cousin became interior minister, in charge of the police. Twice since 2011 a former head of the anti-narcotics police, the FELCN, has been convicted in the United States of working for traffickers, by protecting cocaine loads or steering investigations away from allied gangs.

Foreign traffickers now use the same openings. The Uruguayan cocaine boss Sebastián Marset lived openly in Santa Cruz from 2022, bought a football club, travelled on a false Bolivian identity card issued by an employee of the national identification service, and left just ahead of a police operation in 2023. He later claimed in a video that the FELCN's director had warned him. The director denies it, the minister in charge said he could not rule out police help, and no finding has been made against any officer. Foreign intelligence has also reached this high before: an interior minister of the 1960s said the CIA had recruited him.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Bolivia 6.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and about 4.6 for its courts, police and watchdogs. For people living there, the police unit they would turn to about a trafficking gang has repeatedly been run by someone on a gang's payroll, and investigations have been pointed away from favoured traffickers. Both convictions of anti-drug chiefs came from US courts, not Bolivian ones.

Brunei.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Brunei, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case found so far shows a foreign intelligence service, company, crime group, church or lodge paying or placing people inside its government.

Brunei is a small, oil-rich sultanate on Borneo where the sultan holds executive power and there is no elected parliament, so there are few public channels through which outside influence would come to light. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Brunei 3 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests, low by world standards, and about 4.6 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs.

For people living there, this means there is no documented case of an official acting for an outside interest, and the low score suggests the risk is small. With few public channels and middling oversight, though, such a case would be hard to bring to light, and a documented case would change this estimate.

Cabo Verde.d:
Little is documented for Cabo Verde, so this is an estimate. No case found so far shows a foreign state, company, criminal group or lodge paying or placing people inside its government. The Global Organized Crime Index rates the country low for officials working for criminal interests and comparatively strong in its courts, police and watchdogs, which suggests fewer officials act for outside interests here than in most of West Africa. The islands sit on Atlantic shipping lanes between South America, West Africa and Europe, so the ports are the place most exposed to outside money.

The lack of cases may also reflect how little investigative reporting covers the islands. If outside money does reach officials, it would most likely show up in the ports, in shipping and in public contracts, and residents would pay for it through lost public revenue rather than through anything they could see directly. For now there is no named official, company or group for Cabo Verdeans to hold to account.

Central African Republic.d:
In the Central African Republic a foreign armed group works from inside the state. Wagner, the Russian private military company tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin, arrived in 2018 and placed its own people in the presidency: one of its men, Valery Zakharov, served as President Touadéra's national security adviser and was sanctioned by the United States for his Wagner ties. A US-sponsored research centre, the Africa Center for Strategic Studies, assesses that the old Wagner organisation has in effect taken over the state.

The arrangement has spread into the drug trade. Reporting from Bangui in 2026 describes Wagner's remnants supplying tramadol, an opioid painkiller, to members of the presidential guard and to a youth militia, with senior security officials alleged to control the market and payments flowing to Wagner and allied armed groups along the smuggling route. No one has been charged.

For people in the country, the president's security advice has come from a Wagner man answerable to Moscow rather than to Central African voters or courts, and some of the armed men around them are supplied with opioids by the same network. The Global Organized Crime Index rates the country among the very worst in the world for officials working for criminal interests, with almost no capacity in its courts, police or watchdogs to resist.

Colombia.d:
In Colombia the drug trade and its armed groups have reached every level of the state for over forty years. The cocaine cartels and the AUC, right-wing paramilitaries who were also major traffickers, got people elected, paid into presidential campaigns and bought officials meant to hunt them; in the 'parapolítica' scandal about 30 per cent of Congress was investigated, charged or convicted over collusion with the paramilitaries. At the national intelligence agency, the DAS, two directors and a deputy director have been convicted over killings or help tied to cartels or paramilitaries. Two former Supreme Court presidents and the national anti-corruption prosecutor were convicted of taking money to bury cases. Former commanders also describe, in claims mostly untested in court, controlling board votes and rectors at public universities.

The groups that took over the trade after the peace deals buy protection closer to the ground. The US Treasury says the Gulf Clan, the largest trafficking group, has funded mayoral candidates, and investigators accuse police units of taking its monthly pay. Prosecutors accuse army officers of being paid to move troops off cocaine routes and customs police of taking smugglers' money. Medellín's security chief admitted meeting crime bosses, and a prosecutor at the peace tribunal was convicted of taking money to delay a former FARC commander's extradition. Guerrillas have worked from the other side too, placing an agent inside the army's war college to prepare a car bomb.

Companies reach in through public contracts: US authorities said Brazil's Odebrecht and a Colombian investment company paid more than $23 million in bribes for one toll road. For Colombians, this has meant voting for mayors whose campaigns traffickers helped fund, reporting crimes to officers who may be on a group's payroll, and soldiers going into operations the other side already knew about.

Costa Rica.d:
Costa Rica lies on the route that carries Colombian cocaine north to the United States and across to Europe, and traffickers keep that route open by recruiting people inside the police and the security ministry to tell them what investigators know. The clearest case reaches near the top: the US Treasury found that a former vice-minister of public security, who later sat as a judge, helped move cocaine through the country and used his government contacts to learn about open drug investigations. He was arrested on a US extradition request in 2025 and has not been convicted.

The same method runs through the ranks of the national police. On the Caribbean side, trafficking groups have recruited local officers as lookouts to warn them of raids and checkpoints; in Guanacaste on the Pacific side, local officers have passed information to groups flying drugs out from clandestine airstrips. In 2026 the government said 116 officers of the public security ministry were under investigation after an internal intelligence report found some escorting criminals and coordinating secret drug flights.

Companies seeking public money have reached in too. Prosecutors say the two construction firms that received nearly two-thirds of the national roads agency's funds paid its staff in cash, liquor and vehicles to favour them, and 14 officials were among 30 people detained in 2021.

For people living along the cocaine routes, the officers they would call for help may be the ones telling traffickers when the police are coming, and the roads their taxes pay for may have gone to the firms that paid the agency's staff. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Costa Rica's officials as relatively unlikely to work for criminal interests, with institutions of middling strength.

Cyprus.d:
The deepest outside reach into the Cypriot state came from Greece, and its result is still the shape of the island. In the early 1970s Greece's military government had about 650 of its own officers serving in Cyprus's army, the National Guard, and it funded and controlled an armed group that wanted Cyprus joined to Greece. In July 1974, on the junta's orders, the National Guard attacked the presidential palace and overthrew President Makarios; Turkey invaded five days later and came to hold 37 per cent of the island, which remains divided.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Cyprus low to middling for officials working for criminal interests, but its courts, police and watchdogs score weak for an EU member. For Cypriots, this means a foreign government once used officers inside their own army to remove their elected president, and they still live with the partition that followed. No later case on the map shows an outside party inside the Cypriot state, but the bodies that would find one are weaker than in most of the EU.

Dominica.d:
The one documented case of outside money reaching Dominica's government involves a campaign donation. Al Jazeera reported that an Iranian businessman gave hundreds of thousands of dollars to Prime Minister Roosevelt Skerrit's election campaign and received an ambassador's post and a diplomatic passport in return; the businessman was later jailed in Iran for stealing oil revenue. Skerrit denies any trade, and no court has ruled on the claim.

If the report is right, a post that speaks for Dominica abroad went to a campaign donor, and a diplomatic passport, which carries legal protections overseas, went to a man later jailed for theft. Dominicans have no public record of what campaign donors receive.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Dominica low for officials working for criminal interests, with institutions of middling strength.

El Salvador.d:
In El Salvador the documented case of criminal groups reaching the state comes through local office and the drug trade. The country's two largest gangs, MS-13 and Barrio 18, grew out of Salvadoran communities in Los Angeles and now run neighbourhoods across the country, but the case on the map concerns trafficking along the northern border.

The news site El Faro reported in 2011 that a network moving drugs along that border, known as the Texis Cartel, was led by a sitting mayor, with police, soldiers, judges and prosecutors paid to let shipments through. A court acquitted all nine defendants in 2021, so the account remains a press finding rather than a proven one.

If the reporting is right, a town hall was used to move drugs, and the officers and courts that should have stopped the shipments were paid to let them pass. Salvadorans have had no court finding at home to settle it. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 7.5 out of 10 and the strength of courts and watchdogs at 3.25.

Eswatini.d:
This is an estimate: no case on the map shows a foreign state, company, criminal group or religious body placing or paying people inside Eswatini's government. Eswatini is a small kingdom between South Africa and Mozambique where the king holds executive power and political parties cannot compete for government, so there are few independent sources inside the country that report on officials.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 6.5 out of 10, in its high band, and the courts, police and watchdogs that would resist them at about 3.2. A country with that profile, on the trade routes between South Africa and Mozambique, is one where traffickers and businesses seeking contracts would find officials open to payment and little chance of a case reaching court.

If that is happening, people in Eswatini would pay for it through public contracts that cost more than they should and policing that does not reach those who pay. With no named case, there is no official, company or group they can point to or hold to account.

France.d:
In France outside interests reach government through the people who run it, through political money and through paid insiders lower down the state. Leaked documents, the Uber Files, show Emmanuel Macron, as economy minister in 2015, working behind the scenes for Uber, and a police ban on one of its services was lifted two days after his office was contacted. Political money has come through the state oil company's secret funds, which a former chairman admitted went to parties, and possibly from abroad. In 2025 Nicolas Sarkozy was sentenced to prison for conspiring to seek Libyan money for his 2007 campaign, though the court acquitted him of corruption and illegal campaign financing, saying nothing proved the money arrived; he is appealing.

Foreign spy services recruit insiders. Two officers of the foreign intelligence agency were jailed in 2020 for passing information to China. Investigators accuse an Orly airport border police captain of selling files to Morocco's secret service, and a finance ministry employee of passing data on asylum seekers and opponents to Algeria's consulate; neither case has a verdict. Cocaine networks pay or threaten dockers at Le Havre and, the gendarmerie says, staff at a company working at Roissy airport.

International bodies are targets too. A 2018 inquiry reported strong suspicions that Azerbaijan's money had corrupted members of the Council of Europe's parliamentary assembly, though the accounts of cash envelopes come from witnesses, not a court.

For people in France, rules on taxi services may have been shaped by a firm before ministers presented them, an Algerian who fled to France cannot be sure their file stays inside the French state, and some cargo handlers work for drug networks. The Global Organized Crime Index rates officials acting for criminal interests low and the courts strong.

Germany.d:
Germany has been a main target for foreign intelligence services since the Cold War, and they place or recruit people inside its institutions. East Germany's Stasi had a personal aide to Chancellor Willy Brandt, whose exposure in 1974 brought Brandt down, and agents in parliament and in the foreign intelligence service, the BND. Since Russia's full invasion of Ukraine, Russia and China have been tied to recruits in the BND, the army's procurement office, parliamentary offices and a cargo hub for military flights, some convicted and others only accused. Turkey's intelligence service is suspected of getting police files and exiles' addresses through officers in Cologne and Berlin. Several conservative MPs have resigned or been investigated over payments from Azerbaijan.

The far right has its own people inside the state. Prosecutors allege a serving judge helped lead a coup plot by Reichsbürger, people who reject the modern German state, and an inquiry found eight of the 12 members of one police commando unit linked to Nordkreuz, a network preparing for social collapse, whose members held police ammunition and data from a police computer.

The energy minister appointed in 2025 came straight from running E.ON's largest subsidiary, Germany's risk agency copied glyphosate makers' text into the safety review the EU used to renew the weedkiller, and at Hamburg and Bremerhaven cocaine importers recruit customs officers and terminal staff.

For people in Germany, critics of Moscow, Beijing and Ankara live alongside people those governments are accused of recruiting in parliament, the army and the police, and decisions on energy and farm chemicals have rested partly on people and text from the firms affected. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 2 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs above 7, so many of these cases reach court.

Guatemala.d:
Guatemala's state has been reached from outside for seventy years, first by a foreign spy service and now by traffickers and companies seeking laws and contracts. In 1954 the CIA paid an exiled officer to lead the overthrow of the elected president, whose land reform had taken land from the US-based United Fruit Company, and it kept paid sources in the army in later decades.

The country lies on the land route for South American cocaine going north, and the groups using it buy officials at every level. Since 2005 the people charged or convicted for working with traffickers have included the head of the anti-narcotics police, a town mayor who used his office's letterhead to get cocaine past inspection and a member of Congress. A vice-president and an interior minister were indicted in the United States; she denies it and the drug charge has never been tried. Guards have been arrested on suspicion of helping 20 gang leaders walk out of a high-security jail.

Companies pay their way in at the top. TIGO, a mobile phone company, paid monthly cash bribes to members of Congress from 2012 to 2018 and they backed laws that helped it; it settled with US prosecutors in 2025 and no official has been named. Prosecutors say a minister managed a Brazilian builder's bribes for a highway contract and kept about $9 million; he has been ordered to stand trial.

For Guatemalans this means the police officer, mayor or legislator they would turn to may be working for traffickers, laws on their phone service have been voted through for pay, and the roads their taxes buy may have been awarded for a bribe. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 8 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at 4.

Haiti.d:
Armed gangs control much of Haiti's capital, Port-au-Prince, and large areas of the Artibonite valley, and the line between gangs and state has worn thin from both sides. Canada and the United States have sanctioned a former president, sitting and former senators and other political figures for financing gangs, and a UN panel of experts says former legislators have armed groups and used them to drive violence before elections. Washington has also alleged, without details, that members of the transitional council running the country supported gangs. Several deny it.

The state's own guns reach the gangs too. UN experts report police officers arrested carrying thousands of rounds meant for gangs, close to 1,000 firearms diverted from police stocks in four years, and a former palace security chief accused of arming groups. Cocaine traffickers have paid for protection at the top of the police; former commander Guy Philippe admitted taking millions, and the US Treasury says Michel Martelly worked with traffickers as president, which he denies.

Business reaches in through the ports and state companies. The UN panel says importers bribe customs officers to release their containers or block a rival's, and that one businessman influences who is posted to major ports. A Miami telephone firm's president was convicted in the US of bribing directors of the state phone company. Outside control is old here: a New York bank came to own Haiti's national bank and, under US occupation from 1915, its finances stayed under US control until 1947.

For people in Haiti, the gangs that kill and kidnap them are, on this evidence, paid for by some of the politicians seeking their votes and supplied by some of the police meant to protect them. Courts and watchdogs score 2.2 out of 10 on the Global Organized Crime Index.

India.d:
India's governing party is closely tied to one organisation. The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) is a Hindu nationalist volunteer body; it lends full-time organisers to the governing Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) and places one of its own in the party's top organisational post. A 2020 press count found about seven in ten BJP ministers had RSS roots, and RSS-family groups have had their own people put in charge of public bodies, from the national history research council to the prosecution of riot cases in which their members were accused.

Money and crime reach the state from other sides. Firms seeking contracts or approvals are repeatedly accused of paying officials: US prosecutors allege the Adani Group paid more than $250 million to win solar contracts, which it denies, and federal investigators allege private medical colleges bought inspection dates and favourable reports from health ministry staff. Crime groups buy insiders where it pays, from police who tipped off a gangster, according to a state inquiry, to test-centre officials through whom a gang allegedly got into the 2024 national medical exam.

Pakistan's military intelligence service, the ISI, is accused of recruiting at every level of India's defence establishment, from a diplomat and a missile engineer, both convicted, to a laboratory director and, in recent arrests still untested in court, ordnance factory managers, an aircraft plant supervisor and shipyard workers. In Kashmir a senior police officer is charged with moving militants, and about 80 state employees have been dismissed as collaborators under a rule requiring no inquiry.

For people in India this means most BJP ministers come from an organisation that publishes no membership list, large public contracts may have been won by paying those who award them, and medical colleges and exams may have been passed by paying the people guarding them.

Ireland.d:
For much of the twentieth century, the outsiders inside Irish government were organised bodies of men from Ireland itself, working in private. The Irish Republican Brotherhood, an oath-bound society, re-formed as a faction holding posts inside the new national army, and the fight over those posts led to a 1924 mutiny. Later a member of the Knights of Saint Columbanus, a secretive Catholic men's order, ran the justice ministry and reportedly gave its council private undertakings. In 1951 the cabinet dropped the Mother and Child Scheme, a plan for free health care for mothers and children, after the Catholic bishops privately objected.

Armed republicans also got help from inside the police. A judicial tribunal reported in 2013 that someone in Dundalk Garda station was helping the IRA when two Northern Ireland police officers were killed in 1989, without tying a named officer to the murders. It also found that a sergeant helped the IRA obtain false passports, which he denies.

In recent decades the documented reach has come through money and, possibly, foreign intelligence. An official tribunal found in 2011 that a businessman had made payments to the minister who 'delivered' him the second mobile phone licence, findings he rejects. A newspaper reported in 2024 that Russian intelligence had recruited a serving member of parliament during the Brexit talks; the person was not named and nothing has been proven.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Ireland 4 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and above 7 for its courts and watchdogs. For people in Ireland, that history meant decisions on their families' health care were made in private letters between bishops and ministers, and the police they relied on included people helping an armed group. Voters today cannot tell whether the reported Russian recruit exists.

Japan.d:
In Japan, outside interests reach the governing Liberal Democratic Party (LDP) by supplying what a party in power needs: money, organised votes and campaign workers. The pattern goes back to the 1950s and 1960s, when the CIA secretly funded the party and recruited informers inside it. Since then companies have repeatedly paid those at the top, most clearly the US aircraft maker Lockheed, which paid about ¥500 million to Prime Minister Kakuei Tanaka's office to sell jets to a Japanese airline.

Religious movements and lobbies supply votes and volunteers: Komeito, the party of the Buddhist lay movement Soka Gakkai, governed alongside the LDP for most of 1999 to 2025. Nippon Kaigi, a lobby that wants to rewrite the post-war constitution, and the political arm of the Shinto shrines each run a league of MPs that has counted most cabinet ministers under recent prime ministers.

Foreign spy services and crime groups work lower down, recruiting staff inside companies, the police and the armed forces. Russian intelligence officers posted to their country's trade mission have paid employees of a mobile network and a machine-tool maker for files and trade secrets, and a retired army commander is suspected of obtaining a restricted manual for a Russian attaché. In 2026 a detective in Tokyo's organised-crime division was convicted of sending a 'scout' gang, which recruits women for sex parlours, the locations of police cameras set up to watch it.

For people in Japan, this means those they elect may owe their campaigns to a company with a contract at stake, ministers belong to lobbies whose membership the government does not disclose, an inquiry into a gang can be leaked to it from inside the police, and, as an inquiry found after Fukushima, a regulator can end up serving the power companies it polices.

Kiribati.d:
No case on this map documents a foreign state, criminal group or company paying or placing officials inside Kiribati's government, so this account rests on general conditions.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Kiribati low, 1.5 out of 10, for officials working for criminal interests, but below 5 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. A weak oversight score means there are few institutions in a position to notice outside influence if it came.

For people in Kiribati this means the risk that officials are serving criminal interests appears low, but the means of checking are thin. If outside influence did reach their government, it would most likely show in fishing licences, aid-funded contracts or policing, and with limited courts and press it could go unexamined.

Kuwait.d:
Outside interests reach into Kuwait's government by three routes on the record: an Islamist movement working openly in politics, foreign businesses paying the officials who control visas and arms purchases, and Iran recruiting inside the army.

The Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt that aims to bring its members into power, has a Kuwaiti branch that broke with the international organisation after Iraq invaded in 1990. Its party, the Islamic Constitutional Movement, regularly won seats in parliament through the 1990s and 2000s and at times sent members into the cabinet.

Foreign suppliers have paid officials directly. A Bangladeshi member of parliament whose companies supplied cleaners for government contracts was convicted in 2021, alongside a senior Interior Ministry general, of paying ministry officials to issue visas for more than 20,000 workers, some on fake papers. A parliamentary inquiry in 2024 found that a European helicopter maker paid commissions on a defence contract and named eight senior officials, though parliament was dissolved before any prosecution. In 2011 a Kuwaiti court convicted soldiers serving in the army of passing military information to Iran's Revolutionary Guards.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Kuwait 6 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and just over 5 for its courts and watchdogs. For Kuwaitis this means the officials who decide who may live and work in the country, and those who spend the defence budget, have been paid by foreign suppliers, while migrant workers brought in on bought visas carry the cost. The inquiry into the helicopter deal put the public money wasted at €349 million.

Lebanon.d:
In Lebanon, foreign states have reached into the government for much of the past seventy years, first by choosing who sits in it and later by recruiting in its security forces, phone companies and parties. In the 1957 election a CIA officer later wrote that he carried cash for the president's chosen candidates, and those candidates' side won 51 of the 66 seats. From 1982 Syria's military intelligence chief in Lebanon picked electoral candidates, drew electoral districts and shaped security and judicial appointments, and the head of Lebanon's General Security agency reported to him. This lasted until 2005.

Since 2009 Lebanese prosecutors have arrested more than 100 people accused of working for Israeli intelligence, among them members of the security forces and telecoms staff, and at least five of those convicted were sentenced to death. Military courts have jailed a man inside the state-owned mobile firm and a retired general close to the leader of a large Christian party allied with Hezbollah, though the general was not found guilty of spying and one accused colonel said his confession was untrue.

The US Treasury alleges a further channel from inside the country: that Hezbollah, the Iran-backed armed movement and party, paid or used a former transport minister and a former finance minister to steer contracts and money. These are US accusations, not court findings.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Lebanon 9.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 3 for its courts and watchdogs, close to the worst in the world. For people in Lebanon this means that for long stretches the members they elected, and the officials running their security services and courts, were chosen by a foreign government, and officials say many suspects in the spy hunt identified targets bombed in 2006.

Liechtenstein.d:
Liechtenstein is a small principality between Switzerland and Austria whose banks and trust companies hold money for foreign clients. No documented case yet meets the map's test there: none shows a foreign government, crime group or company getting its people or money inside Liechtenstein's government or courts and steering what they decided.

The Global Organized Crime Index places Liechtenstein among the countries where officials are least likely to work for criminal or outside interests, and rates its courts, police and watchdogs as strong.

For people who live in Liechtenstein, this means the officials they deal with are rated as rarely acting for someone else. If the risk grows, it is most likely to sit in the banks and trustees that manage foreign money and in the officials who supervise them.

Malawi.d:
In Malawi, the documented reach comes through what the state buys, above all for its security forces, where businessmen are alleged to have paid for contracts. Malawi's anti-corruption bureau reported in 2022 that companies linked to Zuneth Sattar, a UK-based businessman, won contracts worth more than 150 million dollars from the police and army over four years, and that he paid officials to secure them. The report named dozens of people, and arrests reached a former police chief, a cabinet minister and the vice president, who denied wrongdoing and died in a plane crash in 2024.

An earlier police contract shows the same route leading to party money. A leaked bureau report alleged that a company supplying police ration packs paid MK145 million into a ruling party account on which the then president was the sole signatory. He called it an honest donation, the party refunded it, and the businessman and a police finance director pleaded not guilty, with no verdict found. A third case did not hold up in court: an inquiry found a minister had acted suspiciously in favour of a private maize trader during a food shortage, but he was acquitted on the charges he faced.

The mechanism is common where the state is a large buyer and details are kept from public scrutiny on security grounds. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Malawi's institutions as weak and finds a moderate level of officials serving outside interests.

For Malawians this means that tax money for police food and equipment may have gone to contractors who bought their way in. These are findings, arrests and allegations rather than convictions, so people still do not know who in their government took part or what the public received for the money.

Malta.d:
In Malta, outside interests have reached the state in two ways: through private companies that win large state contracts with help from the people closest to the prime minister, and through the licences Malta grants to firms that then operate across the European Union.

The clearest example of the first is the gas power station built under a state contract. One of the builder's directors secretly owned a company in Dubai that leaked papers listed as expected to pay into secret Panama companies set up for the energy minister and the prime minister's chief of staff; the journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia was investigating that company when a car bomb killed her in 2017, and the director now faces trial over her murder while all three men face corruption charges. A public inquiry found that the Maltese state had created an 'atmosphere of impunity'.

The second channel runs through Malta's online gambling industry. Because a Maltese licence lets a betting firm operate across the EU, Italian mafia groups, including the 'Ndrangheta from Calabria and Cosa Nostra from Sicily, have secretly owned or run Malta-licensed betting companies to collect bets and launder money, according to Italian investigations over the past decade. Malta's regulator suspended licences once the investigations surfaced.

For people in Malta this means they pay for electricity from a plant whose contract prosecutors say was tied to payments meant for the two men around the prime minister, and the reporter who tried to expose it was killed. It also means their country's licences have served as cover for mafias, and the Global Organized Crime Index finds officials there often serving criminal or outside interests.

Mexico.d:
In Mexico, drug cartels have put officials on their payroll at every level of government for more than forty years. Where a cartel controls a route or a town, it pays the local police, the prosecutors who decide which cases go forward and in several states the governor. Those hired to fight the cartels have been bought most often: the national anti-drug chief, generals, agents in the federal organised-crime unit, prison directors and a federal security minister.

The town hall is where the buying is most common today. Whole municipal police forces have been disbanded because they worked for cartels, and a federal operation begun in 2024 had detained more than 85 officials, including at least 19 mayors, across nine states by mid-2026. Some town halls are accused of working for a cartel's business: in 2026 the mayor of Tequila, in Jalisco, was arrested with his security director, accused of running an extortion ring tied to the Jalisco New Generation Cartel that squeezed drinks makers with inflated taxes and withheld permits.

The reach extends to the ports and the money system. Fuel importers are accused of paying navy officers and customs staff to let tankers of diesel declared as additives dock uninspected and untaxed. The US Treasury said in 2025 that staff at two Mexican banks had helped cartels launder money, which Mexico's finance ministry and the banks dispute. Foreign companies have also paid officials at Pemex, the state oil company, and at other state bodies.

For Mexicans this means the police officer, mayor or governor they depend on may be working for the people they should be stopping, a firm may be taxed by its town hall on a cartel's behalf, and fuel that should be taxed to pay for public services is waved through at the docks.

Mongolia.d:
The documented reach into Mongolia's government runs through mining. Three cases show foreign investors and go-betweens getting money or favours to ministers and senior officials who could decide who mines what. They cover copper, gold and uranium, and they are at different stages of proof.

The largest fight is over Oyu Tolgoi, a copper and gold mine. Swiss prosecutors allege that a businessman paid millions of euros into the account of the finance minister who signed the 2009 agreement for it, and a Mongolian court reportedly convicted him in 2020 of taking kickbacks; he denied all charges. Filings by Mongolian state bodies accused former prime minister Sukhbaatar Batbold of taking kickbacks over the same mine and of steering a state mine's copper to shell companies. His adviser denies it, and the US Justice Department has sued to seize New York flats it alleges were bought with the proceeds. Separately, the French nuclear group Areva paid a chain of consultants while setting up its uranium business, and money reached two senior officials who had helped it; it agreed a €4.8 million fine in France in 2024 under a settlement that involves no conviction.

These cases show money reaching people at the top over minerals. They do not show a foreign government, crime group or religious body placing people inside the state. The Global Organized Crime Index finds a moderate level of officials serving criminal or outside interests and rates courts, police and watchdogs in the middle range. For people in Mongolia, the terms on which their country's minerals were let out may have been shaped by payments to those who negotiated them, and much of what is known has come out through foreign prosecutors and courts.

Myanmar.d:
In Myanmar the army has drawn armed crime groups into the state itself, trading protection and business for their loyalty. Along the borders with China and Thailand, militias the army has formally placed under its command, and armed groups allied with it, control the parts of Shan and Karen states that produce much of Asia's methamphetamine and host compounds where trafficked workers are forced to defraud strangers online. Their leaders hold military rank and state honours while partnering with Chinese-run crime groups and letting them build on the land their forces hold; the commander of the Karen Border Guard Force helped build the scam city of Shwe Kokko and received a top state honour, and the UK and US have since sanctioned him.

A Buddhist nationalist monks' group, Ma Ba Tha, reached into lawmaking. The religious affairs ministry drafted four 'race and religion' laws from texts its members proposed, and parliament passed them in 2015. They restrict religious conversion and marriage between Buddhist women and non-Buddhist men.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds Myanmar's officials serving criminal interests to one of the highest degrees in the world, with almost no court or police capacity to check them. For people in Shan and Karen states this means living beside drug labs and guarded compounds run by forces the army counts as its own. Muslim residents and Buddhist women live under marriage and conversion rules drawn from a monks' movement's drafts.

Netherlands.d:
In the Netherlands, outsiders reach in at three points: cocaine gangs work through the people who move goods and handle information, foreign states have sought people inside the International Criminal Court in The Hague and the country's nuclear technology, and a foreign company once paid an insider to sway a government purchase.

At Rotterdam, Europe's largest port, they have paid terminal workers and IT contractors for the PIN codes that release containers, private security guards to keep searches away, and a customs officer whose job was choosing which containers get scanned. At Schiphol airport they recruit staff whose passes let them move freight past controls. They also buy information from inside the state: police officers and trainees have searched police systems for gangs at a set price per name, and court staff with access to personal records have sold them to suspects. Courts have convicted such insiders many times, and gangs that rely on them have killed people connected to trials against them.

The Hague hosts the International Criminal Court, which tries war crimes, and Russia has tried to get inside it. In 2022 a Russian military intelligence officer with a false Brazilian identity flew in to take up a post there while it was investigating war crimes in Ukraine; Dutch intelligence turned him back. In 1975 a Pakistani metallurgist working inside the Dutch side of a uranium-enrichment consortium took its centrifuge designs home, and they later reached Iran, Libya and North Korea. In 1976 a US aircraft maker was found to have paid the prince consort, a senior military figure, to help it win a Dutch fighter-jet order.

For people in the Netherlands this means their personal details can be sold from a police terminal or a court desk, and violence follows the gangs that have bought insiders.

Nigeria.d:
In Nigeria the people reaching into government are mostly after oil and gas. Foreign oil companies, engineering firms and commodity traders have paid officials, often through local agents, for licences, cargoes, construction contracts and favourable legal outcomes, as many have admitted abroad; one engineering consortium admitted paying about $180 million to officials, from the top of government down to the state oil company, to build a gas plant. The customs service is another steady target. US regulators found that drilling and freight firms paid through brokers for false papers on rigs that never moved. A US diplomatic cable records a Shell executive saying in 2009 that the company had seconded its own staff to every ministry dealing with oil, which Shell denies. Two of the biggest cases ended in acquittal: a Milan court cleared oil companies over a $1.1 billion oil block payment, and a London jury cleared a former petroleum minister.

Pressure also comes from inside the country. Confraternities, secretive brotherhoods that began at universities, are reported to be hired by politicians for election work and rewarded with government posts, which the group named by a BBC investigation denies. In the north-east, a president said in 2012 that Boko Haram, the jihadist group, had sympathisers in the army, police and government, an army commander said in 2016 that soldiers had been selling it arms, and in 2025 soldiers and police were arrested on suspicion of the same. Press claims that generals were convicted of helping it were denied by defence chiefs.

Money lost to a bribed contract or customs fine does not reach schools, clinics or roads, and soldiers and villagers may face guns sold by their own side. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Nigeria high for officials working for criminal interests, with middling courts and watchdogs.

Pakistan.d:
In Pakistan, outsiders reach in through business owners close to government, religious and militant movements and foreign spy services. An official inquiry found in 2020 that sugar-mill owners in or allied to the ruling party took a large share of its export subsidies while sugar prices at home rose about 30 per cent. In 2025 a court convicted former Prime Minister Imran Khan and his wife of taking land for their charitable trust from the property developer Malik Riaz Hussain while their government let £190 million that Britain had sent to Pakistan pay the developer's own court fines; Hussain and Khan's party reject it.

Religious movements, militants and foreign states have reached into the courts and armed forces. Under General Zia, by one journalist's account, members of Jamaat-e-Islami, the main Islamist movement, got many judicial jobs and kept his Islamisation agenda going. Militant and Islamist groups have recruited serving officers, up to major-general, for plans to seize power from inside the army, and a closed tribunal sentenced five navy officers to death for helping militants try to seize a frigate in 2014. Officers up to lieutenant-general have been jailed for passing secrets to foreign spy agencies.

The ISI, the military's spy agency, reaches into elected politics. Pakistan's Supreme Court found in 2012 that army and ISI chiefs had broken the constitution over money passed to politicians in the 1990 election to stop Benazir Bhutto winning, and in 1989 ISI officers tried to win over members of her own party so they would vote her out.

For Pakistanis this means subsidies and money returned from abroad have gone to business owners close to the government, the forces protecting them have held officers working for movements or foreign services, and spy agency money went to politicians in the 1990 vote.

Paraguay.d:
Paraguay's record shows criminal and foreign-linked money reaching the top of government, Congress, the prisons and the courts. The Global Organized Crime Index gives it one of the highest scores in the world for officials working for criminal interests.

At the top, the reach runs through the Tri-Border Area around Ciudad del Este, where free-zone trade lets goods and money move with little checking and where Hezbollah, the Lebanese armed movement and party, has long had finance networks. The US Treasury sanctioned a former president and a sitting vice-president in 2023, saying their representatives collected bribes at private Hezbollah events in Paraguay; the sanctions on the former president were lifted in 2025 without any court ruling either way.

Below that, cocaine networks moving drugs along the Hidrovía river route and across the Brazilian border are accused of keeping legislators, prosecutors, police and court staff on their side. Prosecutors have charged sitting members of the Chamber of Deputies, mostly from the governing Colorado Party, with getting traffickers released, taking their money for campaigns or laundering it. Officials said staff at a border jail helped at least 75 inmates, many from Brazil's largest prison gang, the PCC, walk free, and a former minister and a guard say a Paraguayan crime group bribed and threatened staff at the main prison until it decided shift changes. Prosecutors also allege that officers at the military agency that registers weapons helped supply Brazilian gangs, but four officers sentenced in Brazil were reportedly acquitted on appeal.

For people in Paraguay this means the police who should investigate traffickers, the prosecutors who should charge them, the courts that should try them, the guards who should hold them and the deputies who write the laws have all been accused of having members on the traffickers' side.

Portugal.d:
In Portugal outside interests have reached government mainly through money and the people around the prime minister, while drug networks have reached the ports and foreign states have reached individual justice and intelligence officials.

Banco Espírito Santo had been close to power since the Salazar dictatorship and collapsed in 2014. Prosecutors say money from the group reached a former prime minister, José Sócrates; the trial began in 2025 and all defendants are presumed innocent. In 2023 police investigating a €3.5 billion data-centre project found that its developer had hired a friend of Prime Minister António Costa, and found €75,800 in envelopes in the office of Costa's chief of staff. Costa, not a suspect, resigned and the government fell; a judge later found evidence of influence peddling but dismissed other corruption charges, and all deny wrongdoing.

Foreign money has reached officers of the state directly. Lisbon courts convicted a prosecutor of taking money linked to Angola's then vice-president to shelve an inquiry into him, and an officer of the Security Intelligence Service of selling state secrets to Russia's foreign intelligence service, charges the prosecutor denied. Portugal is also an entry point for cocaine from Latin America, and police say Brazil's largest crime group, the PCC, and Colombian cartels paid customs officials and port staff at Lisbon, Setúbal and Sines to let several tonnes in.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Portugal in the middle range for officials working for criminal interests and fairly well for its courts and watchdogs. For Portuguese people, money from a bank close to power is alleged to have reached a prime minister, a large investor could reach the prime minister's office through his friends, and officials meant to investigate foreign money or stop drugs have been convicted of, or accused of, being paid.

Rwanda.d:
No documented case yet meets the map's test for Rwanda: none shows a foreign government, crime group, company or movement getting its people or money inside a Rwandan public body and steering what it decided.

The Global Organized Crime Index gives the best available estimate. It scores Rwanda in the middle range both for officials working for criminal or outside interests and for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. That places Rwanda neither among the countries where officials are most often bought nor among those where they are least likely to be.

For Rwandans this means the risk that an official is acting for someone else is rated as moderate, and the courts and watchdogs meant to catch such cases are rated as neither strong nor weak.

Saudi Arabia.d:
In Saudi Arabia most of the documented reach runs two ways: foreign suppliers paying the Saudi officials who buy from them, and Saudi intelligence money going out into foreign banks. The suppliers span defence, aviation, telecoms and health, and the money usually goes through consultants or false agency deals.

The clearest case is the communications contract for the Saudi Arabian National Guard, the force that protects the royal family: a British company then owned by Airbus held it from 1994, and British prosecutors said about 12 per cent of its revenue went to Saudi officials, including the Guard's then deputy head, to keep contracts worth at least £1.6 billion. The company pleaded guilty, though two executives were acquitted in 2024 after arguing the British government required the payments. US cases record a Brazilian aircraft maker paying a state company official, a Swedish telecoms maker paying people who could sway a state enterprise, and a German dialysis company paying state doctors and the officials approving its products.

Outward, Kamal Adham, head of Saudi intelligence until 1979, fronted the secret takeover of a Washington bank by BCCI, a bank later closed worldwide for fraud, and paid a $105 million fine in the United States. A Saudi court found in 2016 that Iran ran a spy cell which Saudi media said included former ministry staff; Iran denied it, and Amnesty International called the trial farcical.

The Global Organized Crime Index gives Saudi Arabia one of the highest scores in the world for officials working for criminal interests. For Saudis, this means a share of public money for defence, telecoms and health has gone to the officials choosing the suppliers, the bribery cases have been brought only abroad, and residents have no domestic route to check how state money is spent.

Sierra Leone.d:
Sierra Leone sits on the route that carries South American cocaine to Europe through West Africa, and traffickers using it look for protection inside the state rather than ways around it. They need the people who control an airport or a landing clearance, and the record here shows them reaching both, from ground staff up to the cabinet.

In 2008 a plane carrying about 700 kilograms of cocaine and painted with Red Cross markings landed at Lungi, the international airport, with help from airport and security staff who were later convicted; proceedings indicated that the aviation minister had cleared the landing, and he was dismissed but never tried.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 8 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 4. For people in Sierra Leone that means the convictions have reached baggage handlers and guards while the minister who cleared the landing was dismissed and never tried, so staff who might be approached by traffickers see the risk falling on those at the bottom rather than on those who gave the orders.

Solomon Islands.d:
In the Solomon Islands the record points to foreign governments and resource companies competing for the loyalty of politicians, with money said to go to them directly. Most of it rests on reported accounts rather than findings. When the country switched recognition from Taiwan to China in 2019, MPs told reporters that both Beijing and Taipei had offered them hundreds of thousands of dollars for their votes. The offers came on top of an older arrangement: Taiwan used to pay into a discretionary fund run by the prime minister's office, from which payments go to MPs, and China took over that fund after the switch.

Logging and mining firms appear in the same way. An unnamed industry source alleged in 2008 that Malaysian logging companies paid government MPs to join a new party in order to reach the finance and forests ministries, and a former acting minister has said, in a secondhand account, that two colleagues asked him to approve a Chinese prospecting company for cash before an election. Neither claim was verified. The one court result here is smaller: a logging businessman was convicted in 2004 of offering a bribe to customs officers at a port, and the outcome of his appeal could not be found.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 7.5 out of 10. For voters this means they cannot tell whether their MP's vote on recognition, or a decision about the forests in their province, was made for them or for whoever was offering the money.

Spain.d:
In Spain, outsiders reach the state mainly through payments for contracts and laws, and along the drug routes on its southern coast. Money from businesses seeking public contracts, permits or favourable laws is the most widespread channel, and it has reached the leadership of both main parties. The courts found that the People's Party itself took part in a contractor's kickback scheme from 1989. In the governing Socialist Party, two successive organisation secretaries, the party's third-ranking post, are accused of taking money from companies seeking public business: José Luis Ábalos, also transport minister, was sentenced in 2026 to 24 years, and the Supreme Court is investigating whether the builder Acciona paid kickbacks through his successor while winning works worth more than €537 million, which he denies. Payments from industrial-gas firms to a former finance minister's consultancy are also alleged to have bought changes to tax law.

Along the Strait of Gibraltar, hashish and cocaine groups pay police, customs officers, dockworkers and airport staff around Algeciras to wave loads through, and the reach goes to Madrid: in 2024 the head of the capital's police unit for money laundering was arrested with €20 million in cash in his home, accused of shielding a cocaine network.

Organised groups have also worked from inside institutions. Before the 1936 coup a clandestine pro-fascist society enrolled almost half of Spain's serving officers, and courts found that ETA, the armed separatist group, used the party Batasuna to hold elected seats and passed the public money paid to them on to its own funds.

For people in Spain, public works, tax rules and permits have been decided by who paid the party in charge, and around Algeciras the police and port staff may be on a trafficker's payroll.

St. Vincent and the Grenadines.d:
Nothing is documented here, so this is an estimate. No case has been found of foreign governments, companies or criminal groups paying or placing officials in St Vincent and the Grenadines.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 2 out of 10, and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 5.4, near the middle of the scale. The pressure that exists nearby is the cocaine route north from South America through the eastern Caribbean.

For residents, this means there is no known case of an official here acting for an outside paymaster, and the low score suggests the risk is small. The estimate rests on the index's assessment rather than on any inquiry or court ruling in the country, so it describes what conditions suggest, not what has been checked, and a case that has not yet come to light would change it.

Switzerland.d:
Switzerland is where much of the world's governance sits, and much of the infiltration recorded here is aimed at those bodies rather than at the Swiss state. Geneva hosts the World Health Organization, the UN Human Rights Council and the ISO, which sets world technical standards; Zurich hosts FIFA and Lausanne most Olympic sports federations. Outsiders have worked to get inside each. Tobacco companies spent years working through consultants and other UN agencies to weaken the WHO's tobacco work, according to a WHO expert inquiry. Bid committees have allegedly paid FIFA and Olympic voters for hosting rights, claims the bidders deny and most of which have not been tried. When a software company wanted its document format approved by the ISO, partner companies joined national committees to vote yes, and Sweden's vote was annulled. Leaked emails in 2014 suggested Morocco had people in the UN human rights office, but the senior official named denied it and investigators said they found no evidence.

The country's firms are also a channel for reaching other governments. Swiss-based commodity traders have been convicted of bribing officials who hand out oil contracts abroad. The CIA and West Germany's BND secretly owned a Swiss cipher firm, Crypto AG, so the machines it sold to more than 120 governments let the two agencies read their coded messages, and a parliamentary inquiry found Swiss intelligence knew.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 1.5 out of 10. For Swiss residents, the visible result is that their own prosecutors and courts keep trying firms based there for bribery abroad. For people elsewhere, it means that decisions taken in Geneva, Zurich and Lausanne on health rules, technical standards and which country hosts which games can be shaped by whoever got people or money inside first.

Tanzania.d:
In Tanzania the documented reach-in comes mainly from foreign companies selling power, weapons and finance to the state, which have won or kept contracts by paying officials or people close to them. The pattern has repeatedly reached cabinet level. A British arms maker paid its local agent about $12 million, roughly 30 per cent of the price of a $40 million military radar sold in 1999, and the attorney general at the time later resigned as a minister after British investigators found $1 million in his offshore account, though Tanzania's anti-corruption bureau cleared him. A South African bank's local arm paid $6 million to a 'partner' firm with a government official among its directors while raising $600 million for the state, and $122 million from a power-company escrow account was moved to a private power producer whose associate had paid a minister.

Other outside ties sit closer to the ruling party. Since 2022 a leadership school in Kibaha, paid for by China's Communist Party, has trained officials from Tanzania's ruling party and five others in southern Africa, openly and with government agreement.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials working for criminal interests here at 6 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at about 4.2. For Tanzanians, this means electricity, defence and borrowing have repeatedly cost them more because officials took a share, foreign donors held back almost $500 million in budget support over one scandal, and in most cases no one in Tanzania has been convicted of taking the money.

Tonga.d:
No case is documented of a foreign state, company or criminal group paying or placing officials inside Tonga's government, so this is an estimate based on conditions.

Tonga is a small kingdom where, until reforms in 2008, the monarch held most day-to-day power, and decisions about the country's money could be made by the king and a few advisers. The Global Organized Crime Index places Tonga in its Moderate band, scoring officials acting for criminal interests at 6 out of 10. That score suggests outside money could reach some officials, most likely through public contracts, licences or decisions made by a small circle around the government.

For people in Tonga this means there is no named official, company or group acting for an outside interest that they can point to or hold to account. The estimate rests on the index's assessment rather than on any inquiry or court ruling, and a documented case would change it.

Turkmenistan.d:
Turkmenistan is one of the most closed states on Earth: there is no independent press, no opposition party and no court that rules against the government, and almost nothing about how the state works is made public. The one documented case of outsiders reaching in comes from a foreign court record about companies selling to the government. To keep its vehicle sales to the Turkmen state, the German carmaker Daimler gave a high-level official an armoured Mercedes worth about $300,000 as a birthday present in 2000, paid about $250,000 to translate and print 10,000 German copies of the Ruhnama, the spiritual guide written by President Saparmurat Niyazov, and made other payments to officials. Daimler settled the US case in 2010.

No case shows a foreign state or criminal group placing people inside the government. The Global Organized Crime Index puts Turkmenistan in its severe band, scoring officials acting for criminal interests at 9 out of 10, among the highest in the world, and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at 2.2, among the lowest.

For people in Turkmenistan this means that foreign companies seeking state orders have learned to pay officials and flatter the president's personality cult, and the cost is carried in public spending they cannot see. No journalist, judge or auditor in the country can find out whether officials act for outside interests, and the only account of this case came from prosecutors abroad.

United Arab Emirates.d:
The United Arab Emirates has used a state company to place its own man at the head of an international body. In 2023 the chief executive of ADNOC, the state oil company, presided over the UN's COP28 climate talks, and leaked briefing papers showed his team preparing to raise oil and gas business in meetings with foreign governments; he called the claims false.

The UAE is also a place where outside crime reaches others' governments. Dubai's free-zone companies, whose owners can stay hidden behind a required local sponsor, have been used by foreign drug organisations to employ the men who work for them, including one that prosecutors say paid politicians and worked with a security chief in Bosnia. Inside the Emirates, the engineering arm of the Paris airports group allegedly gave a representative of Fujairah personal commissions on its work there, and settled in France in 2023 for a fine also covering a Libyan tender.

At home, the government has made the accusation the other way: in the 2013 'UAE 94' trial the attorney general said members of Islah, an Islamist group, had tried to infiltrate ministries, schools and universities as part of a plot against the government. Islah denies organisational ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, and 26 of the 94 defendants were acquitted.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests in the UAE at 6.5 out of 10. For people elsewhere, this means a UN climate summit was chaired by the head of a state oil company preparing oil deals, and crime groups can use Dubai companies to employ the people who pay officials in their own countries.

Uzbekistan.d:
In Uzbekistan, foreign companies have entered valuable state business by paying people on the inside, from the president's family down to staff at state companies. Three foreign telecom groups paid companies controlled by Gulnara Karimova, elder daughter of then-President Islam Karimov, to obtain mobile licences and radio frequencies; Uzbek prosecutors put her kickbacks at $869 million, and the three firms later paid about $2.6 billion between them to settle foreign bribery cases. Karimova has been convicted twice in Uzbekistan and remains in prison.

The same habit shows lower down, in the state's oil and rail companies. A steel pipe supplier agreed US penalties after using an agent, whom it expected to pass on money to employees of a state oil and gas producer, to see rival bids and undercut them in four tenders. A French rail engineer settled in France in 2021 after investigators found it had paid nearly $576,000 into an account owned by an official at the national railway, in a tender that a Japanese complaint said was rigged.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 7 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at 3.8, so the conditions that made such deals possible have not gone away.

For people in Uzbekistan, this meant paying for mobile services whose licences were sold privately to the president's daughter rather than to the operator offering the best terms, and for rail and oil work awarded through bought tenders. Most of the telecom settlement money went to the governments of the United States, the Netherlands and Sweden, not to Uzbekistan, and weak courts leave citizens little means to find out whether officials are making similar arrangements today.

Vietnam.d:
In Vietnam, the documented pattern is businesses and criminal networks buying the officials who are meant to regulate, police or buy from them, from provincial party chiefs up to ministers, senior police chiefs and the central bank.

The largest case is in banking. A property tycoon secretly controlled a commercial bank for a decade through nominee shareholders, used it to take about US$12.5 billion in loans for her own companies, and paid the head of the central bank's inspection department $5.2 million to keep it off the watch list; she was sentenced to death in 2024.

Most cases are about public money. Construction, property and medical-equipment companies have paid provincial party leaders and project boards to rig tenders for roads, bridges and hospital supplies. During the pandemic, businesses paid officials in three ministries to approve the repatriation flights that were the only way home for Vietnamese abroad. The reach goes to the cabinet: two communications ministers were jailed after a state phone company bought a private pay-TV firm at a price AP reported as inflated almost ten times. US settlements describe foreign firms working the same way, through agents and slush funds around state refineries and telecoms customers. Two senior police chiefs were jailed for covering for an online gambling ring, and drug-team officers were convicted of shielding a Laos–Vietnam trafficking network.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 7 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at 4.8. For people in Vietnam this means bank savings, hospital budgets, road contracts and even a seat on a flight home have been for sale to whoever paid the official in charge, and officers meant to enforce gambling and drug laws have been convicted of protecting those breaking them.

Albania.d:
Albanian crime groups move cannabis across the sea to Italy and Greece and buy cocaine in Latin America for sale across Europe, and to keep that trade running they reach into the institutions meant to stop it. The record points above all at the police. Since 2023 SPAK, Albania's special anti-corruption prosecutor, has used messages from Sky ECC, an encrypted phone service read by European police, to bring case after case in which a former Tirana police chief, provincial police crime chiefs, a border police head, judges and a prosecutor are accused of working for trafficking groups. The accusations are of warning groups about anti-drug operations, leaking data from the national border database, and suppressing charges or cutting sentences for money. These cases have not reached a verdict in the record here, so they remain allegations.

Higher up, Italian police arrested a cousin of the interior minister in a cannabis probe, and wiretaps mentioned the minister. He was convicted only of abuse of office, so no court has found that the group had him working for it.

SPAK has sent the mayor of Tirana, the capital, to trial on charges that four businessmen gave him and his wife more than €1 million in benefits while he approved construction permits; he denies it. It also suspects that at least 19 tenders at the state IT agency were written for chosen contractors, whose firms gained access to police and prison security systems.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Albania 6.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and about 5 for its courts, police and watchdogs. For people living there, if these charges hold, the officer checking a car or investigating a killing may be passing information to the group responsible.

Antigua and Barbuda.d:
Antigua and Barbuda is a small state with a small civil service, and the documented cases show outsiders with far more money than its government reaching the one official whose signature they needed.

Agents working for Colombia's Medellín Cartel ordered Israeli military weapons in Antigua's name, with forged papers, to arm the forces of a cartel leader. An Israeli diplomatic note said the guns were shipped at the apparent instruction of the minister Vere Bird Jr, son of the prime minister, and after Colombia complained an official inquiry recommended he be barred from public office for life. The island's business as an offshore financial centre, where foreign-run banks take deposits from around the world under Antiguan licences, created the second opening. R. Allen Stanford ran Stanford International Bank from Antigua and was later convicted in the United States of a $7 billion fraud; the head of the Antiguan regulator meant to supervise his bank took cash, private-jet flights and sports tickets from him, left the bank's real assets unexamined and told US investigators his office had no power to help them.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores the country 3 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and about 4.7 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs.
