For people living there, both cases meant outsiders used the state's name and licences for their own business: Antigua's name went on a cartel's arms order, and thousands of savers, on the island and abroad, lost their money in a bank that the regulator had been paid not to look at. In both cases the facts came out through pressure from abroad, from Colombia and from US prosecutors, rather than from Antigua's own institutions.

Austria.d:
Austria sits between east and west, and Vienna has long been a base for foreign spy services. The documented reach-in runs mostly from Russia, into Austria's own security state and into international bodies based here, and the record shows it lasting decades. An Austrian army colonel passed military secrets to the GRU, Russia's military intelligence, from 1992 until 2018 in return for about €280,000, and was convicted in 2020.

The same reach has since appeared inside Austria's domestic intelligence agency, and prosecutors say it ran through more than one person there. A former officer was convicted in 2026 of working for Russia through Jan Marsalek, the fugitive former Wirecard executive: he used police databases to find people Moscow was looking for, including a journalist, and he plans to appeal. Prosecutors allege that the agency's former operations chief, after leaving in 2018, passed that officer orders from Marsalek and Russian operatives; he fled to Dubai and has not been tried. Russian money has also reached sport: an independent inquiry found that the president of the Salzburg-based International Biathlon Union took Russian cash and favours over many years and shielded Russian athletes from doping action.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Austria 4 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 7.5 for its courts, police and watchdogs. For exiles, journalists and others Russia's government wants to find, the risk is that an official with access to state databases may be working for a foreign service and can use the state's records to locate them. For Austrians generally, it means officers in the army and the intelligence service have worked for a foreign power while holding secrets the country shares with its EU partners, and the cases have come to light years after the leaks began.

Bangladesh.d:
In Bangladesh outsiders have reached public institutions from three directions: business groups taking over banks, an Islamist movement reaching into the army, and party networks filling the universities. Foreign firms bidding for large public works have also been accused of paying officials, though the biggest such accusation was not proven.

The banks are where the most money has moved. Under Sheikh Hasina's government, which fell in August 2024, conglomerates close to it came to control lenders holding ordinary people's deposits. From 2017 the S. Alam Group took over Islami Bank Bangladesh and several other Islamic banks, installing its own chairman, board and managers, and holding one bank's shares beyond the legal limit. Media reported huge loans to the group, which the bank denied; the group denies wrongdoing and investigations are open.

A coup attempt by serving and retired army officers, which the army says it stopped in 2012, was linked to Hizb ut-Tahrir, a banned movement seeking a single Islamic state. Since 2024 the interim government has filled the universities from the networks of the BNP and the Islamist Jamaat-e-Islami: 30 of 47 new vice-chancellors had close ties to their teachers' groups. The World Bank cancelled its credit for the Padma Bridge in 2012, alleging a plot by a Canadian engineering firm to bribe a minister and other officials, but Bangladesh's anti-corruption body cleared the accused and a Canadian court acquitted the firm's executives.

For depositors, the bank holding their savings may have been run for the group that took it over. Soldiers have been drawn into a plot to seize power on behalf of a movement outside the state, and students and staff have seen university leadership handed to the networks of the parties now close to government.

Belize.d:
No case of an outside party placing people or money inside Belize's government or companies remains on this map after checking. That is a statement about the documented record, not proof that none exists.

Belize sits between Mexico and Guatemala on the Caribbean coast, on routes used to move cocaine north from South America, and it offers offshore company registration. Those are the conditions under which outside money tends to look for officials willing to help. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Belize 5.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests, in the middle of the range, but only about 3.6 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, which is weak.

For people living there, this means there is no documented case in which they can name an official acting for an outside party. The weak resilience score matters more: if traffickers or foreign buyers did reach officials, the courts, police and regulators that should catch it are rated as poorly placed to do so. The records that would show it first are the ownership of registered companies and how drug cases on the coast and the border are handled.

Bosnia and Herzegovina.d:
Bosnia and Herzegovina sits on the Balkan route by which cocaine and other drugs reach western Europe, and the documented pattern today is criminal networks getting people inside the bodies meant to stop them. Messages on Sky and Anom, encrypted phones used by criminals, led prosecutors to suspect contacts in the police and courts: by early 2023 more than 100 suspects had been detained, among them 14 from law enforcement and a judge. Europol, the EU police agency, said arrests in Sarajevo in 2024 included corrupt officials working for a cocaine boss's inner circle.

The accusations now reach the most senior posts. The United States has said the head of the state intelligence service worked with criminal networks, and that a senior state prosecutor helped hide evidence for drug traffickers; a Bosnian disciplinary body demoted her for abusing her office. The intelligence chief and the president of the state court are on trial over alleged wiretapping of judges and prosecutors, and the judge is also accused of taking a bribe from a Croatian football boss. These are designations and charges, with no verdict reported.

During and just after the 1992–95 war, Iran, a wartime ally, built a presence inside the Interior Ministry. The divided government left by the 1995 peace deal, with separate police and ministries in each part of the country, gives outsiders many offices to approach.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Bosnia 8 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and about 3.9 for its courts, police and watchdogs. For people living there, the prosecutor or judge handling their case may be under suspicion of working for the people they are meant to try, and the bodies that should catch that are themselves under investigation.

Bulgaria.d:
Bulgaria sits on the Balkan route, the main land route by which drugs and smuggled goods enter the European Union, and smugglers get through it by paying the customs officers and border police who are supposed to stop them. The United States sanctioned Bulgarian officials and business figures in 2021, its largest such action against any single country, and several of those named held customs and border posts.

The same sanctions reached the top of the state. The US Treasury said Delyan Peevski, a member of parliament and media owner, used bribes and influence to control key institutions; in 2013 parliament made him head of the national security agency and he quit a day later after mass protests. Claims are also under investigation that compromising files on judges and prosecutors have been used to steer their decisions.

Russian intelligence is accused of reaching the bodies that guard this NATO member's secrets. Prosecutors charged a ring in 2021 that included a senior defence ministry official, two serving military intelligence officers and the former head of parliament's registry of classified information, accused of passing NATO and EU documents to Russian military intelligence; they remain on trial. In 2022 prosecutors also accused a reserve general working at the defence ministry of passing state secrets to a Russian embassy adviser, and investigated two senior officers of the counter-intelligence agency, who were dismissed. Neither 2022 case had been tested in court in the reports available.

For people here, this means goods crossing the border unchecked, a security service open to those it should watch, and allied secrets held by officials who may have been working for Moscow. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Bulgaria high for officials working for criminal interests and its institutions only middling. Few of those named have been charged at home.

Cambodia.d:
One case in Cambodia is on this map, and it is an allegation that both governments reject. The US Treasury says a Chinese state-owned company, Union Development Group, obtained a 99-year lease in 2008 on the Dara Sakor project, almost 20 per cent of the country's coastline, by forming a local company as leaseholder. It says the army used violence to help clear the land and that a senior general and former armed forces chief of staff benefited financially. Treasury imposed sanctions, while a ruling-party spokesman said the state development council had reviewed and approved the plan. If the allegation is right, a foreign company had the use of Cambodian troops, and the people cleared from that land faced soldiers working in its interest.

Beyond this case the entry remains an estimate. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Cambodia among the worst countries in the world for officials working for criminal interests, with weak courts, police and watchdogs to push back. US and British sanctions have named political protection as the reason scam compounds, fenced sites where trafficked workers are forced to run online fraud, can operate in the open. On those scores it is likely that criminal money reaches officials, but the record so far shows owners close to power rather than decisions shown to have been taken inside the state for them. Cambodian courts have prosecuted none of the people sanctioned abroad.

Chad.d:
In Chad outside money reaches in at two levels: foreign oil companies seeking rights go to the presidency and the diplomatic service, and drug traffickers go to the security services. Two cases from the oil side have ended in court abroad. An envoy working for CEFC China Energy, which promoted China's Belt and Road programme, offered President Idriss Déby a $2 million bribe, dressed up as a donation, to win oil rights, and was convicted for it in New York in 2018; the company's chairman denied authorising him. Griffiths Energy, a Canadian company, pleaded guilty in 2013 after paying a $2 million fee to a firm controlled by the wife of Chad's ambassador in North America while seeking an oil contract. The ambassador, his wife and his deputy face US charges that remain unproven.

Lower down, tramadol, a prescription painkiller, is trafficked illegally across the Sahel, and the network moving it through Chad counted high-ranking security and intelligence officials among its members. Analysts who read the court papers when ten people were convicted in 2020 described large sums circulating among them, some used in attempts to bribe judges and the security services.

When intelligence officers are inside a trafficking network, Chadians depend for protection on police and courts that the same network has tried to buy, and when oil rights are sought through payments to the president's circle and the country's diplomats, decisions about the main national resource are made for the payer. The 2020 conviction shows Chad's courts can act, but the oil cases were brought in the United States and Canada. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Chad among the countries where officials most often work for criminal interests, and its courts, police and watchdogs among the weakest.

Comoros.d:
Comoros, a small island state off East Africa, has been reached by outsiders through the men around its president and through its officials. For about eleven years from 1978, its presidential guard was commanded by Bob Denard, a French mercenary who worked for France's secret services: he led the coup that returned President Ahmed Abdallah to power, then ran the force meant to protect him while building up business interests and Comorian citizenship. When Abdallah ordered the guard disarmed in 1989 he was shot dead shortly afterwards, and Denard led another coup in 1995 that French troops ended; the court that later tried him recognised the secret services' role.

The more recent documented reach comes from a tobacco company. Leaked records from British American Tobacco (BAT) show the company arranging bribes for Comorian officials, part of a run of payments in several African countries that included efforts to block tobacco-control laws based on the World Health Organization's tobacco treaty. A British fraud inquiry closed without charges and BAT denies wrongdoing.

For Comorians, this means that for a decade the armed men around their head of state answered to a foreigner tied to another country's spy service, and if the tobacco payments worked as reported, they now live under weaker limits on tobacco sales and advertising than the treaty sets. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Comoros high for officials working for criminal interests, with very weak courts, police and watchdogs.

Cote d'Ivoire.d:
The documented outside reach in Côte d'Ivoire is an international lender placing its own official at the head of the economy.

In 1990 the International Monetary Fund pressed President Félix Houphouët-Boigny to put Alassane Ouattara, who had directed the IMF's African Department, in charge of economic policy; he became prime minister that November while the IMF's programme was still running, later returned to the IMF as its deputy head, and has been president since 2011. For Ivorians this meant that the man running their economy during an IMF programme came from the lender setting its conditions, and the decisions on spending and prices taken under that programme were made by the lender's own former official.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Côte d'Ivoire high for officials working for criminal interests, with courts, police and watchdogs of middling strength. No documented case on the map shows a criminal group paying Ivorian officials.

Czech Republic.d:
The documented outside reach into the Czech state comes from two sides: Russian intelligence, and a lobbyist's network inside public companies. Russia's foreign intelligence service, the SVR, has worked the old way, by recruiting insiders: in 2022 the government confirmed that a long-serving Foreign Ministry employee with top-secret clearance, who had worked at headquarters and in embassies, had repeatedly taken its money for diplomatic information. He was removed, but prosecution was thought unlikely because intelligence material cannot be used in Czech courts. Prague has also been a base for Russian money aimed at legislatures elsewhere: in 2024 the government exposed Voice of Europe, a Russian-funded website that Czech intelligence says passed money to sitting and aspiring European legislators.

At home, police say a group around Michal Redl, a Zlín businessman and lobbyist linked to the STAN party, steered contracts and money at Prague's city-owned transport company, which runs the metro, trams and buses, through a deputy mayor and senior managers of the firm, to benefit businessmen connected to the group, and reached contracts at the state health insurer as well. Thirteen people were charged in 2022, the education minister resigned over his contacts with Redl, and the trial is under way, with the main accused denying guilt.

For Czechs, this means a diplomatic service in which a foreign spy agency was able to pay a cleared official for years, with no trial to show what he passed on, and a city transport company whose contracts, prosecutors say, were decided for a lobbyist's friends rather than for the people who ride it. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Czech officials low to middling for working with criminal interests, with relatively strong institutions.

Dominican Republic.d:
In the Dominican Republic outside money has reached officials through foreign firms seeking state contracts and, far more often, through the drug trade. Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction company, admitted paying $92 million in bribes in the country to win public works, and a former public works minister was convicted over it. Embraer, the Brazilian aircraft maker, admitted promising $3.5 million to a Dominican official to sell military aircraft; a retired colonel and a former defence minister deny any bribe, and their 2022 acquittal is now subject to a fresh trial.

The Dominican Republic is a transit point for cocaine bound for Puerto Rico, the United States and Europe, and traffickers seek protection wherever a shipment can be stopped. Officers of the National Drug Control Agency have been arrested while guarding loads, a navy officer in charge of port security has been accused of moving cocaine, army colonels have been arrested on suspicion of leaking warrants and raid plans, and a fugitive trafficker held a state intelligence card and official gun permits. The reach goes into Congress and the agencies: a congressman and a state agency head were among one cocaine network's contacts, and the congressman was accused of trying to help a man avoid extradition. A convicted trafficker says his money paid for a presidential campaign, a claim never tested in court. Since 2009 the drug agency has removed hundreds of staff and the police well over a thousand officers.

For Dominicans, public works and military purchases have been paid for under deals carrying bribes, and the people meant to stop the drug trade have included some accused of working for it. The Global Organized Crime Index rates the country in the middle range for officials working for criminal interests, with weak courts, police and watchdogs.

Equatorial Guinea.d:
Equatorial Guinea is a small oil and gas producer on the Gulf of Guinea, ruled by Teodoro Obiang since 1979, and the record of outsiders reaching into its government runs almost entirely through oil. The foreign companies that produce and trade its oil have paid the president, his family and the officials who award contracts. A 2004 US Senate inquiry found that American oil companies producing most of the country's offshore oil made payments to Obiang, his relatives and officials for land, office leases, security and scholarships for officials' children, and that Obiang and his family held secret shares in their joint ventures with the government. Later, the Dutch company SBM Offshore admitted that between 2008 and 2012 its local agents passed money on to at least nine officials of the oil ministry and the state oil company, and a Swiss-based commodity trader has pleaded guilty in Britain to bribing officials in five African oil states, this one among them.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 9 out of 10, among the highest anywhere, and the courts, police and watchdogs that would resist them at just over 2. That combination describes a state where the people in office control the main source of money and no independent body can question how contracts are given out.

For Equatoguineans, this means oil revenue that could pay for services has been shared between foreign companies and the ruling family, with officials' children educated abroad on company money. With one president in power for more than four decades and weak courts, they have no domestic route to find out who was paid; every documented case was brought by investigators abroad.

Ethiopia.d:
No documented case in Ethiopia yet meets this map's test of an outside party getting its people, money or control inside the government and steering it. The prime minister's membership of a Pentecostal church is lawful, and no record shows the church directing government decisions.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 6 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at 4.5, which suggests more is going on than has been documented. Civil war in Tigray and continuing conflict in Amhara and Oromia make reporting on officials harder, and the weak watchdogs mean there is little official scrutiny of how decisions are made. The shading here is an estimate from those scores.

Gabon.d:
No documented case in Gabon yet meets the map's test, which asks whether an outside party got its people, money or control inside a government body, international body or company, and whether decisions there served it.

The best available estimate comes from the Global Organized Crime Index. It scores officials acting for outside or criminal interests in Gabon at 7.5 out of 10, and the courts and watchdogs that should catch them at 3.5. Taken together, these scores point to a state where officials can serve outside interests with little risk of being exposed, so the lack of a documented case may partly reflect how little is investigated.

For people in Gabon this means there is no independent record to show whether the officials who govern them answer to someone else.

Ghana.d:
In Ghana the record holds one case of traffickers reaching a senior police officer and one contested case of a foreign company working through a politician's relative. Cocaine moves through West Africa on its way to Europe and the United States, and the traffickers who move it need officials who will look away or help.

In 2006 a large cocaine load landed from a ship and then disappeared. Traffickers were secretly taped meeting the police director of operations at his home about their missing drugs. An inquiry found the police account unsatisfactory and recommended that he be prosecuted, but he was later recalled to duty.

The second case concerns military transport planes. UK court papers said Airbus hired a close relative of a high-ranking elected Ghanaian official as its business partner while selling the planes to Ghana, and Airbus's 2020 settlement with France, Britain and the United States included failure to prevent bribery there. In 2024 Ghana's Special Prosecutor closed its own inquiry, finding no evidence that the official took bribes and clearing the relative, so this is not established as an official being bought.

For Ghanaians, this shows traffickers reaching a senior officer in the police, the body meant to stop them, and that officer returning to duty despite the inquiry's recommendation. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 7.5 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at about 5.3. Two cases cannot show how common any of this is.

Guinea.d:
Guinea holds one of the world's largest untapped iron ore deposits, at Simandou. The documented cases of outside interests getting inside its government are about who controls its minerals, and they run from foreign companies to the president's household and the minister in charge of mines.

In 2008 the government took two blocks of Simandou from one mining company and gave them to a company controlled by Israeli businessman Beny Steinmetz; a Swiss court later found that he got them by bribing a wife of President Lansana Conté, which he denies. The company that lost the blocks, trying to keep its rights, hired a French banker who was a close friend of a former senior Guinean official, and US regulators found that, acting for it, he offered at least $822,000 to a Guinean official; it paid a $15 million penalty without admitting or denying the findings. Separately, executives of Chinese-linked companies paid mines minister Mahmoud Thiam $8.5 million to become first shareholder in a national mining company that would hold Guinea's stakes, and a New York jury convicted him of laundering the money.

In all three the way to national resources ran through payments to people close to power rather than through open bidding. For Guineans, that meant control of the country's main mineral wealth was fought over through the president's household and the officials who negotiated the terms, and years of potential state revenue were lost while the rights were contested. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 8 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at under 3, so cases like these tend to be pursued abroad, if at all.

Honduras.d:
Honduras is one of the main stopping points for cocaine flown and shipped from South America towards Mexico and the United States, and over the past two decades trafficking groups bought protection at the top of the state. According to US courts, traffickers paid a president, his brother in Congress and a national police chief to let cocaine through, and trial evidence said drug money paid for the governing National Party's election campaigns. The clearest single case is Juan Orlando Hernández, president from 2014 to 2022, who was convicted in New York of protecting cocaine shipments and pardoned by the US in 2025.

The police are where the arrangement shows most consistently. Officers who have pleaded guilty in US courts include one who, prosecutors said, led colleagues in escorting tons of cocaine and another who passed police information to the Cachiros, a Honduran trafficking clan, for a decade. Trafficking also worked from the bottom up: on the Guatemalan border, a trafficker became mayor of his own town and, US prosecutors said, paid into the ruling party's presidential campaign in return for protection. The Cachiros laundered money through a business group of one of the country's most powerful political families, whose bank regulators closed after the US imposed sanctions. Suppliers have paid as well: a US uniform maker's chief was convicted in 2025 over bribes for police contracts.

For Hondurans, this means mayors, police, Congress and the presidency have all been used to move cocaine. The main cases were tried abroad, and the former president has been released, though Honduras has an arrest order out for him. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 8.5 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at under 4.

Indonesia.d:
In Indonesia outside forces reach the state mainly through money, business and religious movements. Under Suharto, a Muslim intellectuals' association headed by the minister Habibie moved its members into the civil service and ministries and used that place to set up religious courts and an Islamic bank. Officials say Jemaah Islamiyah, the network behind the 2002 Bali bombings, tried for over a decade to get its people into the military, police and ministries, and one of its advisers sat on the state-recognised Ulema Council's fatwa commission.

Business helps write the law and decide how it is applied. When the government drafted its 2020 omnibus jobs law, which rewrote dozens of laws on labour, land and permits, it put the chairman of the national chamber of commerce in charge of the consultation. Firms have paid the people who buy from them, judge them or guard state assets. Aircraft makers paid the head of the state airline. Power-plant bidders paid MPs, a minister and, in a French group's US settlement, the head of the state electricity company; a later head of that company was acquitted in a separate case. Contractors paid the Speaker of parliament, and prosecutors say palm-oil groups' lawyers paid judges to acquit them. At PT Timah, the state tin company, directors let private smelters mine its concessions under a disguised leasing deal, at a cost put at about 300 trillion rupiah.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Indonesian officials 8 out of 10 for working for criminal interests. For Indonesians this means the rules on their wages and land were drafted with employers at the head of the table, the Bangka Belitung islands were dug up by smelters with the state firm's directors on side, and a court verdict can depend on who has paid.

Israel.d:
In Israel the outside party with the deepest reach into the state is the settler movement, which builds settlements in the occupied West Bank and has long drawn state money to outposts the government's own rules forbade. One of the movement's leaders runs the civil administration that decides on land and building in the West Bank. After the 7 October 2023 attack the movement also came to sit inside the army there: thousands of settlers called up as reservists serve in local defence units staffed largely by residents of the settlements they guard, and the army has dismissed dozens for violations including attacks on Palestinians.

The ultra-Orthodox parties take their decisions from councils of senior rabbis, who used their place in government to protect seminary students' exemption from military service and in 2025 ordered their ministers out after the Supreme Court told the army to start drafting them.

Prosecutors say Benjamin Netanyahu, as communications minister, gave valuable decisions to a telecoms owner in return for favourable coverage, which he denies; a former head of his bureau and a former minister are charged with taking bribes from the Israeli agent of a German shipbuilder whose submarines the state was buying. Iranian intelligence recruits Israelis online, including soldiers in the Iron Dome missile-defence system, and 35 such espionage cases had been made public by the end of 2025.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Israel 5.5 out of 10 both for officials serving outside interests and for its courts and watchdogs. For Palestinians in the West Bank, the official deciding whether their homes stand comes from the movement that wants their land, and the soldiers posted near their villages are often settlers from the settlements nearby. For Israelis, who serves in the army has been set partly in rabbis' councils.

Jordan.d:
In Jordan, outside forces have reached the state through its rulers, its border guards and its parliament. For about twenty years, until 1977, the CIA made secret yearly payments of millions of dollars to King Hussein; President Carter stopped them just before The Washington Post reported them. Today's pressure comes from drug smugglers on the Syrian border. Smugglers moving captagon, an amphetamine pill made in Syria, need the border to stay open to them, so they recruit the people guarding it, and serving and former soldiers have been convicted of carrying pills and weapons across.

The Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement that works to bring its members into power, competed openly through its own party, the Islamic Action Front, which became the largest party in parliament in the 2024 election. In 2025 the government banned all of the Brotherhood's activities and said it would seize its assets, after arrests over an alleged weapons plot that the group said it knew nothing about.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Jordan 6 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and above 5 for its courts and watchdogs. For families in northern Jordan this means living on a smuggling route where some of the soldiers paid to stop the drugs have been caught moving them. For the voters who made the Islamic Action Front the largest party, it means their party's parent movement is now banned and its members face arrest.

Korea, DPR.d:
In North Korea the state itself is the organisation that crosses borders, and the one documented case on this map runs the other way: the government reaching into an international body rather than an outside force reaching into it. In the Pyongyang office of the UN Development Programme, the UN's main aid agency, most local staff were nominees chosen by the government against UN policy, their salaries were paid to the state in hard currency, officials had to be present at project visits, and the government moved its own funds abroad through a UN account. A 2008 US Senate inquiry set this out, and the UN suspended its programme there in 2007 after the government refused new controls.

The Global Organized Crime Index gives North Korea the worst possible score, 10 out of 10, for officials taking part in criminal activity, and one of the lowest anywhere for its courts and watchdogs. The US Justice Department has charged networks that placed thousands of North Korean IT workers, using stolen or fake identities, in remote jobs at foreign companies, with their wages paid into accounts controlled by the state.

For people in North Korea this means that aid meant for them passes through staff picked by the government, and money from work done abroad in their name goes to the state rather than to them. With no independent courts, press or watchdogs, they have no means of learning how the aid or the earnings are spent, or of challenging it at home.

Kyrgyzstan.d:
The record in Kyrgyzstan is small and shows money reaching officials at two points: the customs service and the president's circle. Customs decides what crosses the border and what duty is paid on it, so a smuggling operation with people inside controls both what comes in unchecked and how much revenue the state loses. The clearest case is Raiymbek Matraimov, a deputy head of customs whom journalists tied to a scheme that moved hundreds of millions of dollars out of the country, and whom the US sanctioned in 2020; at home he settled by repaying money and served no prison term at the time.

Foreign companies have also gone to the top. US regulators say a global tobacco trader paid more than $3 million in bribes from as early as 1996 so that its local subsidiary could buy Kyrgyz tobacco, most of it delivered in bags of $100 bills to a high-ranking official; the company settled. After the president was ousted in 2010, officials of the new government said the firm supplying jet fuel to the US air base at Manas had paid his son. That remains an allegation, and these records do not show what a US congressional inquiry found.

Journalists from OCCRP, an organised-crime reporting network, and the Kyrgyz outlet Kloop, who documented the customs scheme, were prosecuted or forced out while the official they wrote about stayed free. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Kyrgyzstan 8.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 4 for the strength of its courts and watchdogs. For people in Kyrgyzstan this means customs revenue that should have paid for schools, roads and hospitals has left the country, and the officials at the centre of it have faced little at home.

Lesotho.d:
Lesotho's largest public project is the Lesotho Highlands Water Project, a World Bank-backed scheme of dams and tunnels that sells the country's water to South Africa, and it is where foreign companies reached in most clearly. Engineering and construction firms from abroad paid Masupha Sole, chief executive of the state authority that ran it, through intermediaries, and Swiss bank records later showed millions of maloti he could not explain. In 2002 Lesotho's own High Court convicted him of bribery and it went on to convict a Canadian engineering firm and a German consultancy. A small, poor country prosecuted the foreign companies itself, which is unusual.

Two later matters are less settled. Prosecutors allege that the head of the German company Frazer Solar and a former minister forged a solar deal after Cabinet declined to approve it; the minister says his signature was forged, no bribe is reported, and the case has been revived on appeal. Even so, the company won an arbitration award of about €50 million and has pursued Lesotho's water royalties to collect it. Separately, the deputy army commander said in 2024 that members of the security agencies escort and associate with famo gangs, rival groups blamed for killings, without naming anyone.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Lesotho 7 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 4 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For people in Lesotho this means the scheme that sells their main natural resource was run for years by an official taking money from the firms building it, income from that same water has been targeted in a dispute over a contract their courts called unlawful, and the forces meant to stop gang killings are said by their own commander to include people close to the gangs.

Lithuania.d:
Lithuania has faced two kinds of reach-in: Russian and Belarusian intelligence recruiting people with access to its armed forces, air infrastructure and security services, and business money reaching politicians and parties.

Russia's military intelligence, the GRU, and its security service, the FSB, have repeatedly tried to buy people with access. The Šiauliai air base, which hosts NATO's Baltic air patrols, has been a repeated target: a GRU agent working as a military surgeon recruited an air force officer there, and later a base worker and an accomplice were convicted of photographing orders and layouts for Russian intelligence. An FSB officer was caught in 2015 trying to recruit members of the presidential guard to plant listening devices. Belarus's military intelligence has used the same method, recruiting an employee of the state air traffic company and, since 2022, two Lithuanians, one of whom joined the Riflemen's Union, a volunteer defence organisation linked to the army, in order to spy.

On the money side, the clearest case is the president removed in 2004: a Russian helicopter businessman who reportedly funded his campaign was then granted citizenship by presidential decree, and parliament impeached him. Domestic business buys in too: in 2024 the Supreme Court made final the convictions of the Liberal Movement's leader, a Labour MP and an executive of one of the largest business groups for bribes paid to get decisions through parliament, after a lower court had acquitted them.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Lithuania's institutions as fairly strong and finds a moderate level of officials serving criminal interests. For Lithuanians this means the soldiers, base staff, volunteers and guards protecting them and the members of parliament voting on their laws have each been targets for payment, and most of those exposed so far have been convicted in Lithuania's own courts.

Malaysia.d:
In Malaysia outside money and networks have reached the state at the top, in the armed forces and at its borders. Goldman Sachs bankers paid bribes to officials in Malaysia and Abu Dhabi to win the bond business of 1MDB, a state investment fund, and billions were then stolen; Najib Razak, prime minister until 2018, was convicted over more than $1 billion found in his own accounts, and is appealing. His successor, Muhyiddin Yassin, is on trial accused of using his office to help firms win contracts under a Covid-era public works programme while they paid money to his party, which he denies.

Defence buying has drawn similar accusations. French investigators allege that French firms paid kickbacks through a defence minister's adviser to sell submarines, which those charged deny. Anti-corruption investigators suspect a cartel of companies paid army officers to rig tenders, and a former army chief has pleaded not guilty to laundering charges. They also allege a smuggling syndicate paid military officers per run.

Traffickers moving methamphetamine from the Golden Triangle pay narcotics officers to release suspects and resell seized drugs, and the commission has prosecuted such officers repeatedly, mostly in Johor and around Kuala Lumpur. The national police chief said in 2021 that 34 members of the force were suspected of working for a single phone-scam gang, and at the main airport the commission says agents pay immigration officers to wave foreigners through.

For Malaysians, a public fund meant to pay for development filled a prime minister's accounts and left the country with the debt, public money for defence may have gone on bribes, some officers paid to stop drugs have sold them back onto the street, and fraud victims have reported to a force in which some officers were suspected of working for the fraudsters.

Marshall Islands.d:
The documented outside reach into the Marshall Islands is an attempt by foreign businesspeople to buy a law that would have given them their own territory. Two China-born businesspeople paid members of parliament and other officials over several years to pass a law creating a semi-autonomous 'special administrative region' on Rongelap Atoll. Both pleaded guilty in the United States, and the US government later barred a former Marshallese president and an MP from entering the country for taking the bribes; the former president denies it.

The scheme shows how a small Pacific state can be approached. A parliament of a few dozen members meant that paying a handful of lawmakers could move a law. The Global Organized Crime Index finds a relatively low level of officials serving outside interests in the Marshall Islands, which fits a country where this was a single scheme rather than a settled arrangement.

For the people of Rongelap this means lawmakers were paid to put their home under a separate set of rules written for the buyers. No one has been charged in the Marshall Islands, so the case was settled in a foreign court, and Marshallese have no ruling of their own on which officials took money.

Micronesia.d:
The record for the Federated States of Micronesia holds one accusation made by its own head of state and one foreign bribery conviction. In 2023, shortly before leaving office, President David Panuelo wrote a long letter saying China was using bribery and threats against Micronesian officials as 'political warfare', with the aim of keeping the Pacific country on Beijing's side, or neutral, if war broke out over Taiwan. China rejected the claims, no court or inquiry has tested them, and no official has been named as taking money.

The proven case is smaller and commercial. US prosecutors said a Hawaii engineering firm gave cash, vehicles, gifts and entertainment to Micronesian officials from 2006 to 2016 to win and keep government contracts worth nearly $8 million. Its owner and a transport department official who oversaw aviation programmes, including airport management, pleaded guilty and were sentenced in the US in 2019.

Both accounts describe a method suited to a small state, where paying or pressing a handful of senior officials can move a large decision, whether that is a contract or which of China or Taiwan the country recognises. The Global Organized Crime Index finds a relatively low level of officials serving outside interests in Micronesia.

For Micronesians, this means at least one official overseeing public services such as airports took payments from a firm seeking government contracts. If the president's account is also true, some officials have made foreign policy decisions after taking money or giving way to threats from abroad, and because that has not been investigated, people cannot tell which officials, if any, were involved.

Montenegro.d:
In Montenegro, organised crime has had protectors at the top of the state for three decades. In the 1990s, when cigarettes were smuggled across the Adriatic to Italy, Italian anti-mafia prosecutors charged that the state itself protected the trade and indicted the country's leader, Milo Djukanovic, in 2008; immunity kept him from trial, and he went on to lead Montenegro until 2023.

The smuggling has continued, cocaine has joined cigarettes, and the protection is alleged to have reached the justice system. Since Europol, the EU's police agency, passed Montenegro messages from Sky ECC, a cracked encrypted phone service used by criminals, former heads of the Supreme Court, the special prosecution office and the police have been charged with protecting crime groups. Prosecutors say a cigarette group using the free customs zone at the Port of Bar had a former national police director and the port city's criminal police chief passing it information; both have denied such accusations and no verdict has been reported. The clearest case is the former Supreme Court president convicted in 2026 of using her position to shield a smuggling network run by her son.

Foreign governments have been accused of reaching in too. Prosecutors accused two Russian military intelligence officers of plotting with pro-Russian opposition MPs to seize parliament in 2016; a first court convicted them, but a retrial acquitted everyone.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials in Montenegro widely serving criminal interests. For people there this means the judges, prosecutors and police chiefs they would turn to may have been working for the groups they were meant to pursue, and anyone whose case reached the Supreme Court in those years cannot be sure it was heard fairly. Most of these charges are still unproven.

Namibia.d:
In Namibia, the documented outside reach is through what the state buys and what it hands out, with foreign companies accused of paying people close to the officials in charge. Neither accusation has been proved in court.

Namibia's fish belong to the public, and the government hands out quotas, licences to catch a set amount. In the case known as 'Fishrot', leaked files published in 2019 indicated that Samherji, one of Iceland's largest fishing companies, had paid people close to the government to obtain horse-mackerel quotas. The fisheries and justice ministers resigned and were arrested with several associates, and they face racketeering, corruption and money-laundering charges under Namibia's organised crime law. Samherji denies paying bribes, and no one has yet been convicted. In an earlier case, prosecutors alleged in 2009 that Nuctech, a Chinese state-owned scanner maker, inflated the price of a deal with the finance ministry to pay millions of dollars in 'commission' to a firm part-owned by a serving public service commissioner. All three accused were found not guilty.

The mechanism alleged is one seen wherever a few officials control who may take a public resource or win a public contract: a foreign company that pays them or their associates gets a share that would otherwise go to local firms or be sold for the public's benefit. The Global Organized Crime Index finds a moderate-to-high level of officials serving outside interests in Namibia and rates its institutions as fairly weak.

For Namibians, if the charges are proved, two ministers sold a public resource to a foreign company, local fishing firms and their workers lost quota they would otherwise have had, and the state lost income for the public budget. The trial has run for years, so people still wait for a court to say who took part.

New Zealand.d:
In New Zealand the documented reach inside government is small and comes from three directions: the Chinese state, which media reports say had people in Parliament whose ties to it were known to the intelligence services but not to voters; drug networks, which police say have paid prison staff; and contractors paying the public managers who buy from them.

The clearest example of the first is Jian Yang, a National MP who had been a Communist Party member and had taught at Chinese army schools that trained intelligence linguists. New Zealand media reported that the agencies had raised concerns about his relationship with the Chinese government; he and a second MP left Parliament at an election. No official finding backs those reports.

Organised crime has generally had little hold on officials, and the Global Organized Crime Index gives New Zealand one of the world's lowest scores on that measure. The exception now before the courts is in Auckland's prisons, where police allege that prisoners coordinating drug imports from their cells had staff take cash to bring in phones and drugs. In 2026 police charged fifteen prison staff, five of them employed by Serco, the private company running one jail. The proven cases are in local government: a road contractor paid more than $1 million over eight years to a senior manager at a local council and then Auckland Transport, and both were jailed.

For New Zealanders, this means they elected MPs whose links to a foreign government were reportedly known to the security services and not to them, some officers paid to keep prisons closed may have been working for the people held inside, and spending on Auckland's roads was for years overseen by a manager taking money from the firm doing the work.

North Macedonia.d:
In North Macedonia outsiders have reached into politics and the justice system by paying or directing individual office-holders, most visibly around the 2018 agreement that renamed the country so it could join NATO, which Russia opposed. Interior ministry documents seen by investigative reporters say Ivan Savvidis, a Russian-Greek billionaire and former member of Russia's parliament for the ruling party, paid at least €300,000, some carried across the Greek border in cash, to more than a dozen politicians from several parties, nationalist groups and football hooligans ahead of protests in which a petrol bomb was thrown at parliament; he denied funding the protests. Leaked counter-intelligence files from 2017 say a Serbian intelligence officer at Serbia's embassy gave instructions to an MP in the ruling coalition and that Russian intelligence officers tried to recruit army and interior ministry staff.

The justice system has been bought from inside as well. The Special Prosecution Office, set up to pursue high-level crime after a wiretapping scandal, was compromised when a television personality close to its head sold the country's richest man milder treatment in his case; in 2020 a court jailed him for bribing her and jailed her for misuse of office. Separately, the foreign minister joined the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders network in 2025, which is lawful and shows no decision taken for it.

The Global Organized Crime Index gives North Macedonia a fairly high score for officials working for criminal or outside interests and middling strength in its courts and watchdogs. For people in North Macedonia this means a decision about their country's name and alliances was contested with foreign money paid to their own politicians, and the office created to prosecute the powerful was itself for sale.

Palau.d:
The record for Palau, a Pacific island country that hosts US airstrips and radar sites, is one allegation from a foreign government, so it can show only what the United States says happened and what the accused man answers.

In February 2026 the US State Department barred Hokkons Baules, president of Palau's Senate, and his family from entering the United States, saying he accepted bribes for supporting 'government, business, and criminal interests from China'. Reuters reported in 2025 that three Palauan officials said Baules phoned a customs officer after a Chinese investor allegedly arrived with $119,000 in undeclared cash; Baules said he did not recall that. He denies wrongdoing, says he was accused because he helped Chinese investors, and says Palau's authorities could charge him if they have evidence. China called Reuters's claims fabricated.

For people in Palau, this means the head of one chamber of their legislature stands accused by a foreign government of taking money from Chinese interests while helping to make their laws, and the record shows no charge or court ruling that has tested the claim.

Peru.d:
In Peru, money from builders has reached the presidency and the transport ministry, and criminal networks have bought people inside the offices that keep the country's records, grant its pardons, guard its ports and store its weapons.

Public works are where the money has gone deepest. Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction group, paid former president Toledo about $35 million for the contract to build the Interoceanic Highway, and he has been sentenced over it. Peruvian firms have done the same at home: prosecutors say a cartel of construction companies paid transport ministry officials so that 30 public works went to its members, four of the firms have admitted responsibility, and in 2025 another former president, Martín Vizcarra, was convicted of taking money from two builders while a regional governor; he is appealing.

Lower down, staff of the national property registry rewrote the recorded owners of disputed land, officials of the board advising the president on pardons sold early release to traffickers, cocaine groups were reported to pay security staff and dockworkers at Callao, and an army lieutenant is accused of supplying rifle ammunition to Ecuadorian gangs. Police disciplinary records from 2019 to 2024 show 96 officers implicated in 37 cases of helping illegal gold miners, with only six ending in sanctions fully upheld. Unnamed witnesses on television made similar claims about a later national police chief, which he rejects and which are unverified. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Peru high for officials working for criminal interests.

For Peruvians this means they have paid for roads, irrigation and hospitals awarded in return for bribes, a land title has been changed for whoever paid the registrar, traffickers have bought early release, and police have been accused of warning illegal miners of raids.

Qatar.d:
Qatar's documented cases run in two directions: foreign arms makers paying the officials who buy for its armed forces, and Qatar's own money reported to have reached inside another country's government.

The clearest case is in arms buying. The US Justice Department found that Raytheon, the American missile maker now part of RTX, paid at least $2 million from 2012 to 2016 through sham contracts with a company owned by the official who ran procurement for the Qatar Emiri Air Force, and won additions to an air-defence contract in return; RTX agreed in 2024 to pay a $252 million criminal penalty for the bribery. Going the other way, Israeli prosecutors are investigating aides of the Israeli prime minister over money reported to have come from Qatar to promote its image from inside his office.

Qatar's residents have no elected body able to ask how state money is spent, whether on weapons at home or on influence abroad, and the air-force case came to light only through a US prosecution. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Qatar fairly high for officials working for criminal or outside interests.

Samoa.d:
No case of outside groups paying or placing officials in Samoa is documented yet, so this account is an estimate based on general conditions. The only outside organisation recorded as present is Shincheonji Church of Jesus, a South Korean religious movement, and its presence is lawful and not evidence of wrongdoing.

The Global Organized Crime Index places Samoa in its low band, scoring it low for officials working for criminal or outside interests and in the middle range for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. Neighbouring Pacific states have seen bribes for business deals, and small island governments with few investigators are the kind of place where such pressures can go unnoticed.

For residents, the absence of cases means there is no specific harm to point to, not that none exists. The bodies that would bring such cases to light, the courts, police and audit office, are the ones whose middling scores leave that question open.

Senegal.d:
In Senegal the one documented claim of an outside group getting inside the state concerns a drug ring and the police. In 2013 the country's anti-drug chief accused his predecessor, by then national police chief, of having worked with a drug ring while he ran the anti-drug office. The police chief was removed, but an inquiry found no evidence, and the claim remains contested.

It does not show a pattern, and no other case on the map shows a foreign state, crime group or company getting its people or money inside a Senegalese public body.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Senegal in the middle range both for officials working for criminal interests and for the strength of its courts and watchdogs. For Senegalese, this means the officials they deal with are rated as neither often nor rarely acting for criminal interests, and the one serious accusation against a police chief was investigated and not upheld.

Singapore.d:
Singapore appears on the map mainly as a base from which other governments are reached. For years a Singapore ship-supply firm run by Leonard Francis bribed US Navy officers with cash, travel and gifts for ship schedules and inside information, while a civilian Navy contracting officer in Singapore stopped an early inquiry; US prosecutors charged 33 people.

At home, the government treats foreign influence, most often linked to China, as something that works through ordinary community life: business chambers, clan and grassroots associations and universities. Its response is to name the people it believes are being used, and it does this by ministerial decision, not by trial. Since 2024 a foreign-interference law lets it designate residents, so far a business-chamber leader who had attended a Chinese Communist Party united front body, and make them report each year their political donations and foreign ties.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 1.5 out of 10, among the lowest in the world, and courts and watchdogs at about 7.8. For residents this means the bribery on record ran through a local firm into a foreign navy rather than into their own government, while people who lead community or business groups with ties to China can be publicly named and made to disclose their links without the evidence being tested in court.

Somalia.d:
In Somalia the outside force reaching furthest into the state is al-Shabaab, the al-Qaeda-linked armed Islamist group fighting the federal government, which places its own people inside the government it is trying to overthrow. Its members take public jobs, sometimes under false names, to collect information for taxing businesses and choosing targets, and in 2019 a woman working under a false name in the Mogadishu mayor's office blew herself up at a meeting there, killing the mayor and other officials. In 2023 the national intelligence agency said it had arrested ten al-Shabaab spies inside government agencies in Mogadishu, and opposition parties have urged the president to purge the agency itself.

Its reach extends to the systems that carry money and goods. UN monitors reported that it got inside the institutions running Mogadishu's port and used cargo manifests to tax importers, and that it moved funds through a mobile-money company, two of whose staff were prosecuted over a 2017 truck bomb. Monitors also reported government commanders supplying ammunition that reached the group, and in 2014 alleged that a man they called a presidential adviser steered state weapons to it, which he and the president denied.

Foreign states compete at the top as well: from 2019 to 2021 the intelligence agency was run by a former reporter for Qatar's state-funded Al Jazeera, whom Somali media and analysts accuse of channelling Qatari money and interests into government, which Qatar denies.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 8 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 1.9. For people in Somalia that means paying tax twice, to the government and to the group fighting it, and working in offices where a colleague may be passing on who should be taxed or killed.

Sri Lanka.d:
In Sri Lanka three kinds of outside force are documented inside the state: organised crime, which is accused of buying officers in the army and police; foreign companies paying the heads of state enterprises; and a Buddhist nationalist movement, whose leader was given a hand in writing the law.

The crime side came to light in 2025, when the gang leader Kehelbaddara Padme was returned from Indonesia with four associates. Investigators say his network had people across the security forces, with army officers detained over allegedly selling firearms and ammunition to the gang and a police sub-inspector arrested over close ties to him. The public security minister said police and immigration officials helped the gang obtain forged passports.

A UK settlement with Airbus described a US$2 million bribery arrangement through a firm in the name of the wife of the chief executive of SriLankan Airlines during a 2013 aircraft sale. Sri Lanka's bribery commission alleges money went on to the Rajapaksa family; the son it names denies it, and that part is unproven. In 2021 President Gotabaya Rajapaksa put Gnanasara, leader of Bodu Bala Sena ('Buddhist Power Force'), a monks' group accused of stirring violence against Muslims, in charge of a task force to draft a single legal code, work the Bar Association said belonged to Parliament and the Justice Ministry.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 7 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 3.7. For people in Sri Lanka this means guns from army officers and passports obtained with officials' help may have reached a gang, the state airline's aircraft deal involved a bribe, and Muslims and other minorities saw their law being drafted by a cleric whose group was accused of violence against them.

Sudan.d:
In Sudan armed and political movements have repeatedly taken over the state from inside. The longest-running is the Islamist movement derived from the Muslim Brotherhood. Led by Hassan al-Turabi, it spent the decade after he became attorney general in 1979 placing members in high posts, took power through army officers in 1989, and under Omar al-Bashir filled state jobs with its own people. A committee set up after Bashir fell in 2019 began removing them, but after the army's coup of 2021 a special court reinstated scores of officials in the central bank, the judiciary, the prosecution service and the foreign ministry.

Since the war between the army and the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary began in 2023, the Islamists have gone back inside the army itself. Military sources said thousands of men from Bashir's former intelligence service, with ties to the movement, joined the army, the US says one Islamist brigade has supplied more than 20,000 fighters, and the army chief relies on Islamist backing.

Armed Darfur movements entered by another door: a 2020 peace deal gave them about a quarter of the cabinet, and one rebel leader has run the finance ministry since 2021, staffing it with his movement's members.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 8.5 out of 10 and courts, police and watchdogs at about 2.3. For people in Sudan, this means the courts, the central bank and the ministries that handle their money are staffed by the appointees of movements rather than chosen for the job, officials removed for their party ties can be put back by a court after a coup, and the army fighting the war is partly run by a movement that the US says has obstructed a ceasefire.

Syria.d:
Syria's state was taken over in the 1960s by a closed group that built its own structure first. The Military Committee, a secret body of army officers formed in 1958 and hidden even from their own Ba'ath party's leaders, used army units to carry out the 1963 coup and held the real power inside the new government. One of its founders, Hafez al-Assad, seized power in 1970, and he and his son Bashar ruled until December 2024.

That ruling circle was itself reached from outside. By 1965 Israel's Mossad had planted an agent, Eli Cohen, under a false identity among Syria's leaders, where he heard officials discuss army plans and reported them to Israel.

The Global Organized Crime Index gave Assad's Syria 10 out of 10 for state-embedded crime and about 2 for courts and watchdogs. For people in Syria, this meant decades of rule by a group that had organised in secret inside the army, with police and courts that answered to it rather than to them, and no independent court or elected body able to hold it to account.

Thailand.d:
In Thailand criminal businesses reach into the state mainly through the police, who have been accused of selling protection to gambling, drug and visa rackets. In 2023 the deputy national police chief was removed and investigated over alleged protection of an online gambling network, splitting the police leadership in public.

Chinese crime groups in Thailand have used the same route, and local government too. In a crackdown that began in late 2022, investigators charged at least 80 immigration police, three of them generals, with demanding bribes over visas issued to about 5,000 Chinese nationals. A linked case against a Chinese businessman ended in his acquittal in 2025 for insufficient evidence, though six officers had been dismissed over links to him. Investigators allege that district chiefs and village headmen took bribes to grant citizenship to Chinese nationals, and a newsletter's claim that scam networks paid a deputy finance minister's wife led to his resignation; he denies it and is suing.

Foreign companies have paid for state business through middlemen. Rolls-Royce's 2017 British settlement described about US$36 million paid to intermediaries, some reaching state airline staff and agents of the state, though a Thai court dismissed the resulting case for weak evidence. A Japanese court case showed a power-equipment maker's executives paying a transport official 11 million baht.

Groups outside the elected system have also decided who holds power: the People's Party, founded by Siamese students in Paris, ended absolute monarchy with army units in 1932, and the army's habit of coups dates from then. The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime at 7 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at about 5. For people in Thailand, the officer or district chief who decides on a visa, a card or a complaint may be working for the businesses involved.

Trinidad and Tobago.d:
In Trinidad and Tobago the documented reach-in has come through people holding public posts while serving outside interests: contractors on the country's largest public works, an international sports body, and now armed gangs. The clearest case is the new terminal at Piarco International Airport, built in the late 1990s: contractors, led by a Miami engineering firm, worked with the then finance minister to rig bids and charge inflated prices. In 2023 a Miami jury found the former minister and two businessmen liable for racketeering and fraud, awarding the country US$131.3 million. Jack Warner, meanwhile, was a vice-president of FIFA, world football's governing body, while he served as works minister and then national security minister until 2013; US prosecutors later charged him with taking bribes in his football roles, charges never tried because Trinidad's High Court blocked his extradition in 2025.

The gangs reach in through the prisons. When the government declared a state of emergency in July 2025 over a plot, hatched by jailed gang leaders, to kill public officials, it detained a prison superintendent it said had used his post to get contraband to the plotters and support the gangs' leaders inside.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores both officials acting for criminal interests and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 5 out of 10. For people in Trinidad and Tobago this means the airport they paid for cost far more than it should have because their finance minister was working with the contractors, that the minister once responsible for their police was also an officer of a body later accused of selling votes, and that gang leaders the state has locked up can still plan killings with help from the officers guarding them.

Tuvalu.d:
No case of outside groups paying or placing officials in Tuvalu is documented, so this account is an estimate based on conditions. Tuvalu is a nation of about 11,000 people on low-lying atolls, and its government depends heavily on foreign aid and on agreements with larger partners. Elsewhere in the Pacific, payments for business deals have drawn smaller states into larger powers' rivalries; none of this is documented in Tuvalu.

The Global Organized Crime Index places Tuvalu in its Minimal band, scoring officials acting for criminal interests at 1.5 out of 10 and courts, police and watchdogs at 5.9. For Tuvaluans this means there is no known current harm from hidden outside influence. The risk is that a country this small has only a handful of officials, auditors and police, so if an outside interest did reach in, there would be few people in a position to notice it.

United Kingdom.d:
In Britain outsiders reach in through foreign intelligence services recruiting inside the state, fraternities placing members in office, paramilitary and far-right groups entering the security forces, companies entering the departments that regulate them, and crime groups buying port staff. Soviet intelligence had agents inside MI6, MI5 and the Foreign Office last century; today China and Iran are most active. MI5 says a solicitor working covertly with China's United Front gave donations to an MP.

In Northern Ireland every prime minister from 1921 to 1969 belonged to the Orange Order, a Protestant fraternity. Loyalist paramilitaries drew on the security forces for men and information: a 1973 army estimate put up to 15% of a local regiment in loyalist groups, and a government review reported a 1985 MI5 assessment that 85% of the intelligence held by the UDA, a loyalist group, came from security force sources, while finding no overarching state conspiracy. Neo-Nazi National Action tried to grow inside the army, and a serving corporal was convicted of belonging to it. In England, a detective has said Masonic officers took him off an inquiry that pointed to the lodges.

Firms have paid MPs to lobby, the big accountants lend tax staff to the Treasury to help draft law they then advise on, and a Conservative peer pushed her husband's firm through the pandemic contracts 'VIP lane'. At the ports, cocaine importers recruit port security guards and Border Force officers to pass their vans and couriers.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials serving criminal interests at 3 out of 10 and courts at 7.6. For Britons, this means rules drafted or enforced by those they apply to, drugs passing checkpoints staffed by a gang's recruits, and, in Northern Ireland, families still seeking inquiries into killings in which soldiers and police took part.

Vanuatu.d:
No case of outside groups placing people inside Vanuatu's government or paying its officials is documented, so this account is an estimate based on general conditions.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests in Vanuatu at 3 out of 10, a low score, but scores its courts, police and watchdogs at only 4.9, in the middle of the range. That means experts judge that officials are not often working for criminal or outside interests, but that the bodies meant to catch it if they were are only moderately able to do so.

For ni-Vanuatu, as the country's people are called, the absence of cases means there is no named official or company to hold to account, not proof that none exists. With courts and watchdogs in the middle of the range, it would take time for any hidden outside influence on officials to come to light.

Yemen.d:
Yemen's case on the map is a neighbouring government paying Yemen's own leaders. A Saudi government body, the 'Special Committee', kept about 2,700 Yemeni political, tribal and military leaders on monthly pay, as records from 2012 show, and directed named sheikhs and a serving brigade commander, so people holding Yemeni office and command were also answering to Riyadh.

Yemen has been at war since 2014, and its state has split. In the north, the Houthi movement, a Zaydi Shia armed group, took over the capital Sanaa and its state institutions in 2014–15 and still rules most of Yemen's population through its own council. In the south, the internationally recognised state is run by the commanders of the forces fighting the Houthis, several of them backed by Saudi Arabia or the UAE.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Yemen's courts, police and watchdogs at 1.9 out of 10 and officials acting for criminal interests at 8. For Yemenis, this means the sheikhs and commanders who decide local matters may be paid by a foreign government, and there is no court or police force they can turn to when an armed group takes their land or money.

Algeria.d:
In Algeria the documented reach-in comes from two directions: foreign firms paying officials for state contracts, and the cocaine trade buying protection inside the security state. Contractors have worked on the public works ministry and Sonatrach, the state oil and gas company, through agents. The clearest example is the East-West motorway, begun in 2006 by Japanese and Chinese consortia: in 2015 an Algiers court jailed an adviser to the Chinese group, a former director of highways and other ministry staff over kickbacks on the project, whose cost rose from $6 billion to at least $13 billion. Bribery charges brought in Italy against a foreign oil-services firm over Sonatrach contracts ended in acquittal, but Algeria's energy minister from 1999 to 2010 was later sentenced in absentia to 20 years for corruption.

The cocaine trade reached into the police. When 701 kilograms of cocaine were found at the port of Oran in 2018, hidden in a cargo of imported meat, press reports tied the importer to judges, prosecutors, mayors and the children of senior politicians. The seizure brought down the head of the national police, and he and several generals were later convicted of corruption and illicit enrichment rather than drug offences; Algeria has published little about who protected the shipments.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Algeria 7.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and about 4 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For Algerians, this means public money for roads and energy has passed through officials who took a share, while the officials who let cocaine through a state port have not been named in court, and residents cannot tell whether they are still in post.

Argentina.d:
Argentina's state has more than once been run from inside by secret circles. Officers' lodges made and unmade the first governments after 1812 and, by most historians' account, organised the 1943 coup behind Juan Perón's rise. In the 1970s P2, a secret Masonic lodge run from Italy, listed an interim president, ministers, a junta member and generals among its members, and they gave its grand master a diplomatic post.

Since the 1990s the route has run more through business and money. A team of economists from a business-funded think tank took over the economy ministry in 1991, and its programme ended in frozen savings and the 2001 collapse. Firms have paid for state business under governments of left and right: a German engineering company admitted paying more than $100 million in bribes for a national identity-card contract, and in the notebooks case 87 people, including former president Cristina Fernández de Kirchner, who denies it, are on trial over contractors' cash allegedly paid to officials. Other charges concern insurance commissions steered to a president's circle and, under the current government, kickbacks at the disability agency, which the accused deny.

Crime reaches police, courts and city halls. Around Rosario, drug and gambling bosses have had a provincial police chief, detectives who warned of raids and the city's chief prosecutor on their side. In Paraná a court found that a drug clan financed the winning mayor's campaign and was then given control of a municipal unit, which he denied. Federal judges, who hear drug cases, have been convicted of selling traffickers rulings or house arrest. For people in these places, the detective, prosecutor or judge may be on the gangs' side, and money for disabled people's medicines is alleged to have gone to people close to those spending it.

Azerbaijan.d:
Azerbaijan's economy rests on oil and gas, and the state oil company, SOCAR, is closely bound up with the government. Outsiders have got in by sharing state wealth with the officials who control it, or with people close to them. In the late 1990s foreign investors trying to buy SOCAR in a privatisation they expected to be rigged made senior Azerbaijani officials their secret partners, promising them two-thirds of the profits. French investigators determined that a French rail engineering firm won its Baku metro contract corruptly, paying about 30 per cent of its invoices from 2009 to 2017 to an agent with close access to the minister in charge, and the firm settled in France.

The oil sector and Azerbaijani money have also reached outward, into international bodies that set rules for them. When Azerbaijan hosted the UN climate summit, COP29, in 2024, its president had been a SOCAR vice-president, and its chief executive was secretly filmed discussing oil and gas deals with campaigners posing as investors. An inquiry for the Council of Europe's parliamentary assembly, Europe's human rights body, reported in 2018 a strong suspicion that some members had acted for Azerbaijan in return for money or gifts, known as caviar diplomacy.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Azerbaijan 8.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 4 for its courts, police and watchdogs. For people living there, oil wealth and public works budgets that belong to the country have been treated as something to share privately with foreign firms, and most of what is known came from abroad. For people elsewhere whose coasts and harvests depend on emissions falling, the talks on phasing out oil and gas were chaired by people from the industry that sells them.

Barbados.d:
Barbados has one documented case of an outside party reaching into its government, and it came from a company seeking state business rather than from organised crime or a foreign state. Senior executives of the Insurance Corporation of Barbados Limited paid the island's Minister of Industry, Donville Inniss, about $36,000 in 2015 and 2016 to help the company win two government insurance contracts covering more than $100 million of state property. The money went through a US bank account in the name of a friend's dental company in New York, which is why a US jury, not a Barbadian court, convicted him of money laundering in 2020; he was sentenced to two years in prison.

No other case of a foreign government, company, crime group or lodge placing people or money inside the state remains on this map. The Global Organized Crime Index gives Barbados 3 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests, low by world standards, and about 6.1 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, better than most of the Caribbean. Barbados is also an offshore financial centre that registers international companies, the kind of business that can draw outside money.
