For Barbadians, this means a minister used his office to steer the insurance of public property to a company that paid him, and the case came to light only because the money passed through the United States. The likeliest places for outside money to reach in are the ones this case shows: who wins public contracts, who funds politicians and who owns the companies registered on the island.

Benin.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Benin, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case found so far shows a foreign state, company, criminal group or lodge paying or placing people inside its government. Two French Masonic bodies, the Grand Orient de France and the Grande Loge Nationale Française, are thought to have members in Benin but are not documented.

Benin is a coastal West African state whose port at Cotonou handles goods for its larger neighbour, Nigeria, and for landlocked states to the north, so much of the trade that crosses it belongs to outsiders. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Benin 6 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 3.8 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. That combination describes officials under real pressure and weak checks on them.

For people living there, this means that if outside interests are paying or placing officials, it is likely to show up in port and customs work, public contracts and policing, and residents would pay through lost public revenue and weaker protection. With no named case, there is no official or company they can yet challenge.

Botswana.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Botswana, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case found so far shows a foreign state, company, criminal group, church or lodge paying or placing people inside its government, and no outside organisation is recorded as present.

Botswana's economy rests on diamonds, mined mainly through a long-standing partnership between the government and the De Beers company, and on that kind of single, valuable export outside interests often seek influence. Against that, the Global Organized Crime Index scores Botswana 4.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 5.4 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. That puts it in the middle of the range and ahead of most of its neighbours. The lack of cases may also reflect limited investigative reporting.

For people living there, this means there is no named official or company to hold to account, and no evidence that public decisions are being bought. If a case exists, it would most likely surface through mining and other licences, public contracts or policing of the borders, and those are the records residents would need to see.

Burkina Faso.d:
No documented case in Burkina Faso yet meets the map's test, which asks for an outside party that got its people, money or control inside a government body or company and had decisions there serve it. This entry is an estimate.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Burkina Faso high for officials working for criminal interests, and very weak in the courts, police and watchdogs that would check them. On those scores, a criminal group or foreign interest trying to place people inside the state, or to buy officials already there, would meet little resistance at home, and the record of it would be thin. The country has been under military government since 2022, and nothing here reaches into that government.

Cameroon.d:
No documented case in Cameroon yet meets the map's test, which asks for an outside party that got its people, money or control inside a government body or company and had decisions there serve it. This entry is an estimate.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Cameroon among the countries where officials most often work for criminal interests, and rates its courts, police and watchdogs as weak. On those scores, an outside group that paid officials or placed its own people in a ministry or state company would be unlikely to be traced by Cameroon's own institutions, and any such case would more likely come to light through reporting or courts abroad. Paul Biya has held the presidency since 1982, so an inquiry would also have to start from inside a government that has not changed hands in that time.

Chile.d:
In Chile, outsiders have reached the state through three routes: foreign intelligence money during the Cold War, companies paying the officials who write laws, collect taxes and decide court cases, and crime groups buying the officers who police them.

Between 1963 and 1973 the CIA spent about $13 million on Chilean parties, candidates and a newspaper, and under General Pinochet it kept the head of the secret police as a paid contact.

Since the return to democracy the money has come mostly from companies, and it has reached each branch of the state. A holding group used employees inside the tax service to help pass campaign money through fake invoices, and a lawyer's business clients had bribes paid to officials of the tax service and the Treasury, some of whom have since been convicted. A fishing company paid a senator, later jailed for bribery, who voted its way on the 2012 fisheries law that handed a large share of the national catch to companies controlled by a few families. In 2026 a Supreme Court justice was detained, accused of taking money from a Belarusian-Chilean mining-truck consortium over a ruling in which her chamber ordered Codelco, the state copper company, to pay the consortium $20 million rather than the reverse.

As Chile has become a drug transit route, the buying has reached the police and prisons: national police officers have been charged with reselling seized drugs and protecting dealers, and in 2025 about a tenth of the guards at Santiago's main remand prison were charged with smuggling drugs and phones to gangs held there. For Chileans this means laws, tax checks and court rulings that can be bought by the firms they concern, and in some places officers who work for the groups they guard.

Congo, Dem. Rep..d:
Congo has been reached from outside in two ways: by neighbouring armies and the armed groups they back, and by foreign companies paying for its mines and state contracts. In the 1960s the CIA paid Joseph Mobutu, who went on to rule until 1997. After a Rwandan-backed rebellion ended his rule, a Rwandan officer served as chief of staff of Congo's army, and a later rebel group was folded into that army.

The live case is M23, a rebel force that took the eastern cities of Goma and Bukavu in 2025. UN sanctions monitors report that Rwanda's army commands it and that Rwandans have been put in charge of mining, tax, banking and border control; Rwanda denies it. Kinshasa says the reach goes into its own state: military courts have sentenced to death a sitting MP who owned a coltan mine and, in his absence, Joseph Kabila, president until 2019, and a former eastern commander is on trial for treason. All three deny it, and reports from the general's trial say the prosecution has struggled to prove contact with Rwanda.

Companies use intermediaries. US authorities say a commodity trader and a New York hedge fund sent money through third parties to reach Congolese officials and win mining business; both settled. A French settlement covers commissions allegedly paid to officials around the state power company, and a Belgian identity-document firm, presumed innocent, has been sent to trial over the passport contract.

For people in the east, the governors and tax collectors over them have been appointed by a group that UN monitors say a foreign army commands. Across Congo, money from mines and state contracts has gone to insiders, and the Global Organized Crime Index rates the country among the worst in the world for officials working for criminal interests.

Croatia.d:
Croatia's documented cases show companies reaching the state through the people at the top of government, to win control of national assets or public money. The clearest is the national oil company, INA. MOL, a Hungarian oil company in which the Hungarian state has influence, wanted to run it, and Croatian courts found that Prime Minister Ivo Sanader took a 10 million euro bribe from MOL's chief executive to give it that control. MOL denies the bribe, and Hungary has not handed the executive over to Croatia.

The pattern continues in health. In 2024 the health minister was arrested and sacked, accused of taking bribes from a group selling medical equipment to approve hospital purchases at inflated prices; prosecutors say tenders were fixed at least four times, two hospital directors are among those charged, and the minister denies it.

For Croatians, the national oil company they part-own is still managed by the firm the courts found paid their prime minister for that control, and hospitals may have paid more for equipment because the minister in charge was paid by the sellers, money that would otherwise have gone on patients. Croatian courts can punish the officials who take the money but not always those who pay it: the MOL executive lives in another EU country that will not send him back, which leaves the harmed country able to try its own politicians while the company and its managers stay out of reach.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Croatia in the middle range for officials working for criminal interests and for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. The courts have reached a former head of government, though it took most of a decade.

Denmark.d:
Very little outside reach into the Danish state or Danish companies is documented on the map, and what there is comes from two directions: a foreign spy service working through an insider, and a business-led network at the head of state.

Russian intelligence has paid people working inside Denmark to collect information. In the clearest case, a Russian man employed by a Danish fuel cell maker spent several years gathering information on energy technology from that company and from the Technical University of Denmark and passing it to Russian intelligence for money; a court in Aalborg sentenced him in 2021 to three years in prison and permanent expulsion. Russia called the case a witch hunt.

King Frederik X is listed among alumni of the World Economic Forum's Young Global Leaders programme, which he joined as crown prince. The Forum is the Swiss-based organisation behind the annual Davos meeting of business and political leaders, and its programme gathers people under about 40 into a five-year network of meetings and courses. The king's role is ceremonial, so the membership does not show the Forum deciding anything for Danes, only that its network reaches the office that formally heads the state.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Denmark among the very lowest countries in the world for officials working for criminal interests, and among the strongest for its courts, police and watchdogs. For Danes, this means the officials they deal with are unlikely to be working for criminal or foreign interests, and the documented risk sits with the research and energy firms that foreign intelligence wants to learn from.

Ecuador.d:
Ecuador sits between the two largest cocaine-producing countries, Colombia and Peru, and its Pacific ports have become one of the main exits for cocaine bound for Europe and the United States. The gangs that run this trade pay the officials at each point the drugs, the money and their own members pass through. At the coast they recruit port workers and customs officers so that cocaine hidden in banana shipments leaving Guayaquil passes inspection, and at the Peruvian border soldiers have allegedly been paid to wave smuggling convoys through. Inland they buy judges, prosecutors, the staff of prosecutors' offices, police commanders and prison staff, so that members are released, cases are delayed and the gangs learn what investigators know. Since 2023 investigations have traced this reach inside courts and prisons; decrypted messages on one trafficker's phone led to the conviction of 20 people, among them the former head of the council that oversees Ecuador's judges.

Foreign companies and businessmen reach in through the money. Oil traders, contractors and builders from abroad have paid officials at Petroecuador, the state oil company, and in the ministries above it to win and keep contracts, and US courts have convicted several people involved. The bribes have reached two vice-presidents: one now in prison, and another, later president, charged over a Chinese-built dam, which he denies.

For people in Ecuador a court ruling or a release may have been bought, and the soldiers, port staff, police and prosecutors' clerks around them may be on a gang's payroll, while the bribes came out of the oil money and loans that pay for schools, hospitals and power. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials working for criminal interests at 7.5 out of 10, with the courts and watchdogs meant to resist them at under 4.5.

Eritrea.d:
This is an estimate: no case on the map names a foreign government, company or criminal group placing or paying people inside Eritrea's government. Eritrea has been governed by one party, the People's Front for Democracy and Justice, since independence in 1993, has held no national election in that time and has no independent press, so very little can be checked from outside.

What reporting there is points to criminal business run from inside the state rather than reaching in from outside. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 9.5 out of 10, one of the highest scores in the world, and says military officers and ruling-party members dominate smuggling of people, gold, alcohol, tobacco and counterfeit goods, much of it across the border with Sudan, and that officials involved are rarely prosecuted. A 2013 report presented at the European Parliament said the army's border surveillance unit took part in smuggling Eritreans into Sudan, where thousands are reported to have died in captivity.

If that picture is right, Eritreans who try to leave the country pay the same officers who are meant to guard the border, and money from gold and trade ends up in private hands. The strength of courts and watchdogs scores 2.2 out of 10, and there is no independent body inside the country where a resident could take a complaint.

Fiji.d:
Fiji sits on the shipping and air routes that carry methamphetamine and cocaine across the Pacific to Australia and New Zealand, and traffickers moving those drugs have got inside its police and customs. The minister for policing told parliament in 2025 that 27 police officers had been involved in 33 drug cases since the start of 2023. Two officers of the counter-narcotics unit and a senior customs manager were among seven people charged with helping methamphetamine through Nadi airport in air cargo, and the unit was later disbanded. Leaked chats published in late 2025 appeared to show senior officers discussing drug shipments and payments with traffickers; the police commissioner confirmed that seven senior officers were under investigation, and the claims have not been tested in court.

Business money has also tried to reach officials. Two men from a Chinese company in Fiji pleaded guilty in 2010 to offering the top civil servant in the finance ministry money and tea for help with a water project; both received prison terms. The anti-corruption commission has more recently charged a businessman with earlier drug and trafficking convictions with bribing officials of the iTaukei Land Trust Board, which manages land owned by Fiji's indigenous people; the outcome of that trial could not be confirmed.

For people in Fiji, the officers responsible for stopping drugs at the airport and the border may be working for those bringing them in, and indigenous landowners face an allegation that the body handling their land was paid by a businessman. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 4 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at about 5.4, a middle position in which cases are being investigated and charged rather than ignored.

Gambia.d:
Under Yahya Jammeh, president from 1994 to 2017, The Gambia's state businesses were handed to a small circle around him, and part of that circle was tied to a foreign armed movement. Lebanese businessmen whom the United States designates as financiers of Hezbollah, the Lebanese Shia party and armed group, received state monopolies, including the national fuel supply and half of the state telephone companies. OCCRP, a network of investigative reporters, estimated that more than $100 million from Gambian telecoms reached Hezbollah.

For Gambians, this meant they paid for fuel and telephone calls through monopolies given to the president's associates, and some of that money left the country to fund a foreign armed group rather than reaching the treasury. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 7 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at about 5.

Greece.d:
Greece's record shows two lasting ways in: organised groups getting inside the armed forces, police and ports, and bankers buying their way into the state's finances. A secret society of army officers, IDEA, grew inside the army, and its members led the 1967 coup. More recently the neo-Nazi party Golden Dawn built support inside the police: after the May 2012 election, polling stations used by Attica police officers gave it just over 20 per cent of the vote against about 6 per cent at civilian stations nearby, and its leaders were convicted in 2020 of running a criminal organisation.

The reach into the uniformed services and ports goes on today. Foreign intelligence services recruit serving officers, among them an air force colonel charged in 2026 with passing NATO plans to Chinese handlers. Criminal groups recruit the people who control access: an Athens ring selling 'protection' to brothels, casinos and clubs had at least 11 police officers among its members, and cocaine networks, one allegedly led by an Albanian gang, have used workers at Piraeus, the largest port, to find and empty containers.

Money has been the other way in. A bank owner later said he had paid the prime minister and ministers, who in return had state companies deposit public money in his bank; two were convicted in 1992.

For people in Greece, this means migrants and opponents were policed by officers many of whom backed a criminal organisation, nightlife businesses in Athens paid a ring that included the police meant to protect them, and some of the workers handling cargo at the country's main port are accused of working for traffickers. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 7.5 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at about 5.1.

Guinea-Bissau.d:
Since the mid-2000s Guinea-Bissau, a small West African country with weak central control, has been a transit point for South American cocaine headed to Europe. The trafficking networks reached the commanders of the armed forces themselves. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, a research group, reports that Latin American trafficking cells were paying the military for protection by about 2006, that this protection went right to the top, and that senior military figures took control of bulk transit and kept a share of the profits, reportedly 13% to 15%. Those are the group's findings from its sources, with no court verdict behind them.

In 2013 US prosecutors charged the heads of the navy, the air force and the army with offering their positions to help move cocaine. The army chief, who had led a coup the year before, was also charged with offering to store cocaine for the FARC, the Colombian guerrilla army, and sell it weapons. Only the navy chief was caught, in a sting at sea; the other two stayed in Bissau and were never handed over.

The armed forces have repeatedly overthrown or threatened elected governments, so the people accused of taking traffickers' money are the same people who decide who governs. The reach also extends to the justice system: traffickers convicted over the country's largest cocaine seizure reportedly got out of prison on fake sick notes.

For people in Guinea-Bissau, this means the officers commanding their army, navy and air force have been accused of working for foreign traffickers, and those accused have remained free and in some cases in power. With the courts and watchdogs scoring under 2.7 out of 10 on the Global Organized Crime Index and officials acting for criminal interests at 8.5, the cases against them have been brought abroad.

Hungary.d:
Hungary's documented cases show foreign intelligence services working through Hungarians who hold European posts. Russia's services had a Hungarian member of the European Parliament working for them: Béla Kovács, elected for the nationalist party Jobbik, was convicted in Hungary in 2022 of spying on EU institutions for Russia and lives in Russia. Hungary's own intelligence service has used its position in Brussels in a similar way, with officers under diplomatic cover at Hungary's mission to the EU trying for years to recruit Hungarians employed at the European Commission, the EU's executive, a network the Commission has confirmed.

Both run through the same opening: Hungarians who hold seats or jobs in EU institutions have access to information and decisions that affect all 27 member states, which makes them worth recruiting for Moscow and for Budapest's own government. Hungary has also been on the receiving end of a foreign power placing its own people in charge. In October 1944 Nazi Germany detained the regent and installed the leader of the Arrow Cross, Hungary's fascist movement, as head of government; in under three months its death squads killed up to 38,000 Hungarian Jews.

Inside Hungary today, the Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 7.5 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at about 4.8, a weak position for an EU member. For people in Hungary, this means a representative they elected to the European Parliament was working for a foreign intelligence service, and Hungarians working in EU institutions have been targeted by their own country's spies, so decisions that affect their rights, funds and trade are taken with a foreign or partisan service listening in.

Iran.d:
In Iran the documented reach into the state has come above all from foreign intelligence services, along with foreign oil money. In 1953 the CIA, with British help, bribed members of parliament and organised the security forces to remove the elected prime minister, Mohammad Mossadegh, after he nationalised Iran's oil; the Shah then ruled as a US ally until the 1979 revolution.

Since the revolution, the agency Iran most often accuses of recruiting people inside its state is Israel's foreign intelligence service, Mossad. Iranian officials said in 2024 that Mossad had hired guards from the Revolutionary Guards unit that protects senior officials to plant the bombs that killed the Hamas leader Ismail Haniyeh in a Guards guesthouse in Tehran; Israel neither confirmed nor denied it. Iran has also hanged a nuclear institute scientist as a Mossad agent, without making the evidence public, and a former deputy defence minister as a British spy, a charge he said was extracted under torture.

The oil sector has also been reached with money. A Paris court convicted a French oil company in 2018 of corrupting foreign officials through about $30 million in disguised consulting payments connected to a deal on the South Pars gas field; prosecutors said much of it was meant for a former president's son, who then ran subsidiaries of the national oil company.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Iran 9.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and about 3 for the strength of its courts and watchdogs. For people in Iran this means no independent court or free press can examine which foreign services or companies have people inside the state, and anyone accused of spying is tried, and may be executed, by courts that are not independent of the government bringing the charge.

Italy.d:
Italy's mafias get inside the state mostly at the level of the town hall and the local health service. They supply votes to local politicians and in return take a say over public jobs, building contracts, permits and hospital services. Since 1991 the national government has dissolved town councils and local health authorities 402 times after finding them under mafia control, mostly in Calabria, Campania, Apulia and Sicily but also in the north and in Rome's own seaside district; in 2021 Foggia became the second provincial capital dissolved. In 2026 police said a Camorra clan ran the café, vending machines and private removal of the dead at a Naples public hospital with help from staff and administrators.

Companies and secret networks have reached further up. In the early 1990s the 'Mani pulite' inquiry found that firms paid the governing parties a cut of public works contracts, and at one point more than half of parliament was under indictment; in 2024 Liguria's governor took a plea deal over campaign money from a port tycoon seeking a terminal concession. In 1981 police seized the membership list of P2, a hidden Masonic lodge, naming dozens of members of parliament, serving ministers, nearly 200 senior military officers and the heads of all three intelligence services. Foreign services reach in as well: Russian military intelligence has paid a navy officer on the defence staff for classified documents.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Italy 7 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and above 6 for its courts and watchdogs. For people in southern Italy especially, their elected council can be replaced by commissioners for up to two years, and public works and hospital services can go to firms a clan controls.

Kazakhstan.d:
Kazakhstan's state draws most of its money from oil and gas, and nearly all the documented cases of outsiders reaching in run the same way: Western companies competing for the country's fields and pipelines paid consultants and agents, knowing the money would reach the Kazakh officials who decided who got the work. US and British settlements record a US oilfield services company and a British engineering group paying, or intending to pay, officials of the state oil company and of a pipeline venture owned by the Kazakh and Chinese governments.

US prosecutors charged in 2003 that an American adviser to President Nursultan Nazarbayev had moved about $20 million through Swiss accounts to the president and a former prime minister for Western firms' oil contracts. The adviser pleaded guilty only to a tax offence in 2010, so the bribery claims against Kazakh leaders were never proven in court. Kazakhstan itself now claims, in a confidential London arbitration, that foreign contractors bribed its officials to approve costs at the Karachaganak gas field; leaks say the panel accepted some of this, but no ruling has been published.

Evidence of a foreign state getting someone inside is thinner. In 2019 a China expert at a state-run institute, reported to advise on border talks, was jailed for treason. Media reports said he passed documents to China, but details were never published, he pleaded not guilty, and he was later pardoned.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Kazakhstan 6 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 5 for its courts, police and watchdogs. For people in Kazakhstan, this means the contracts for the oil and gas that fund their state have repeatedly been won by paying officials, and most of what is known comes from foreign prosecutors and leaks.

Korea, Rep..d:
In South Korea, three kinds of outside force have reached into politics and the state: religious movements, through gifts, cash and mass sign-ups to a party; business, through payments and deals with officials; and the spy services of North Korea and China, through recruits in parties and the armed forces. In 2026 the leader of the Unification Church, a Korean-founded movement, was sentenced for arranging luxury gifts for the first lady and cash for a senior lawmaker of the then-governing People Power Party; the church will appeal. Investigators say thousands of its followers and at least 56,000 from another movement, Shincheonji, joined that party. A minister from the rival Democratic Party resigned over similar cash claims, which he denies.

Samsung, the largest family-run business group, has been found by courts to have bribed two presidents' circles, and those convicted were later pardoned. Developers worked with a planning chief at a city-owned company to fix a housing project's terms, costing it about 490 billion won, a court found.

North Korea's ruling party has run cells that placed members in the leadership of a party with seats in the National Assembly. Both neighbours recruit in the military with cash, and the record reaches the bodies meant to catch them: an employee of military intelligence sold a Chinese agent the identities of undercover officers abroad, while two heads of its secret operations team and a counter-espionage officer have been accused of leaking secrets, with no reported verdict.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials working for outside interests at 4 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at 8. For South Koreans this means churches have sought influence through a first lady and a party's membership, and companies have bought favours from presidents and city officials, though courts have convicted many involved.

Laos.d:
No documented case in Laos yet meets the map's test, which asks whether an outside party got its people, money or control inside a government body, international body or company, and whether decisions there served it.

The best available estimate comes from the Global Organized Crime Index. It scores Laos 7.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 4 for the strength of its courts and watchdogs. Taken together, these scores point to a state where officials can work for criminal groups with little risk of being exposed, so the lack of a documented case may partly reflect how little is investigated.

For people in Laos this means there is no independent record to show whether the officials who govern them answer to someone else.

Liberia.d:
In Liberia, outside bodies have shaped how state money is spent, and traffickers have reached into the police. After the civil wars, international lenders reached directly into the state firms. Under a 2005 programme designed and funded by the IMF, the World Bank and the US government, foreign financial controllers sat inside the port authority, the main airport, the state oil refiner and the forestry agency with power to co-sign their major transactions, until signing authority returned to Liberian hands in 2009.

Today the documented pressure comes from cocaine traffickers using Liberia as a stop on the route from South America to Europe. After the country's largest recorded seizure in 2026, nearly four tonnes bound for Europe, police charged the head of their own major crimes unit, named a senior airport security officer as a participant, and said senior government officials were involved; these are charges, not convictions.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Liberia 7.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 4 for its courts and watchdogs. For Liberians this means that, if the charges hold, the police unit meant to fight serious crime and the officer guarding the main airport were working with traffickers, and they cannot rely on those offices to stop drugs passing through their country.

Luxembourg.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Luxembourg, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case found so far shows a foreign state, company, crime group or lodge paying officials or placing people inside its government.

The Global Organized Crime Index, which scores every country on how far its officials work for criminal or outside interests, rates Luxembourg among the lowest in the world on that measure. That means experts judge that officials there rarely act for criminal interests.

For people living there, this means no named official or company can be shown to be acting for an outside party, and the index suggests officials face less of this pressure than in most countries. If outside money did reach in, it would most likely show up in who funds politicians, who wins public contracts and who sits on the boards of companies the state regulates, and residents are best protected when those records are public.

Maldives.d:
The Maldives sits between India and China's shipping routes in the Indian Ocean, and the one recorded claim of an outside power reaching inside its politics comes from that rivalry. In December 2024 the Washington Post reported that Maldivian opposition politicians had planned to pay 40 members of parliament, including some from President Mohamed Muizzu's own party, to vote to impeach him, using about $6 million to be sought from India. Muizzu had won office promising to reduce India's influence. The paper said an officer of India's foreign intelligence agency explored ways to remove him through two intermediaries, who confirmed the plan existed. No money is reported to have been paid, Muizzu's coalition won a parliamentary majority in 2024, and a former president denied any Indian role.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates the Maldives in the middle range for how far officials work for criminal or outside interests, and rates its courts, police and watchdogs as fairly weak. Conditions like that usually mean some officials can be paid to serve business or criminal interests and the bodies meant to catch them have gaps.

For Maldivians, this means the members of parliament they elect have been treated, at least in planning, as votes a foreign-backed group could buy to remove their president. In daily life the weak institutions are more likely to show as bribes asked for ordinary services and state contracts going to favoured firms.

Mauritania.d:
No case has yet been documented of a foreign state, company or crime group paying Mauritanian officials or placing people inside the government, so this account is an estimate based on general conditions.

Mauritania lies on the route by which South American cocaine crosses the Sahara and the Sahel towards North Africa and Europe. The UN Office on Drugs and Crime reported in 2024 that across Mauritania and its Sahel neighbours, traffickers include members of the political elite and use their profits to get into state institutions and avoid prosecution, and Mauritania itself has made some of the largest cocaine seizures in the region. The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials there often serving criminal interests and rates its courts, police and watchdogs as weak.

If the estimate is right, the pressure would show most in policing and border control, and people in Mauritania would face traffickers who are protected by officials rather than stopped by them. Without a named case there is no official or company they can yet hold to account.

Moldova.d:
Moldova's courts, banks and elected offices have been used by outside money, most of it Russian, on a scale few countries match. In the scheme known as the Global Laundromat, Russian companies signed fake debts that Moldovan judges ordered paid into a Moldovan bank, moving tens of billions of dollars out of Russia; prosecutors later charged judges who approved them. In 2014 about $1 billion, roughly 12 percent of the country's economic output, vanished from three banks including the state savings bank, and a former prime minister was jailed for taking money to let a businessman's investors take control of it.

Russian money has also paid for political parties and candidates, and the accusations reach as high as the presidency. Igor Dodon, president from 2016 to 2020 and leader of the pro-Russian Socialist Party, was filmed saying his party received monthly funding from Russia and has been charged with high treason and illegal party financing; his trial is being restarted. Courts have banned a party for serving a foreign state's interests and sentenced a regional governor and a member of parliament for channelling undeclared money to that network in elections. The MP, who denies it, was sentenced in his absence. Prosecutors also say an assistant to Russia's military attaché ran the head of parliament's legal division and a senior border police officer at Chișinău airport; both are on trial for treason.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials in Moldova widely serving criminal interests. For Moldovans this means a court ruling could be bought by a foreign client, the savings they and the state held in the banks were taken with help from people running the government, and some of those they elected owed their campaigns to foreign money. If the charges against Dodon hold, that includes a president.

Morocco.d:
Morocco is one of the world's main producers of cannabis resin and lies on routes that carry cocaine across the Sahara and North Africa to Europe. Traffickers on these routes need officials and elected figures who can protect property, permits and shipments, and the record shows one network reaching them. A drug-trafficking network linked to a Malian trafficker known as the 'Escobar of the Sahara' drew Moroccan elected figures and security staff into its operation: in 2026 a Casablanca court jailed a former president of the Oriental regional council, a former member of parliament and the former president of the Wydad Casablanca football club, and gave shorter terms to local officials, security officers and gendarmes, a military police force, for helping drug lorries pass through. The case is under appeal.

The other documented case involves a foreign company. US regulators found that the German dialysis firm Fresenius bribed the chief kidney specialist at two state-owned military hospitals for about four years to win contracts there, and it paid a settlement covering Morocco and other countries in 2019.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials in Morocco often serving criminal interests. For Moroccans this means that, in the trafficking case, the court found the head of a regional council and gendarmes at the roadside working for traffickers rather than for the people who elected or employ them, and in the hospital case contracts were won by paying the hospitals' senior kidney doctor. These are the only two documented cases on the map for Morocco, so how far either pattern reaches beyond them is not shown by the record.

Nauru.d:
In Nauru, a small Pacific island state whose main export is phosphate, outside money arrives mainly from Australia, and it has reached the island's politicians through the two things Australia buys there: phosphate and the hosting of asylum seekers.

Australian businesspeople seeking phosphate deals have been prosecuted in Australia for paying Nauruan politicians; one Sydney businessman was jailed in 2018 for paying an MP and a minister, and a Gold Coast phosphate trader is still awaiting trial on a charge of conspiring to bribe them. The second channel is the asylum detention centre that Australia pays contractors to run on the island. In 2023 the Sydney Morning Herald and The Age reported that subcontracts worth millions went to firms tied to Nauru's leaders, with banking records showing suspect payments to the justice minister and to a company of a man who later became president. The reporters said they were not claiming the payments were bribes, the minister denies wrongdoing, and Australia's Home Affairs department had been warned of bribery allegations for more than a decade.

In a country this small, a few contracts from one foreign government make up a large share of the money in circulation, and the politicians who decide on them can also benefit from them.

For people in Nauru this means that phosphate, one of the few sources of national income, has been sold through deals prosecutors say were bought, cutting what reaches the public. Ministers who benefit from Australian contracts have a private reason to keep the detention centre open whatever residents want.

Nicaragua.d:
In Nicaragua the reach into the state has come from two very different directions: the United States in the past, and drug traffickers more recently. In 1911 and 1912 New York bankers, backed by Washington, lent Nicaragua money in return for its National Bank as collateral and a majority stake in the National Railway, while the US president appointed the collector of its customs. When the president they dealt with faced a revolt, US Marines landed, and they stayed, with one short break, until 1935. In the 1980s a foundation funded by the US Congress paid for opposition groups and the newspaper La Prensa, and Congress added more for the opposition campaign before the 1990 election, which the opposition won.

The recent cases point to traffickers reaching the bodies that issue identities and hand down sentences. In 2012 a court convicted a magistrate of the Supreme Electoral Council, which oversees elections, for giving members of the network of Alejandro Jiménez, known as El Palidejo, false identity cards; he got 17 years. Two years earlier the interior minister said she held a list of judges who had granted releases or shorter sentences to 1,000 traffickers, though the report names no judge, no payment has been proven, and leaked US cables alleging that the ruling Sandinista party took traffickers' money have no reply on record.

The Global Organized Crime Index gives Nicaragua one of the lowest scores in the world for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, and one of the highest for officials working for criminal or outside interests. For people in Nicaragua this means an official of the body that runs their elections has been shown to work for traffickers, and if others are doing so, there is little domestic power to examine it.

Norway.d:
Norway is one of the countries where outside forces have the least documented hold on government. The Global Organized Crime Index gives it one of the world's lowest scores for officials working for criminal interests.

The exceptions the record shows are foreign spy services recruiting people with access, and a drug importer working with the police. The spy cases run from the Cold War to today. The KGB had an agent in Arne Treholt, a Labour Party official who sat in fishing and Law of the Sea talks with the Soviet Union and became head of the Foreign Ministry's press department before his arrest in 1984 and conviction for treason. The same approach is still used on people with less senior posts but useful access: in 2025 an Oslo court convicted a Norwegian security guard at the US embassy who had sold Russian and Iranian intelligence the embassy's floor plans, security routines and the home addresses of diplomats and their families.

Inside the police, drug enforcement depends on officers handling informants with little outside oversight. Eirik Jensen ran the Oslo police narcotics section for years while helping an informant he managed bring around fourteen tonnes of hashish into the country, and was jailed for twenty-one years, the most senior police conviction of its kind in Scandinavia.

For Norwegians, this has meant that a man passing information to the KGB took part in their country's sea-boundary talks with the Soviet Union, that the unit meant to stop the drug trade in Oslo was protecting one of its suppliers, and that foreign services can still find a guard or clerk willing to sell what he sees at work. In each case the courts held the person to account.

Panama.d:
Panama's place in the record comes from its role as a corridor for ships, money and companies, and from the people who have paid their way into its government and its ports because of it. Its law firms set up companies for clients abroad, its free zone in Colón lets goods pass without entering customs, and its banks have held money for traffickers and rulers alike; each of these has drawn foreign buyers of influence.

Under military rule in the 1980s the state was rented out from the top. Manuel Noriega, the army commander who ran the country, took money from Colombia's Medellín cartel to make Panama a shipping platform for cocaine while also being paid as a CIA source.

The largest recent reach came from Odebrecht, the Brazilian construction group that admitted paying bribes across Latin America and Africa to win public contracts. It says it paid Panamanian officials during the 2009–2014 government, and the trial of more than 20 people, including a former president who joins by video from asylum abroad, opened in 2026. Lower down, trafficking groups recruit the people who check the roads and load the ships. A gang federation has paid police officers, including one who opened checkpoints and escorted its drug shipments, and in 2026 police arrested 26 workers at the Port of Balboa, at the canal's Pacific end, accused of hiding cocaine bound for Australia and Europe in refrigerated containers.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Panama high for officials working for criminal interests. For residents, public contracts and protection from the law have been on offer to the corridor's biggest users, Panamanians paid for the public works on which the bribes were earned, and the canal's own docks have been worked by staff on a trafficking network's side.

Philippines.d:
In the Philippines, the groups that reach into government are mostly the ones that can deliver cash: illegal gambling operators, the contractors who live off public works, and foreign firms and intelligence services seeking contracts or secrets.

Gambling money has bought protection and, at times, the police themselves. Operators of jueteng, an illegal numbers game, were accused of paying President Joseph Estrada 5 million pesos a month. From 2016 Chinese-run online gambling hubs were helped by brokers who paid immigration officers to wave Chinese workers through Manila's airport, and by allies placed in local office, including a mayor later found by a court to be a Chinese citizen; Congress banned the industry in 2025. In December 2025 prosecutors ordered charges against a businessman tied to cockfighting arenas and 21 others, 14 of them serving police officers, over the abduction of cockfight workers who went missing in 2021 and 2022; his defence calls the ruling unfair.

Public works are the largest channel today. In 2025 flood-control contractors told the Senate that lawmakers and public-works officials demanded 10 to 25 percent of each project as 'advance commissions', and the Speaker stepped down; US prosecutors also charge that executives of a voting-technology firm bribed the head of the elections commission for the 2016 vote-counting contract, which they deny, and Chinese intelligence has recruited analysts in the defence department, navy and coast guard for money.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores the Philippines high for officials working for criminal interests. For Filipinos this has meant flood defences skimmed by the people who approve them, towns run by officials whose loyalty was to a gambling compound, police officers accused of abducting people for a gambling network, and an election counted on machines bought, prosecutors allege, with a bribe.

Romania.d:
In Romania, the clearest documented case of a movement getting its people inside the state comes from 1940. That year the fascist Iron Guard was given the Interior Ministry, the Bucharest police and every county prefecture, the offices that run each county for the central government. Its men used that state power to kill opponents and Jews until the movement was expelled after a failed coup.

The case shows how a movement handed the police and local administration can turn them against the people they are meant to protect. No more recent case on the map shows a foreign state, crime group or company getting its people or money inside a Romanian public body and steering what it decided.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Romania in the middle range both for officials working for criminal interests and for the strength of its courts and watchdogs. For Romanians today, this means the record holds no documented case of their police or ministries working for an outside group, while the middling scores leave room for cases not yet found.

San Marino.d:
In San Marino, the documented reach into government comes from builders and bankers who paid politicians for the permits and licences they needed. In a state of about 34,000 people, a small number of politicians decide who may build and who may open a bank, and the courts have found that those decisions were bought.

In the case known as Conto Mazzini, named after an account held under the name 'Giuseppe Mazzini' at a Sammarinese bank, prosecutors showed that construction and banking entrepreneurs paid politicians, including former government ministers, with cash drawn from that account. About 200 million euros were seized, and an appeal court upheld most convictions in 2022.

For residents, it meant building permits and banking licences went to those who paid, while builders and bankers who did not pay competed against firms that had bought their approvals, and the buildings and banks approved that way are still part of daily life. It also shows the courts reaching former ministers.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores San Marino in the middle range both for officials working for criminal or outside interests and for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs.

Serbia.d:
In Serbia the reach into the state comes mostly from Belgrade's organised crime groups, and they work through the security services. Gangs with a share of the Balkan heroin, cocaine and cannabis trade have recruited or merged with police and intelligence units, which gives them state identity cards, entry to protected buildings and warning of investigations. The clearest case came in 2003, when a commander of the interior ministry's special operations unit, which had fused with the Zemun clan, shot dead the elected prime minister, Zoran Đinđić. Since then prosecutors have charged a gang that carried state security identification and a businessman close to the ruling party whose cannabis farm, they say, was guarded by police and intelligence officers; both trials are still open. A court has convicted a former deputy head of the organised-crime police of demanding the return of a seized car to an associate of that gang's leader.

The intelligence service has also been tied to Russia. In 2023 the US sanctioned the head of the Security Intelligence Agency (BIA), saying he helped Russia's activities in the region and supported a drug-trafficking network and illegal arms shipments; he resigned under Western pressure and became deputy prime minister the next year. Around the First World War, secret societies of army officers decided much of Serbian politics.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 8 out of 10, near the top of Europe, and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 4.9. For people in Serbia that means the units meant to protect them have been used by gangs, once against the government they had voted for, and the agency that guards the country's secrets has been run by a man a foreign government accuses of helping Russia and drug traffickers.

Slovakia.d:
In Slovakia businessmen and their fixers are accused of reaching into the police, courts, prosecution service and prime minister's office, and the public has mostly learned of it from journalists and leaks before any court acted. A leaked secret-service wiretap file published in 2011 reportedly recorded executives of a large investment group discussing kickbacks on privatisations with ministers, which the group called fiction.

The clearest picture came after journalist Ján Kuciak and his fiancée were shot dead in 2018. Prime Minister Robert Fico resigned after mass protests, and messages on the phone of the businessman later charged with ordering the murder showed judges and a deputy justice minister working for him. In 2020 police detained more than a dozen judges in two operations, among them the acting head of the Supreme Court, and a lawyer was charged with corrupting them. Prosecutors charged a former police president and the heads of the national crime agency's top units with belonging to another businessman's criminal group; that trial continues.

Not all of this has held up. The head of the office that prosecutes organised crime was convicted of taking a bribe to free an underworld boss, but the Supreme Court annulled those judgments in 2025 and ordered a retrial. The former intelligence chief was acquitted in 2025 of taking part of a bribe, and prosecutors have appealed. Separately, police charged a former military academy vice-rector in 2022 with passing information to the GRU, Russia's military intelligence.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 7 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at about 4.9. For Slovaks this has meant police chiefs accused of working for a businessman, court rulings that may have been bought, and top prosecutors and spies under suspicion for years without a settled verdict.

South Africa.d:
South Africa's state has been run from inside by private networks twice in living memory, first a secret society and then a business family with foreign firms alongside it. Every prime minister and state president from 1948 to 1994 belonged to the Afrikaner Broederbond, a secret all-male society that placed its members in top posts; by the late 1970s it held almost every cabinet seat as well as the heads of the army and the intelligence service.

After apartheid the reach came through money. Foreign arms makers paid large commissions to win the 1999 arms deal, and under Jacob Zuma's presidency the Zondo Commission, a judicial inquiry, found that ministers and the heads of Eskom, the state power company, and Transnet, the state rail and ports company, acted corruptly for the Gupta brothers, Indian-born businessmen who offered cabinet posts to officials willing to cooperate. Foreign consultancies and engineering and software firms also paid officials at Eskom, Transnet and government departments to win contracts.

Today the reach also runs through the police, the prisons, local councils and public hospitals. Crime bosses have bought officers up to the national commissioner, and in Cape Town gang leaders have paid a police brigadier and got gun licences through staff of the police firearm registry. Supplier syndicates pay health officials to buy from them: at one Gauteng hospital investigators found more than R2 billion drained by suppliers working with at least 15 current and former officials, from clerks to senior managers.

For South Africans, the bribes paid to win power, rail and hospital contracts came out of the public money meant for electricity, transport and health care, and people who report gang crime cannot be sure whether the officer taking the statement, or the clerk issuing a gun licence, works for the gang.

St. Kitts and Nevis.d:
Nothing is documented yet for St Kitts and Nevis, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case found so far shows an outside government, company, crime group or lodge paying Kittitian officials or placing people in office.

The Global Organized Crime Index, which scores every country on how far its officials work for criminal or outside interests, places St Kitts and Nevis near the middle of its scale, at 5 out of 10. It gives about 5.4 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. That describes officials under some pressure, with checks on them that are neither strong nor absent.

For people living there, this means no named official or company can be shown to be acting for an outside party. If outside money did reach in, it would most likely show up in who funds politicians, who wins public contracts and how licences are granted, and residents are best protected when those records are public.

Suriname.d:
In Suriname the cocaine trade did not need to buy officials from outside the government: for years it reached the presidency and the security services through the country's own leaders. Suriname lies on the Atlantic coast between Guyana and French Guiana, and the US Treasury says semi-submersible boats carry cocaine across the ocean from its ports and Guyana's.

Desi Bouterse, the former military ruler, was convicted in absentia in the Netherlands in 1999 of smuggling more than 450 kilograms of cocaine, never served the sentence because there was no extradition treaty, and was then elected president twice. While he held office his son Dino ran the country's counter-terrorism unit and used it to traffic cocaine; US agents arrested him in Panama, and he pleaded guilty in New York, including to offering a base in Suriname to people he believed were from Hezbollah, the Lebanese armed group.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 8.5 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 3.2. For the Surinamese, this meant that a counter-terrorism unit paid for by their taxes was used for drug trafficking, and that a court verdict against the man they twice elected president was never enforced.

Taiwan.d:
In Taiwan the main outside effort comes from China, through its intelligence services and united front work, the Chinese Communist Party's system for winning over or recruiting people abroad. A Chinese government office has paid for trips by elected village chiefs, and Chinese officials used the trips to urge them how to vote.

Since at least the late 1990s Chinese intelligence has placed people inside Taiwan's state, and its main target now is the armed forces and coast guard. Investigators and courts have found agents in the presidential guard, military intelligence and the senior ranks, up to retired lieutenant general Kao An-kuo, jailed in 2025 for trying to build an armed group to help an invasion, which he denies. In 2024, 64 people were prosecuted for Chinese espionage, two in three of them serving or retired military.

Retired officers sign up former subordinates, loan sharks and pawn shops find officers in debt, and others are reached through temples, gangs, paid tours and a juggling association. Two journalists have been convicted or charged as go-betweens. Pay runs by the value of what is handed over: classified documents, missile data, or videos in uniform pledging to surrender. Not all of this succeeds: in one ring twelve people agreed and twelve refused, and courts have acquitted a former legislator and others.

Business money reaches Taiwan's own governments too. In 2026 a court found that a developer's bribes to Ko Wen-je as mayor of Taipei led the city to let it build far more; he can appeal. For Taiwanese voters this means the soldiers and aides meant to defend them against the government that claims their country have, in case after case, been working for it, and a city's building limits were raised for the developer who paid the mayor.

Timor-Leste.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Timor-Leste, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No case found so far shows a foreign state, company, crime group or lodge paying officials or placing people inside its government.

Timor-Leste depends on oil and gas from the Timor Sea to fund its budget, and that kind of single, valuable source of public money is where outside interests often seek influence. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 4.5 out of 10 and the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs at about 3.9. That describes moderate pressure on officials with weak checks on them.

For people living there, this means no named official or company can be shown to be acting for an outside party. If a case exists, it would most likely surface through oil and gas deals, public contracts and policing, and those are the records residents would need to see.

Tunisia.d:
No documented case in Tunisia yet meets the map's test. The best-known charge, that Ennahda, the Islamist party that led the government after 2011, ran a 'secret apparatus' inside state institutions, ended in a life sentence for party leader Rached Ghannouchi in June 2026, but Ennahda calls the charges political and rights groups called the trial part of a crackdown on opponents, so the map does not count it.

No case found so far shows a foreign state, company or crime group paying Tunisian officials. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 6.5 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at 4.3, which describes officials under real pressure and weak checks on them. If outside interests are paying or placing officials, it is most likely to show up in public contracts, customs and policing.

Uganda.d:
In Uganda outside influence reaches the state through a foreign religious lobby working with legislators on its laws and through companies and brokers paying the men at the top for oil, arms and infrastructure deals.

The religious reach runs from the United States. Before Uganda passed the Anti-Homosexuality Act in 2023, Family Watch International, an Arizona-based Christian lobby that had coached African politicians for a decade, ran a private group of over 150 campaigners in which the Deputy Speaker said the ground was 'ripe' to bring the bill back; the group says it did not support the final version.

Money reaches the same level. A US jury convicted an agent of CEFC China Energy of arranging $500,000 for Uganda's foreign minister and urging a cash 'campaign donation' for President Yoweri Museveni so that both would steer business to the firm. Earlier, a judicial commission found that the president's brother took $800,000 from an arms broker over the purchase of unfit helicopter gunships, and MPs in 2011 tabled documents alleging an oil company paid the prime minister and two ministers for its concessions, claims never tested in court.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests here at 8 out of 10 and courts, police and watchdogs at 3.7. For gay Ugandans, the effect is a law that can send them to prison for life, shaped with lobbyists from abroad. For everyone else, oil and arms deals have been shaped by payments that came to light only in commissions without consequences or in foreign courts.

United States.d:
In the United States the most common way outside interests get inside government is to write its laws and staff its offices. Industry-funded groups led by the American Legislative Exchange Council, where companies and legislators draft 'model bills', produced at least 10,000 bills introduced in state legislatures between 2010 and 2018, more than 2,100 of which became law, and Christian nationalist groups now supply ready-made bills the same way. A conservative lawyers' network supplied most of Trump's first-term appeals-court judges, and since 2025 many federal agencies have been put under people from the industries they regulate, as when the securities regulator under a crypto adviser dropped many lawsuits against crypto companies.

When it turns into bribery, it is often a utility, developer or contractor buying the official who decides on it. In Ohio, FirstEnergy paid about $60 million to a group around the House Speaker for a law rescuing its nuclear plants, and more than $4 million to the man who then chaired the state's utility regulator; in San Francisco and Los Angeles, a public works chief and a planning committee chair were jailed for taking money from contractors and developers.

Foreign intelligence services, most often China's, recruit people in the State Department, the CIA, the FBI, the Federal Reserve and the armed forces, including soldiers paid for secret documents. Political movements have got in too: in at least four states, activists disputing the 2020 election got at county voting equipment often with local officials' help, and a Washington police lieutenant fed the Proud Boys leader inside information.

For Americans this means Ohio electricity prices set by a law that was bought and a regulator who was paid, and in some counties election officials who let people set on overturning the result handle the machines that count the vote.

Vatican City.d:
The Vatican is both the centre of the Catholic Church and a sovereign state, with its own bank, the Institute for the Works of Religion (IOR), and its own courts that answer to the Pope. Outsiders have reached it in two ways: financiers tied to organised crime and secret lodges who were given control of its money, and Cold War intelligence services that placed informants among the clergy around the Pope.

The money route opened in 1969, when the Holy See made Michele Sindona, a Sicilian banker who laundered heroin money for Mafia families, its financial adviser, and large sums moved from his banks through the Vatican to Swiss accounts. Sindona belonged to P2, a secret Masonic lodge that had enrolled Italian intelligence chiefs and politicians, as did the chairman of Banco Ambrosiano, the Milan bank whose collapse in 1982 still shapes how the Vatican is seen. The IOR was Ambrosiano's main shareholder and was tied to the offshore companies that held the missing money; it paid creditors $224 million while denying liability, and when Milan magistrates sought to arrest its president in 1987, Italy's top court ruled that the Lateran Treaty shielded him, so he was never tried.

On the intelligence side, communist Poland's secret police had an informant among the priests who looked after Polish pilgrims close to John Paul II during the 1980s.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 7 out of 10. For Catholics who give money to the Church, and for savers at the banks it deals with, this means losses caused through the IOR can fall outside the reach of ordinary courts, and any case against Vatican officials is heard by judges the Pope appoints.

Zambia.d:
What the record holds for Zambia is one contested allegation, about timber. In its 2019 report 'The Mukula Cartel', the Environmental Investigation Agency said traffickers supplying China with mukula, a protected rosewood, used the state forestry company as cover and shared profits with people around President Edgar Lungu, including his daughter and two ministers. It estimated that more than 50 containers a month left illegally over two years, with about $7.5 million a year paid in bribes and informal fees. The government denied the report, and the daughter and both ministers sued the agency in 2021, though she later withdrew. No court finding against them appears in the record, and Transparency International Zambia says most prosecutions are still ongoing.

If the report is right, protected timber left Zambia illegally with the help of people in government, using a state company as cover, which has not been proven.

The Global Organized Crime Index places Zambia in its Moderate band, scoring officials acting for criminal interests at 6.5 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at 4.7. Beyond this one report, no case is documented of a foreign state, company or crime group placing people inside the Zambian government, so what is shown here rests on those scores and a disputed account.

Andorra.d:
Andorra is a small mountain state between France and Spain whose economy has long relied on private banking for foreign clients. That makes its banks the obvious place for outside money to try to get in, and the documented pattern here is crime-group money handled by bank insiders rather than by politicians.

The case on the map is Banca Privada d'Andorra, whose senior managers, the US Treasury found in 2015, knowingly moved money for professional launderers working for transnational criminal organisations. Andorra took the bank over the next day and wound it up within a week. The US later withdrew its finding, but an Andorran court sentenced eighteen of the bank's executives in 2025; they are appealing, and shareholders argue the bank was closed on an administrative finding never tested in court.

Outside banking there is little on record. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Andorra 1 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests, the lowest possible score, and 8 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For people living there, the cost of the bank case fell on its ordinary clients, who had to prove their money was legitimate before they could get it back, some waiting years, while the country's standing as a banking centre, which much of its income depends on, was put in question.

Armenia.d:
The cases on record in Armenia are accusations of spying for a foreign state, and most of them point to its neighbour and enemy, Azerbaijan. Since the 2020 war, in which Azerbaijan retook much of the territory around Nagorno-Karabakh, Armenia has opened several treason and spying cases against its own personnel. Investigators describe a former serviceman, reported to have commanded an army detachment, passing on troop deployments and commanders' names during the war. In 2022 the National Security Service said Azerbaijani operatives had posed as Armenian women on social media, befriended officers with access to state secrets and then offered them money; it said dozens of servicemen were involved and detained nineteen people.

In 2025 the accusations moved beyond the armed forces, when an unnamed Foreign Ministry employee was charged with treason for passing state secrets to a foreign state. Officials have not said which state and say no other ministry staff were implicated, and a newspaper's claim that the case involves Azerbaijan is unconfirmed. No case here shows an outside party placing people or money inside other ministries or companies.

The Global Organized Crime Index gives Armenia 3.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests, low by world standards, and about 5.6 for its courts, police and watchdogs, around the middle of the range. For Armenians, the documented danger is that people passing on the positions of their own units, if the accusations hold, put soldiers and border villages at risk during and after a war. Elsewhere the scores suggest institutions that work moderately well, and the places to watch are who wins public contracts, who owns the companies running essential services and who funds political campaigns.

Bahamas.d:
The Bahamas lie on the sea and air routes between South America and Florida, and since the cocaine boom of the late 1970s traffickers moving drugs through the islands have paid the officials who police them. In the early 1980s Colombian smugglers used the Exumas as a base and paid ministers and police to let them through. A Royal Commission of Inquiry reported in 1984 wide corruption in the cabinet and the police; it found that Prime Minister Lynden Pindling had spent eight times his reported income and had received at least $57.3 million in cash, and while it did not find him guilty, five ministers resigned or were dismissed.

The pattern has returned. A US indictment filed in November 2024 says that since at least 2021 two high-ranking officers of the Royal Bahamas Police Force and a Bahamian military official helped cocaine arriving on charter flights from Colombia and Venezuela pass through Bahamian airports and onto boats for Florida, for bribes of $10,000 to $2 million, and that one officer demanded $2 million on behalf of an unnamed senior politician. The police commissioner, who was not accused, resigned the following week.

The Bahamas is also an offshore financial centre, where foreign banks and companies register to hold money. The Global Organized Crime Index gives it 3 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 5.6 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. For Bahamians, this means that forty years apart, the officers responsible for guarding the islands' airports and coasts have been accused of selling that protection to traffickers, the case was brought by a foreign court rather than their own, and the politician named as wanting a share has not been identified to them.

Belarus.d:
The documented cases in Belarus are few and all come from the state's own prosecutions, so they show only what the authorities have made public. They concern bribes paid to people running state bodies and state firms, and in two of the three the money came at least partly from Russian companies. A Belarusian court found that a Russian company paid a deputy state secretary of the Security Council, previously head of President Alexander Lukashenko's protection service, about $148,000 to promote its interests in the country, and jailed him for 12 years. The director of Beltelecom, the state telephone operator, admitted guilt in a bribery case whose charges included €15,000 from a Russian firm over equipment supplies.

The third case is in health. Officials allegedly took bribes of $10,000 to $450,000 from those seeking medical equipment and drug contracts, with prices inflated by up to 60%. Thirty-three people were held, among them a former deputy health minister and the head of the state medical importer, who was jailed for bribe-taking.

Lukashenko has ruled since 1994, and power is concentrated around the presidency and the security services. The Global Organized Crime Index gives Belarus 9 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 3.1 for its courts, police and watchdogs. The KGB, the state security service, made the arrests in the health and Security Council cases, and no free press, independent court or opposition party can test them or say how far such payments go beyond these cases. For people in Belarus, this means public money for medicines and hospital equipment has gone partly on bribes, foreign firms have paid officials close to the president, and residents have no independent channel for raising it.

Bhutan.d:
Nothing is documented yet for Bhutan, so this is an estimate based on conditions. No foreign intelligence service, company, crime group, church or lodge has a documented presence in its government or companies, and none is listed as likely to be present.

Bhutan is a small Himalayan kingdom between India and China, which limits foreign investment and tourism, and it became a parliamentary democracy only in 2008. The Global Organized Crime Index, which scores every country on how far its officials work for criminal or outside interests, gives Bhutan 3 out of 10 on that measure, low by world standards, and about 4.7 out of 10 for resilience, meaning the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. The estimate rests on that index alone.

For people living there, this means no known cost from outside groups placing people in Bhutan's offices or firms, and the index rates this as a smaller problem than in most of the world. The middling resilience score means that if outside influence did arrive, through its large neighbours or through investment, the institutions that would have to catch it are not rated as especially strong. A documented case found later would replace this estimate.

Brazil.d:
Brazil has more documented cases of outsiders inside its institutions than almost any other country, and they come from three directions: organised crime, churches and business money.

Crime groups have bought police, judges and legislators for decades, and they now put their own people into elected office and into the workplaces they need. The PCC, a São Paulo prison gang that runs much of the drug trade, is accused of paying police for protection, financing candidates and placing allies in town halls around São Paulo, and has recruited ground staff at Guarulhos, Latin America's largest airport. Rio's militias, armed groups that began as off-duty police running protection rackets, and the Comando Vermelho drug faction are accused of having allies in the state assembly and Congress.

Churches reach in through seats and appointments: pastors of the Universal Church of the Kingdom of God founded the Republicanos party, which a church bishop leads and through which a bishop became a federal minister. Business money reaches state firms, lawmakers, regulators and the courts. Brazilian and foreign traders, shipbuilders and engineering groups have admitted or settled claims of paying Petrobras staff for contracts, and advertising agencies accepted responsibility for bribes to win state accounts. Companies have also bought rules: an airline paid officials to pass two laws cutting its taxes, and a petrochemical firm's settlement covers official rules produced by improper payments. Associations allegedly paid insiders at the pensions agency to take about R$6.3 billion from retired people.

For people living there, a bus fare or a tank of petrol can feed a crime group, a town's mayor may owe the seat to a faction, pensioners have allegedly had money taken from their payments with officials' help, and tax laws and state contracts have been bought by those with a stake in them.

Burundi.d:
In Burundi the documented reach comes from a foreign tobacco company working on the officials who write tobacco law. Leaked records from British American Tobacco (BAT), one of the world's largest cigarette makers, show payments to Burundian officials who handled tobacco control, part of a run of such payments in several East and Central African countries that researchers read as aimed at blocking laws modelled on the WHO tobacco treaty, which commits governments to restrict tobacco sales and marketing. A British fraud inquiry closed without charges and BAT denies the allegations, so these remain reports rather than findings.

If the payments worked as the records suggest, Burundians live under weaker tobacco rules than the treaty asks for: more advertising, cheaper and easier access, fewer health warnings, and over time more illness from smoking. No Burundian inquiry is recorded, so residents do not know which officials were paid or what they did in return.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Burundi among the countries where officials most often work for criminal interests, and its courts, police and watchdogs among the weakest. On those terms, an official who takes money from a foreign company is unlikely to be investigated at home, which is why the only account of these payments came from a British broadcaster and a British university.

Canada.d:
Most of what reaches inside Canadian government comes from foreign states, as it has since a Soviet spy ring reaching into Parliament was exposed in 1945. China's reach now extends into state science: Canada's intelligence service has said a scientist at its highest-security pathogen laboratory worked to benefit China's government, and a researcher at Hydro-Québec, Quebec's state power company, is accused of passing its battery research to Chinese bodies through a Chinese state scheme for recruiting scientists, which he denies.

In politics China and India are the most active, working through proxies.
