Canada's public inquiry into foreign interference found intelligence that India's proxy agents may have given illicit money to politicians to elect pro-India candidates, and a parliamentary intelligence committee reported that some MPs and senators had knowingly or half-knowingly helped foreign states, including by taking disguised money from foreign missions. For voters, a candidate on the ballot may have had a foreign government's help getting there, and for taxpayers, publicly funded research can end up serving another state.

Organised crime reaches in where money or goods change hands. In Quebec, construction firms rigged bids for city public works and paid both the Mafia and the parties that ran city hall; mayors of Montreal and Laval fell over it. At the busiest land crossings into the United States, border officers have been convicted of waving smugglers through, and police say the ring behind a C$20 million gold theft from Air Canada's cargo building at Toronto's airport had airline staff on the inside. Earlier, the Orange Order, a Protestant fraternity, placed its members in office: for decades every Toronto mayor belonged to it. Canada's courts and watchdogs rank among the strongest measured by the Global Organized Crime Index, and most of this came to light through its own inquiries.

China.d:
Reaching-in runs several ways in China. The Communist Party places its own bodies inside companies, foreign ones included: any firm with three or more party members must set up a party organisation, and nearly three-quarters of private companies had one by 2018.

Businesses buy the officials who are meant to regulate or lend to them, and the record reaches the top: convictions for taking money from companies and smugglers have reached a Politburo member, the railway minister and the officials overseeing police, medicines and finance. State banks, which decide who gets credit, are a main route: in 2024 a central bank deputy governor and the chairman of Bank of China both received suspended death sentences for bribes from companies seeking loans. Foreign firms have hired officials' relatives to win business, and gangs have bought deputy police chiefs and village party secretaries.

Foreign spy services are reported to have reached deep into the state, though little of this can be checked. US officials told the New York Times that the CIA had recruited insiders deep in China's bureaucracy and that China killed at least a dozen of them from 2010 to 2012. China's Ministry of State Security regularly announces that foreign agencies recruited students and state employees, some of whom it says were executed or sentenced to death. The Wall Street Journal reported in 2026 that the top general Zhang Youxia was accused of passing nuclear data to Washington; this is unproven, and the party's statement on him does not mention it.

The party answers with its own arrests and executions, untested by any independent court. For people in China, this means loans, medicines and trains overseen by officials who may have been paid by the firms involved, and no open way to judge who has really passed secrets abroad.

Congo, Rep..d:
The Republic of Congo's state runs on oil, and the documented reach-in comes through the circle around President Denis Sassou-Nguesso, who has ruled for most of the period since 1979. Foreign oil traders have obtained the national oil company's crude by dealing with intermediaries close to his family. The clearest case is Gunvor, a Geneva oil trader, which between 2010 and 2012 lent the national oil company $750 million to be repaid in oil while paying nearly $30 million in commissions to two fixers close to the president's family; according to the case record the money was meant for his relatives, and a Swiss court convicted Gunvor in 2019.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates the country among those where officials most often work for criminal interests, with weak courts, police and watchdogs. For Congolese, this means oil that belongs to the state has been sold on terms set by foreign traders and the president's relatives, the case came to light in a Swiss court rather than their own, and little inside the country would check such dealings.

Cuba.d:
Cuba is a one-party state whose own intelligence and security services control most of public life, and both documented cases of outside reach involve organised crime getting to the people at the top.

Before the 1959 revolution the American Mafia, through its financier Meyer Lansky, had an arrangement with Fulgencio Batista: Lansky's associates ran Havana's casinos and racetracks and Batista took kickbacks. After his 1952 coup Batista made Lansky an adviser on gambling reform, and the law was changed to let any hotel worth $1 million host a casino. The arrangement ended with the revolution, when the casinos were looted and then nationalised.

The second case ran through the revolutionary state itself. In 1989 General Arnaldo Ochoa, and an Interior Ministry colonel who ran the state's hard-currency businesses were convicted of letting the Medellín cartel move cocaine to Florida through Cuban waters and airspace, and both were executed by firing squad. It showed that a Colombian cartel could reach senior officers inside a state that tightly controls its own territory, and that they used state channels to help it. The trial was held by military courts that Cubans have no independent way to check, so the public record of how far the network reached is the one the government chose to give.

For Cubans, both episodes meant that decisions about their country, from who ran the hotels to what crossed their coastline, were sold by people in power to criminal outsiders. The Global Organized Crime Index rates Cuba's officials as relatively unlikely to work for criminal interests, with institutions of middling strength. No more recent case on the map shows outsiders inside the Cuban government, though the closed nature of the state means little would be reported if one did.

Djibouti.d:
Djibouti's documented case is a foreign company paying the state's own officials for a state contract. Ericsson, the Swedish telecoms equipment maker, admitted paying about €2.1 million to high-ranking Djibouti officials to win a contract with Djibouti Telecom, the state-owned telephone company, as part of a US settlement covering bribery in several countries. The payment went to the people inside the state who decide which foreign supplier builds a national network, so the contract was settled by the bribe rather than by price or quality.

For Djiboutians, the telephone network they pay for was built under a contract won by bribing their officials, and they learned of it from a US settlement rather than from any process at home. The officials who took the money were not named in public, and no case against them in Djibouti is recorded.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Djibouti in the middle range for officials working for criminal interests, with weak courts, police and watchdogs. The Ericsson payments are the only case on record.

Egypt.d:
In Egypt the outside forces that have reached the top of the state have mostly come through the army and through creditors. In 1952 the Free Officers, a secret network of junior officers recruited inside the army, seized power and ended the monarchy, and the body that succeeded their ruling council, the Supreme Council of the Armed Forces, still sits at the top of the Egyptian state. Since then the army has been the place where others try to get in: an armed Islamist group built a cell inside it that killed the president in 1981, and a member of two presidents' inner circles was a source for Israel's foreign intelligence service.

The other outside force that came close to the top is the Muslim Brotherhood, a Sunni Islamist movement founded in Egypt in 1928 that works to bring its members into power. In 2012 Mohamed Morsi won the presidency as the candidate of the Brotherhood's own party; the army removed him in 2013, most of the movement's leaders were jailed, and membership alone can now bring a prison sentence.

Creditors set the older pattern. After Egypt fell behind on its loans in 1876, its European lenders placed their own commissioners over its finances, and the debt fund they ran lasted until 1940; from 1883 to 1907 a British controller from the banking family that held Egyptian debt, effectively ruled the country. For Egyptians the result is a state run by officers who arrived through a secret network, which treats an organised religious movement as an enemy within, and where people who voted for the Brotherhood saw their president removed by the army. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 8.5 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at 3.75.

Estonia.d:
Estonia is a NATO and EU member on Russia's border, and the most serious documented reach into its state is Russian intelligence recruiting people inside the institutions meant to keep its secrets. Over two decades Estonia has caught a series of Russian agents in its own defence and security bodies, paid by the SVR, Russia's foreign intelligence service, the GRU, its military intelligence, or the FSB, its security service. The clearest case is Herman Simm, who headed the defence ministry's security department, the office that protected NATO and EU classified material, and passed those secrets to the SVR for thirteen years until his arrest in 2008. The recruiting continues and now reaches lower: in 2025 a member of the Defence League, the volunteer force that forms part of national defence, was convicted of reporting to the FSB on fellow volunteers, soldiers and local politics in the border city of Narva. Estonia also convicted its first spy for China in 2021.

The second route runs through the banks, which money from Russia and the former Soviet states has used as a gateway into the EU. In the Azerbaijani Laundromat, about $2.9 billion moved in 2012–2014 through accounts at Danske Bank's Estonian branch, and part of it reached European politicians who defended Azerbaijan in the Council of Europe, Europe's main human rights body.

For Estonians this means that people trusted with state secrets, and neighbours in their own volunteer defence units, have been working for the power those secrets are guarded against, and that their banks were used to pay politicians elsewhere to speak for a foreign ruling family. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Estonian officials acting for criminal interests at 2 out of 10 and its courts and watchdogs above 8, and the spy cases have ended in convictions.

Finland.d:
Finland today has one of the cleanest records on the map. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal or outside interests at 1.5 out of 10 and the strength of its courts and watchdogs at over 8.4, among the highest in the world, and no current case shows a foreign state, company or criminal group paying Finnish officials.

During the Cold War it was different. The Soviet KGB assigned its officers in Helsinki, working under diplomatic cover at the Soviet embassy, to individual Finnish politicians and officials, so that many of them had a personal Soviet contact known as a 'kotiryssä', or 'home Russian'. The system reached President Urho Kekkonen, and a former Soviet diplomat later said the KGB general who ran it backed a candidate to succeed him. It is tied to what became known as Finlandization, the bending of Finnish policy to Moscow's wishes, and a leading Finnish newspaper reported in 2015 that the practice had almost ended.

What is documented now is the reach of a private elite network. The World Economic Forum, the Swiss foundation behind the annual Davos meeting, picks rising politicians under about 40 for its Young Global Leaders network, which brings them together with business executives over several years. President Alexander Stubb joined in 2009 and lists it on his official CV, and former prime minister Sanna Marin is also listed. Membership is lawful and public, and no finding says the network directed Finnish decisions.

For Finns, this means the foreign power that once had a contact for each senior politician has largely lost that access, and the open question now is whose views leaders hear in private meetings funded by large companies.

Georgia.d:
In Georgia, criminal and armed groups reached inside the state in the years after independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, Russia has kept trying to recruit people inside its armed forces and diplomatic service, and the newest case reaches the security service. In the early 1990s a militia, the Mkhedrioni, was made the country's interior forces and was accused of extortion and drug smuggling until it was outlawed in 1995. Alongside it worked the 'thieves in law', a criminal fraternity born in Soviet prison camps, which 1990s governments treated as part of the power structure, Georgian analysts say. Membership became a crime in 2005, but police arrested more than 100 people in a crackdown in late 2025 and early 2026.

Russia's approaches centre on the 2008 war. A former counsellor at Georgia's mission to NATO was sentenced to 20 years, after a closed trial, for reporting arms purchases and troop movements to Russia; he denied it and said his confession was forced. In 2010 Georgia arrested air force pilots and a naval radio operator accused of giving Russian military intelligence its codes and readiness. Scam call centres, which phone people abroad and talk them into fake investments, have operated from Tbilisi, and in December 2025 prosecutors charged the State Security Service's chief from 2020 to 2025, a ruling-party member, with taking about $1.4 million in bribes, partly for protecting such centres. It is untried.

For Georgians this means armed men accused of extortion were once the state's interior forces, the army facing a neighbour that occupies part of their land is accused of holding that neighbour's informants, and the agency meant to protect them is accused of being paid to protect fraudsters. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 4 out of 10.

Grenada.d:
Grenada has given ambassador titles to foreign businessmen, and the documented allegations here come from foreign investors dealing directly with the prime minister's office. In 2019 an Al Jazeera investigation reported that one foreign investor said he had paid about half a million dollars to Prime Minister Keith Mitchell, who said he received only $15,000 to cover travel. A US businessman said a partner had been offered a diplomatic post in return for kickbacks on state projects, which the government denies. No charge has been brought, and the claims rest on the investors' own statements.

For Grenadians, this means public contracts and diplomatic posts can be traded with foreign investors, and only the government's word stands between residents and that trade. If a kickback was asked for, it raised the cost of work done for the public. With no court test, residents are left with conflicting accounts. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 3.5 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at about 5.2, better than most of the region.

Guyana.d:
Guyana produces gold in its interior and has become a route for cocaine moving from South America by air and sea, and the people in both trades pay officials to keep their business moving. According to the US Treasury, the largest gold trading family in the country bribed customs officials to leave more than 10,000 kilograms of gold off customs declarations, paid officials for help in court matters and to win state contracts, and was helped by the top civil servant at the home affairs ministry, who took cash and gifts for contracts, gun permits and passports. The family denies wrongdoing.

Cocaine networks reach the police in the same way. In 2025 the Treasury sanctioned a serving police officer it says arranged safe passage for Mexican and Venezuelan traffickers, along with trafficking bosses and Colombians managing hidden jungle airstrips. None of these cases has been tried, and the US State Department calls corruption in Guyana a significant obstacle to stopping drugs.

Outside interests choosing who governs is older than the drug trade. Before independence the CIA secretly paid opposition parties to remove the elected premier Cheddi Jagan, and kept funding their leader Forbes Burnham, who became the first prime minister of independent Guyana in 1966.

For Guyanese, this means the customs officer, court official or ministry clerk they deal with for a permit or passport may have been paid by a large private business, and duty lost on undeclared gold, more than $50 million by the Treasury's count, was public money. People in the interior live near airstrips used for cocaine, policed by a force that traffickers have reached. The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 8 out of 10 and the courts and watchdogs at about 4.3.

Iceland.d:
No documented case in Iceland yet meets the map's test, which asks whether an outside party got its people, money or control inside a government body, international body or company, and whether decisions there served it. No case shows a foreign government, a company or a crime group placing people or money inside the Icelandic state.

The Global Organized Crime Index puts Iceland among the lowest anywhere for officials working for criminal interests and near the top for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. On that estimate, an official serving outside interests would be both unusual and likely to be caught.

For Icelanders this means they are unlikely to meet an official quietly serving a foreign state or a crime group, and if one were found, the courts and watchdogs are well placed to examine it.

Iraq.d:
Since 2003 Iran's reach has been written into the Iraqi state, from the security forces to the cabinet and now the town halls. Badr, a militia formed in Iran in 1982, held the Interior Ministry, which runs the police. The Popular Mobilization Forces (PMF), about 67 mostly Shia militias almost all backed by Iran's Revolutionary Guards, were made a branch of the armed forces by a 2016 law and are paid from the state budget; their own chief of staff has said they take orders from Iran's supreme leader. The PMF has its own state company to win public contracts, and Iran-aligned armed groups hold ministries, including Badr and Kataib Hezbollah nominees in the cabinet formed in May 2026.

The militias also use their state seats and state-paid units to take over local government. The political arm of one PMF brigade won all four provincial council seats reserved for Christians by mobilising mostly Shia Arab voters, then used its majority on the Nineveh council to remove 15 mayors and directors in Christian and Yazidi towns. In Baghdad in 2025, gunmen from Kataib Hezbollah's state brigades raided an agriculture office to keep their ally in charge, and three people were killed.

Money flows the same way: about $2.5 billion was taken from a tax account through fake refunds, with the director of the prime minister's office among those convicted.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Iraq 8.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 3 for its courts and watchdogs. For Iraqis this means their taxes pay militias that follow a foreign cleric, those militias run ministries, a state company and local councils, and Christian and Yazidi towns can have their officials removed by an armed group's party.

Jamaica.d:
In Jamaica the documented case of an outside party reaching inside government involves money from a company that did business with the state. In 2006 the oil trader Trafigura, which lifted oil for the Jamaican government, paid $31 million into an account linked to the governing party. The party called it a donation and said it was returned. Dutch prosecutors investigated the payment as possible bribery of officials.

The concern in a case like this is that a firm paid the people in charge of the government it was earning from, so that decisions on its business could go its way.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Jamaica 7.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and just over 5 for the strength of its courts and watchdogs. For people in Jamaica this means a firm holding government oil business paid into an account tied to the party running that government, and the question of whether it was a bribe was taken up by prosecutors in the Netherlands.

Kenya.d:
In Kenya the documented reach into the state comes from three directions: drug traffickers moving heroin through the port of Mombasa, armed groups and smugglers working the border with Somalia, and foreign companies seeking public contracts.

The traffickers have bought protection where they needed it. The Akasha brothers, who ran a Mombasa heroin business, admitted in a US court that they had paid Kenyan judges, prosecutors and police for two years to block their extradition, and none of those officials has been named or charged in Kenya. Along the Somali border the record is less firm. UN monitors reported that al-Shabaab, the Somali insurgency, paid security officials on both sides to help a 2018 car-bomb plot through, without naming any official. A rights group has accused army units fighting al-Shabaab in Somalia of sharing in a sugar and charcoal smuggling trade with the militants; the military denies it.

Company money has reached the bodies that run elections and exams. A British security printer and its owner were convicted in London of paying officials at Kenya's electoral commission and national exams council to win contracts for ballot papers and exam materials. A former commission chief charged in Kenya denies it, and the commission's chair was cleared by the anti-corruption body.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Kenya 8 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests. For Kenyans this means the judges, prosecutors and police paid by traffickers have still not faced a court at home, and contracts to print their ballots and exam papers were won with bribes, as a British court found.

Kosovo.d:
Kosovo's record shows two ways outsiders have got inside its security services: a foreign government working through them, and a crime group accused of paying them. In 2018 Turkey's government had Kosovo's police and intelligence service seize six Turkish nationals it wanted and fly them to Ankara, without the knowledge of Kosovo's own prime minister. A Pristina court later jailed the former intelligence chief for abuse of office.

The second comes from northern Kosovo, where the United States says a crime group run by a Kosovo Serb businessman bribed Kosovar and Serbian officials to smuggle goods, money, drugs and weapons, and that politicians gave it protection in return for campaign support. In 2021 Washington sanctioned the businessman, a vice-president of the Belgrade-backed party Srpska Lista and a former police operations chief for the north. An earlier indictment accused the businessman and the party official of leading a group behind a Kosovo Serb politician's killing, which they denied; in 2024 a Pristina court convicted four others, two of them policemen. The US sanctions are a government finding and not a court verdict.

The Global Organized Crime Index does not score Kosovo separately; North Macedonia's figures, 6.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and just over 5 for courts and watchdogs, stand in for it here. For people in Kosovo this means the police and intelligence officers meant to protect them have acted for another government without their elected leaders being told, and in the north some officers are accused of serving the people who smuggle through it.

Latvia.d:
Latvia has been reached from outside in two ways: Russia's intelligence services recruiting inside its parliament, ministries and key companies, and private bank owners paying the official who supervised them. By January 2024 Latvian public media counted ten people found guilty of espionage in the country, and the cases run from the interior ministry to a railway employee who was jailed for sending videos of NATO supply trains to a contact in Moscow.

The recruiting has reached elected politicians over many years. Leaked emails published in 2024 show Tatjana Ždanoka, who represented Latvia in the European Parliament for twenty years, reporting to officers of the FSB, Russia's main security service, from at least 2004; a criminal case is open but she has not been convicted. Jānis Ādamsons, a former interior minister who sat on parliament's defence and anti-corruption committee, was convicted in 2023 of passing material on NATO units and on Latvia's own security service to the FSB through a former KGB officer.

Bank owners have reached the top of the regulator. In 2023 a court sentenced the former governor of the Bank of Latvia, who also sat on the European Central Bank's governing council, to six years for taking a bribe from a Riga bank's shareholders in return for help with the financial regulator.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Latvia 2.5 out of 10 for officials working for outside interests and above 7.5 for its courts and watchdogs. For people in Latvia, this means an MP on the committee overseeing their police and security service was passing information to the neighbouring power those services guard against, and the official meant to keep banks honest took money from a bank's owners. Courts here have caught such people, often years later.

Libya.d:
Libya is split between a government in Tripoli and Khalifa Haftar's forces in the east, and on both sides armed groups have become the state bodies meant to police them. In Tripoli, militias formed in 2011 have been given official status as security agencies while staying loyal to their own commanders. One, Radaa, has held the capital's only commercial airport and its prisons as a state force; another, the Stability Support Apparatus, was placed under the Presidential Council in 2021 while its chief's associates controlled the internal security agency, public companies and transfers from the central bank.

Smuggling networks have their own people in coast guard units, ports and fuel distribution, so the officials who should stop fuel, migrants and drugs leaving are the ones moving them. The Sentry, an investigative group, estimates that about $20 billion of subsidised fuel was diverted in 2022–24. Followers of a Saudi cleric whose Salafi teaching demands obedience to rulers, known as Madkhalis, hold strong positions in a Tripoli security force and in Haftar's army and run the eastern mosques authority.

Foreign companies have paid for access to Libya's oil money. Under Muammar Gaddafi, a Canadian engineering firm was convicted over bribes to officials linked to his son, and a French bank settled over commissions that partly reached officials controlling state investments.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Libya 9.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal interests and below 2 for its courts and watchdogs. For Libyans this means the airport, the prisons and the police in their district may answer to a militia commander, they pay for a fuel subsidy that is resold abroad, and migrants picked up at sea can find themselves held by the people trafficking them.

Madagascar.d:
Madagascar's documented outside reach comes through elections, from a foreign network that courts several candidates at once. In the 2018 presidential race, political strategists tied to Yevgeny Prigozhin, the businessman behind the Russian private military company Wagner, worked with as many as eight candidates, offering cash or promises of money, according to the Russian outlet Proekt and the BBC; the winner denied being Russia's candidate and no evidence showed he took Russian money.

This is the approach Prigozhin's network used across much of Africa: back several contenders, so that whoever wins may owe something. In Madagascar it met a state that the Global Organized Crime Index rates as highly exposed, with officials often serving criminal or outside interests and weak courts, police and watchdogs to check them.

That weakness is why no Malagasy court or official inquiry has set out who took money or what was promised in return. For Malagasy voters it means they chose a president in a race where a foreign network was paying or courting candidates, and they have no official record of which of the people they elected, if any, owe that network anything.

Mali.d:
In Mali, those reaching into the state are mostly cocaine traffickers crossing the Sahara and the Sahel, the dry belt south of it and the armed groups protecting them. Where the routes cross desert airstrips and border posts, traffickers pay local officials and armed groups to let the cargo through, and the UN Office on Drugs and Crime has found that traffickers include members of the political elite. The clearest example is the 2009 'Air Cocaine' flight from Venezuela, unloaded at a northern desert strip under protection investigators traced to local officials and armed groups; no senior figure was convicted.

Armed groups have also had their own members in official posts. UN sanctions listings say an influential member of a pro-government armed group sat in the National Assembly for the president's party while coordinating an armed blockade of talks on the 2015 peace deal, and that a member of a rebel group became special adviser to the governor of Kidal and used the role to control regional aid projects and extort aid organisations. These findings are untested at trial.

The military government, which turned from France to Russia from 2021, presents foreign intelligence as the threat from inside. In August 2025 it arrested two generals and a French national, saying he acted for French intelligence to turn officers against it. France has not commented, and the charges have not been tested in an open court.

The Global Organized Crime Index rates Mali's courts, police and watchdogs among the weakest in the world. For people in Mali this means traffickers and the officials who shelter them are rarely brought to court, aid meant for them in the north has passed through armed groups' hands, and those accused of working for a foreign power are judged by the government accusing them.

Mauritius.d:
Outsiders have reached into Mauritius in two ways on the record: foreign builders paying officials for public contracts, and a foreign financier getting close to the head of state while seeking a licence from the state.

The contract route runs through middlemen. The money passes through agents or consultants, so the official who decides the contract never appears on the company's books. The African Development Bank, which lends for infrastructure, found that a Danish power-plant builder had more likely than not paid members of the Mauritian administration in this way during the tenders for the state electricity company's Saint-Louis power station, and barred it from its projects for nearly two years. That is a lender's decision, not a court verdict, and it names no Mauritian official.

The second case reached the presidency. President Ameenah Gurib-Fakim was vice-chair of a charity run by an Angolan banker, Álvaro Sobrinho, and used its credit card for private spending while he was seeking a banking licence from the Mauritian financial regulator, which she asked to issue it. After a newspaper published her card statements in 2018 she repaid the money and resigned, and the government set up a commission of inquiry into her conduct.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds a moderate level of officials serving outside interests in Mauritius and rates its institutions in the middle range. For Mauritians this means part of the electricity they pay for comes from a station whose builder was found to have paid officials, and their head of state was spending a licence-seeker's money while pressing the regulator on his behalf. No official has been named in the power case, so people do not know whether those involved are still in the public service.

Monaco.d:
The cases that touch Monaco come from the international bodies and wealthy foreign residents who base themselves there. The principality hosts sports federations and some of the world's richest people, and the documented problems arise where their money meets the decisions made in Monaco.

The clearest case is World Athletics, the governing body of track and field, which has its headquarters in Monaco. Its former president, Lamine Diack, was convicted in France of taking money from Russian sports officials to delay doping cases against Russian athletes, so that suspected dopers could compete at the 2012 London Olympics. In the second case, Dmitry Rybolovlev, a Russian billionaire who owns the AS Monaco football club, was suspected of courting Monaco officials, including a former public prosecutor; the case was closed after the courts ruled that the phone messages it rested on had been obtained unlawfully, so no court has decided whether officials were influenced.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds a fairly low level of officials serving outside interests in Monaco. For people there, the athletics case shows a body run from their city selling decisions to a foreign state, at the expense of athletes everywhere who competed clean. The Rybolovlev case leaves residents with no finding either way on whether a wealthy resident could buy favour from their prosecutors.

Mozambique.d:
Mozambique has been reached from outside by foreign lenders and contractors who paid its officials, by timber traders who are accused of doing the same, and by criminal gangs with police and justice staff on their side.

The clearest case is the 'hidden debts'. Foreign banks, including Credit Suisse and Russia's VTB, lent about 2 billion dollars to three state companies for fishing and maritime security projects under state guarantees kept from parliament and the International Monetary Fund. US prosecutors said hundreds of millions went in bribes and kickbacks to bankers and Mozambican officials, the former finance minister was convicted in the United States, and Mozambique's constitutional council declared the loans void. The state airline shows the same route on a smaller scale: a foreign aircraft maker admitted bribes on a jet sale, and a Maputo court sentenced a former transport minister, whose defence planned to appeal.

In the northern forests the claims are weaker. Campaign group reports say Chinese timber traders pay officials to move wood to port, and traders told undercover investigators that two agriculture ministers helped them. The ministers deny it, the anti-corruption office found no shareholdings by Mozambicans, and no charges are reported from these claims. In Maputo the country's own criminal investigation chief has said justice staff take part in kidnappings for ransom.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials serving criminal interests to one of the highest degrees anywhere. For Mozambicans the hidden loans meant debt their parliament never approved; when they surfaced in 2016, the IMF and World Bank froze support, and one study estimated that two million people were pushed into poverty. Families whose relatives are abducted cannot be sure the police investigating are not working with the kidnappers.

Nepal.d:
The documented cases of outsiders getting inside Nepal's state come from crime networks, a foreign spy service and a foreign company, and they work through the politicians and officials who control the borders, customs and state purchases.

Crime networks reach in through the same people who make and enforce the law. In the 1990s an MP who held ministerial posts was reported to work with D-Company, Dawood Ibrahim's Indian crime syndicate, and with Pakistan's ISI spy agency, in gun-running, forgery and sheltering fugitives, a claim never tested in court. The current case is a gold-smuggling network: Nepal's anti-graft commission charged 28 people in 2026, including the chief customs administrator at Kathmandu's international airport and a former Speaker of parliament, after seized gold was swapped out of the sealed customs warehouse.

A foreign firm selling to the state has paid officials as well. A US aviation-services company admitted in 2024 that it had paid Nepali officials through intermediary companies to win the sale of two Airbus A330 jets to Nepal Airlines Corporation, the state airline, and paid more than $55 million to settle with US prosecutors over this and a South African deal.

The Global Organized Crime Index finds officials in Nepal widely serving criminal or outside interests and rates its institutions as weak. For Nepali people this means smuggled goods can pass the country's main airport because the officers checking them, and politicians above them, are alleged to work for the smugglers; a minister they elected was reported to be serving a foreign crime syndicate and spy service; and the state airline's purchase of aircraft, made with public money, was won with bribes to officials.

Niger.d: Niger lies on a Sahel route that the UN drugs office describes as a natural stopover for South American cocaine heading to Europe. Where a trafficking route crosses a thinly policed country, traffickers make use of local officials, whose vehicles and offices are less likely to be searched; the clearest example is a mayor caught in early 2022 with more than 200 kilograms of cocaine in his vehicle, with no outcome recorded since. Higher up, a researcher has reported that a cocaine-linked businessman known as 'Cherif Cocaine' funded the ruling party's campaigns and was protected by officials at the highest levels, though the claim is hard to document. The Global Organized Crime Index scores Niger high for officials working for criminal interests and low for the strength of its courts and police, so residents have little reason to expect a trial that shows who else was involved.

Oman.d:
The clearest documented reach into Oman's state came from Britain, and its effect is still felt: the sultan whom British officers helped put in power in 1970, Qaboos, ruled for half a century. At the time Oman's armed forces were under de facto British command. On 23 July 1970 the British commander briefed the Omani officers who carried out a palace coup in Salalah that removed Sultan Said bin Taimur and installed his son, who was then under house arrest and had been sent the plan on cassette tapes by British officials. Accounts based on British records say MI6, the Foreign Office and the Ministry of Defence planned it and the prime minister approved it; Britain denied involvement for forty years, saying its officers had acted on their own.

Nothing documented since then shows a foreign state, company, crime group or secret society with people or money inside Omani offices or firms. The Global Organized Crime Index places Oman in its moderate band, scoring it in the middle range both for officials working for criminal or outside interests and for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs. Read together, those scores suggest that outside interests have some room to reach officials and that the bodies which would expose them are of middling strength.

For Omanis, this means the ruling line they have lived under for most of the past five decades began with a decision made largely in London, by officers commanding their own army. Today they cannot see whether contracts go to favoured firms or whether crimes linked to officials go unpunished; published court records, audits and lists of who owns the companies doing business with the state would be the first places such a pattern would show.

Papua New Guinea.d:
In Papua New Guinea the longest documented reach into the state is by logging companies, and officials have been found to help them at many levels. A government inquiry led by Justice Thomas Barnett reported in 1989 that some companies paid politicians and leaders to log forests while ignoring the law, with corruption, fraud and incompetence across the industry. The forests minister of the time was found to hold a secret stake in a foreign timber group he gave a permit to, and he was convicted of misconduct by a tribunal in 1991. A second inquiry in 2013 found that farm leases covering more than five million hectares, over a tenth of the country, had been hijacked by developers and people with vested interests, with corruption at all levels. Nearly all the operations were run by foreign companies, according to the campaign group Global Witness, which reported no prosecutions by 2014.

Other outsiders have used similar routes. A former executive of the contractor running Australia's asylum centre on Manus Island has alleged that some of that money reached a businessman close to senior officials, which is denied and untested. Drug traffickers have also allegedly relied on police help: after a plane carrying 548 kilograms of cocaine crashed near Port Moresby in 2020, the police commissioner said there are criminals in uniform in the constabulary, yet the officers alleged to have helped were not charged.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores PNG among the highest in the world for officials working for criminal interests and low for its courts and police. For people in PNG, this means decisions on who logs their forests have been made by officials working with the companies concerned, and they have little reason to trust the police to police themselves.

Poland.d:
In Poland, the documented cases of outsiders getting their people inside the state come mostly from Russia, Belarus and China and are aimed at people who hold secrets or useful records; one more came from private brokers selling faster visas.

Russian recruitment inside Polish ministries has been coming to light for more than a decade. Courts have convicted a defence ministry officer as a source for the GRU, Russia's military intelligence, and a ministry employee working on energy projects and on reducing reliance on Russian gas. Those now accused, who have not been convicted, include a defence ministry employee who had worked there since the 1990s, a Territorial Defence Forces radio operator, and a Warsaw registry official said to have sent records that helped build false identities for Russian deep-cover officers. In 2024 a Warsaw judge who ruled on whether military and intelligence officers could see classified information fled to Belarus; officials say he worked for Russia, which has not been proven. Prosecutors say Chinese intelligence worked through a Huawei employee and a former Polish security officer to win access to government data systems; both deny it.

The visa affair ran through the foreign ministry. Brokers got their clients' names passed from the ministry to consulates for quick approval: the state audit office found that a deputy foreign minister forwarded lists of people 'third parties' wanted approved, and he has been charged with taking bribes, which he denies.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores Poland in the middle range for officials working for criminal interests. For Poles, this means people handling military secrets, gas supplies and civil records have reported, or are accused of reporting, to Moscow, much of the evidence is heard behind closed doors, and a visa could depend on which broker an applicant paid.

Russia.d:
In the 1990s, after the Soviet Union ended, Russian crime groups took over enterprises through their own people and ties with managers. The named leader of the Tambov crime group became deputy president of St Petersburg's main fuel company, one of up to 100 enterprises the interior minister said the gang controlled, and crime groups took control of the largest carmaker's sales network through its managers.

Now the FSB, Russia's security service, is accused of being used to settle business fights: an American investor says a rival used connections inside it to have him arrested in a fight over a bank, and his conviction was later vacated. The same services reach into bodies meant to be independent: reports for the World Anti-Doping Agency found that the sports ministry and the FSB ran a system through the Moscow testing laboratory that hid doped athletes, protecting more than 1,000 competitors between 2011 and 2015. Foreign companies buy their way in through officials at state bodies: a US transport firm paid an official at the state's sole uranium exporter, and an Israeli drug maker, US prosecutors say, paid a high-ranking official to boost sales in health ministry auctions. In the regions, a gang operated for years under protection from local police and authorities, until its members murdered 12 people.

For Russians, a business can be lost through an arrest rather than a court case the owner could win, public money for medicines can follow a payment rather than the best offer, and in some regions the police have protected gangs rather than the people they threatened. The Global Organized Crime Index gives Russia one of the highest scores in the world for officials working for criminal interests and low marks for its courts and watchdogs.

Sao Tome and Principe.d:
São Tomé and Príncipe is a small island state in the Gulf of Guinea that shares an offshore oil zone with Nigeria, and its one recorded case of outsiders reaching in comes from the race for those oil rights. ERHC, a small Houston oil company controlled from 2001 by a Nigerian businessman who was a major donor to Nigeria's ruling party, obtained unusually favourable terms, including the right to pick the best blocks without the usual fee. In 2005 São Tomé's attorney general reported that bidding in the shared zone showed serious procedural deficiencies and political manipulation and that ERHC may have made improper payments to government officials. The FBI raided ERHC's Houston offices in 2006, the company denied wrongdoing, and no charges were reported.

The Sovereign Military Order of Malta, a Catholic order with diplomatic relations with many states, is also present; that is lawful and not evidence of wrongdoing. The Global Organized Crime Index scores the country low for officials working for criminal or outside interests, though its courts, police and watchdogs are also rated below the middle of the scale, which means fewer bodies able to find outside pressure if it were there.

For people in São Tomé and Príncipe, this means the oil under their waters, potentially the country's largest source of income, was parcelled out in a process their own attorney general found manipulated, and no court has said who was paid. They are best protected when they can see who wins resource rights and public contracts and who owns the companies that hold them.

Seychelles.d:
Little has been proven about outsiders reaching into the Seychelles state, and what has been reported centres on the heroin that moves through the islands of the western Indian Ocean. People who use drugs, prison staff and former anti-narcotics officers interviewed for research published in 2021 described police who release dealers after a payment, resell seized drugs and protect some traffickers while pursuing their rivals, and they said corruption in the anti-narcotics bureau reaches high. A parliamentary committee separately found irregular payments of about US$6 million, involving the drug-enforcement agency and the financial intelligence unit, sent to offshore companies in Mauritius.

None of this has been tested in court: as of 2021 the Anti-Corruption Commission had no active case of drug-related corruption. The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 4 out of 10 and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 5.4, both near the middle of the scale.

For residents this means the agencies they are told are fighting the drug trade are described as compromised by the people who work closest to them, while no court has yet said who was paid or by whom. In a 2017 survey by the Anti-Corruption Commission, more than four in five of the roughly 15,000 people who answered said corruption was very high.

Slovenia.d:
The documented attempts from outside to get inside Slovenia's state have come through two doors: arms buying, where a single contract is large and the details are kept from the public, and the office that prosecutes organised crime. In 2006 Patria, a Finnish state-owned arms maker, won a deal worth 278 million euros to supply 135 armoured vehicles, and the Finnish broadcaster YLE later alleged that bribes were paid partly aimed at Prime Minister Janez Janša. A Slovenian conviction of Janša was annulled by the Constitutional Court and the case lapsed; defendants in Finland were acquitted and one middleman was convicted in Austria. No court has a standing finding that Janša took money, and he denies it.

Organised crime has reached the prosecutors themselves. In 2021 police said an official who had worked for about five years in the Specialised State Prosecutor's Office, which handles organised crime, had photographed files on live investigations, including orders for house searches and covert surveillance, and passed them through her partner to the Slovenian cell of the Kavač clan, a Montenegrin cocaine-trafficking syndicate. Two of the cell's key members avoided arrest, and the official had passed every background check.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 6.5 out of 10, higher than most of its EU neighbours, and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 6.2. For Slovenians this means an organised-crime investigation can reach the gang it targets before the police knock on the door, taxpayers paid for the country's largest arms purchase while a foreign broadcaster said it had been won with bribes, and voters have judged the prime minister at several elections since without a final answer from any court.

South Sudan.d:
No documented case for South Sudan yet meets the map's test of an outside party getting its people, money or control inside a government body and having decisions there serve it.

The wider picture suggests the risk is high. Oil is the state's main income, and Glencore admitted in a UK court in 2022 to paying bribes for oil business in five African countries, South Sudan among them. The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 9 out of 10 and courts, police and watchdogs at about 2, among the worst in the world.

For South Sudanese this means that if oil revenue or state contracts are being steered by outside payments, there are few courts, police units or watchdogs able to find out or to act.

St. Lucia.d:
Nothing is documented here, so this is an estimate. No case has been found of foreign governments, companies or criminal groups paying or placing officials in St Lucia.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 3 out of 10, which is low, and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 5.5, near the middle of the scale. The main risk in the eastern Caribbean is the cocaine route north from South America, which passes through these islands.

For residents, the absence of a documented case means there is no known instance of officials here being paid or placed from outside. It also means the estimate rests on the index's own assessment rather than on any investigation or court case in St Lucia, and it would change if a case came to light, most likely through the drug route.

Sweden.d:
In Sweden the reach into the state comes from two directions: criminal networks working through ordinary public administration, and foreign intelligence services recruiting people inside Sweden's own security agencies and its companies.

The criminal route is the larger one today. A 2023 research review for the SNS think tank found that criminal networks have people inside government agencies, run companies in the welfare sector, such as home care, schools and assistance services, and draw on social insurance; wrong welfare payments are estimated at 13 to 16 billion kronor a year. Municipalities are most exposed, as they spend much of the money with less oversight. Courts have convicted police employees of passing data from police registers to these networks, and police reporting calls insider access a systematic weakness.

Russian military intelligence, the GRU, has had agents inside the Swedish state in two separate generations. During the Cold War an air force colonel in the defence minister's office passed it about 20,000 pages including Sweden's air defence plans, and from 2011 to 2021 a man who had worked for both the Security Service and military intelligence passed it information for money, for which he was jailed for life in 2023. The same interest extends to industry: a technology consultant at the truckmaker Scania was sentenced in 2021 for passing manufacturing material to a Russian diplomat suspected of being an intelligence officer, which he denied.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 2 out of 10 and courts and watchdogs at about 7.4. For Swedes this means their taxes fund welfare companies that criminal groups run, losses fall on municipal budgets, police register data on people can reach those groups from inside the police, and the agencies meant to catch foreign spies have had a spy on their staff.

Tajikistan.d:
Tajikistan's long border with Afghanistan is one of the main routes for Afghan heroin and hashish heading north to Russia and Europe, and the record shows the drug trade reaching the officials who are meant to stop it: anti-drug police, the border service and, by some accounts, the head of the anti-drug agency. Analysts and diplomats cited by EurasiaNet in 2012 said some estimate drug money at the equivalent of 30% of the economy, and that major traffickers enjoy high-level protection.

The cases are few, but most sit inside bodies responsible for stopping drugs. In 2004 the head of the national Drug Control Agency, a former commander of the presidential guard, was jailed for life on charges that included drug trafficking; many saw the arrest as political, though critics who accepted that also said he had links to the trade. In 2012 a district anti-narcotics police chief was convicted of trafficking after investigators said he protected a smuggler's group, apparently for bribes, and the head of the Interior Ministry's anti-narcotics police was arrested in the same inquiry. That year the authorities also said a former civil war rebel leader, who had been running a border unit on the Afghan frontier, was leading a smuggling operation; how his case ended is poorly documented.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores state-embedded crime here at 9 out of 10, among the highest in the world, and the strength of courts, police and watchdogs at about 2.5.

For people in Tajikistan this means the officer in charge of the local drug police or border post may be working with the smugglers, police and prison guards are reported to control street and prison sales, and if drug money makes up a large share of the economy, many families depend on it for work.

Togo.d:
Togo's one documented case of outsiders reaching into its government comes from a foreign conglomerate and the country's main economic asset, the deep-water port of Lomé. French investigators allege that subsidiaries of the Bolloré Group, the conglomerate of the French billionaire Vincent Bolloré, provided President Faure Gnassingbé's 2010 election campaign with communications work at below its real price through its advertising agency, and that the group then secured control of the port. Bolloré admitted the facts in 2021 under a guilty-plea procedure, but a Paris court refused the deal, and in 2026 he was ordered to stand trial in Paris. A similar arrangement is alleged in Guinea. The group sold its African ports business in 2022.

The Global Organized Crime Index puts Togo in its high band, scoring it 7.5 out of 10 for officials working for criminal or outside interests and about 4.4 out of 10 for the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs, below the middle of the range. Read together, those scores suggest outside interests have room to reach officials and the bodies that would expose them are weak.

For Togolese, this means the concession to run the port through which much of their trade passes is alleged to have been handed to a company that helped the president win re-election, a family that has held the presidency since 1967. The case is being tried in France, and no Togolese court has examined it, so residents depend on a foreign trial to learn how the deal was made.

Turkiye.d:
In Turkey, secret networks inside the army, police and courts have shaped the state for more than a century, since an oath-bound society seized the Ottoman government in 1913. The largest recent one is the religious movement of the preacher Fethullah Gülen, which placed followers as judges, prosecutors, police and military officers. Courts have convicted people over a leaked state entrance exam whose questions, prosecutors say, went to followers.

The government blames those followers for the failed coup of July 2016, and it dismissed about 150,000 people, including about a third of the judges in one day, without a court ruling on each, so for most the evidence was never tested. Journalists say the Menzil Sufi order has filled many emptied police posts, which the government denies, and leaked files suggest a youth foundation close to President Erdoğan's family listed members as candidates for state security and judicial jobs, which it calls forged.

A second pattern links police and politicians to crime groups and armed movements, among them the Grey Wolves, youth wing of the president's ultranationalist coalition partner, the MHP. The 1996 Susurluk crash put a wanted Grey Wolves gunman in a car with a police chief's deputy and an MP, and in 2026 police officers and a court clerk were held for allegedly warning a gang of raids. Business money reaches in too: a German dialysis company gave public doctors free shares and they sent it business, and prosecutors accused a gold trader of bribing ministers, a case parliament ended.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 9 out of 10. For people in Turkey this means state jobs and courtrooms have been staffed by whichever network held the hiring, and a public servant can lose a career on an untested accusation.

Ukraine.d:
Ukraine is fighting Russia while networks reach into its parliament, security services, state companies and border posts. The deepest reach is Russia's own, running through the security service since well before the full invasion. People charged as Russian agents inside the SBU, Ukraine's main security service, have included a major general said to have worked for the FSB since 2014, senior officers of its Kherson and Kharkiv offices accused of helping Russian troops in 2022, and the colonel who had headed the staff of its own Anti-Terrorist Center, sentenced to life in 2026. In 2024 two colonels in the State Guard, which protects the president, were detained over an FSB plan to kill him. In parliament, at least three sitting MPs, among them the leader of the main pro-Kremlin party, have been charged with treason.

The other lasting pattern is business circles reaching state firms and ministries for a cut. In 2025 the National Anti-Corruption Bureau said a group led by a businessman and friend of President Zelensky took about $100 million in kickbacks from contractors of Energoatom, the state nuclear power company, and it has charged a former deputy prime minister with seeking flats far below market price from a Kyiv developer in return for help with a land plot, which he denies. Customs and border officers in the west have been charged with running smuggling channels into the EU.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 8 out of 10. For Ukrainians, this means the officers meant to protect them and their leaders may be passing information to the army invading them, and kickbacks at the nuclear company raise the cost of keeping electricity on while Russia bombs the grid.

Uruguay.d:
Uruguay has strong courts and watchdogs by world standards, and no current case shows outside groups with people inside its government. The Global Organized Crime Index puts it in the Low band, scoring officials acting for criminal interests at 3.5 out of 10 and the strength of its courts, police and watchdogs at 7.5. The two cases on record date from 1970 and 1981.

In 1970 the Tupamaros, an urban guerrilla movement, reportedly had a sailor on guard duty inside the navy's training centre in Montevideo, who helped let in the raiders who left with hundreds of weapons. The longer-lasting case came under military rule. In 1981 the Unification Church, the Korean-founded movement of Sun Myung Moon, bought 49% of Banco de Crédito, one of the country's oldest banks, and started a daily newspaper that declared itself 'fully identified' with the military government. A later parliamentary commission found that the bank had lent about US$100 million, about a sixth of all its loans, to companies linked to Moon's movement before it closed in 2002.

The effect of that bank case reached Uruguayans who kept savings there or depended on its stability: a foreign group that owned almost half of it had its companies take a large share of the lending, under a government that faced no free press or opposition able to ask questions. Those cases are the reason the risk is not shown as zero, but in present-day Uruguay the courts, parliament and press are able to investigate such an arrangement if it happened again.

Venezuela.d:
Venezuela's state has been accused of becoming a channel for drug trafficking, run by the military circle around Hugo Chávez, with its security partly run by Cuban officers. Communist and far-left parties had links to officers behind a 1962 rising, and Chávez built a secret army movement from 1982, then put fellow plotters in charge of intelligence once elected. Since 2008 the United States has named officers from his circle, including intelligence chiefs, as working for the FARC, the Colombian guerrilla army funded by cocaine, and one intelligence chief pleaded guilty in New York in 2025. US prosecutors call the network 'Cartel de los Soles'; analysts dispute that it is a cartel. Nicolás Maduro, seized by US forces in January 2026, has pleaded not guilty.

Cuba's reach went deepest. Under secret agreements from 2008, Cuban officers rebuilt Venezuela's military counterintelligence, which then watched Venezuela's own soldiers, and Cuban officers worked in the security around Maduro: Cuba says 32 of them were killed in the US raid. The US says a diplomat used his post to raise money for Hizballah, and the prison ministry left the leader of the Tren de Aragua gang in charge of Tocorón prison, its headquarters until 2023. A US asphalt trader admitted paying officials of PDVSA, the state oil company, for inside information and contracts, and a Spanish telecoms group's Venezuelan arm paid officials for rationed dollars.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests at 9 out of 10 and courts, police and watchdogs at 1.9. For Venezuelans this has meant anti-drug agencies led by men accused of working for traffickers, soldiers watched under foreign supervision, a prison run by the gang inside it, oil contracts handed out for bribes, and no domestic court able to examine any of it.

Zimbabwe.d:
In Zimbabwe the record points to the country's minerals and to the state's spy agency, the Central Intelligence Organisation (CIO), which appears in the cases from more than one direction. All of it remains allegation or unfinished case rather than proven fact.

A 2012 report by the campaign group Global Witness, quoting CIO sources, said the Hong Kong businessman Sam Pa gave the agency money and equipment, put at $100 million and 200 pick-up trucks in one CIO document, in return for access to diamonds, cotton and property, and that CIO members jointly controlled a company with him. The US later sanctioned him and the company. Money of that kind sits outside the state budget, so parliament and voters cannot see it.

Gold, the country's main source of hard currency, follows a similar path. In 2020 police said two CIO operatives and two police officers were among those arrested in a smuggling case at the main airport. In 2023 undercover reporters recorded the preacher Uebert Angel, whom the president had appointed ambassador-at-large and presidential envoy, apparently offering to use his status to bring illicit cash into the country, swap it for gold and sell the gold abroad as clean money. The government's financial intelligence unit said it found no evidence for the claims.

The Global Organized Crime Index scores officials acting for criminal interests in Zimbabwe at 8 out of 10 and its courts, police and watchdogs at 3. If these accounts are right, Zimbabweans' diamonds have helped fund a spy agency outside the state budget and their gold has left the country with help from officers meant to stop it, and weak courts make it hard for people to find out which accounts are true.
